docs.title: Databricks Mastery Path
docs.text:
Mastery Path BOOTCAMP VINOD BHANUJA

Databricks is Apache Spark and Delta Lake plus a lot of platform: a governance layer (Unity Catalog), compute you do or don't manage, pipelines and jobs, SQL warehouses, ML tooling and AI features. It's easy to click through and hard to know what is actually happening underneath. A one-row DELETE that rewrites 49,999 other rows. A partition column that turns 2 MB into 86,665 files and a seven-minute write. A deleted checkpoint that duplicates every record. An INSERT * merge that silently drops a new column. An ALTER TABLE ... CLUSTER BY that rewrites nothing. A window function whose result changes with tied sort keys. None of these are platform bugs. They follow from how Delta and Spark work, and this course shows each one with something you can run.

It assumes you know SQL and some Python. It doesn't assume any Databricks experience, and most of Levels 1, 2 and 4 runs on your own laptop with open-source Spark and Delta Lake.

Level 1 is the foundation: the lakehouse and its control and compute planes, compute types and notebooks, Spark DataFrames and SQL, reading and writing files, Delta tables, the Delta log, time travel and VACUUM, tables, views and volumes, ending with a local sales lakehouse. Level 2 is Delta and data engineering: MERGE and the change feed, schema enforcement, OPTIMIZE and clustering, partitioning, how Spark executes and why joins skew, Structured Streaming, Auto Loader and the medallion architecture, ending with an incremental bronze/silver/gold pipeline. Level 3 is the platform: Unity Catalog's object model, privileges, storage governance, row filters and masks, lineage and system tables, declarative pipelines, jobs, OpenSharing and SQL warehouses, ending with a governance-as-code project. Level 4 is building and operating: bundles and CI/CD, testing, MLflow and model serving, AI features, cost, performance, table maintenance and migration, ending with a platform plan and checker.

Every lesson has a How It Actually Works section: why Delta commits are atomic, why a file can be vacuumed out from under a rollback, why Z-order can cut files read from 16 to 2 on one column and not another, why AQE can fix partition counts but didn't fix a hot key on a small test, and why a deletion vector hides a row without erasing it.

Versions and what was actually run

This course was written without access to a Databricks workspace, and no output is presented as coming from Databricks. What was run, and is labelled in each lesson: Apache Spark 4.2.0 and Delta Lake 4.4.1 (open source) on a laptop for the Spark and Delta behaviour and the local pipeline project; the open-source Spark Declarative Pipelines runtime that ships with PySpark; MLflow 3.17.2, scikit-learn, pytest, sqlglot 30.24, and the delta-sharing and databricks-sql-connector clients (API checks only). Unity Catalog, jobs, SQL warehouses, Auto Loader, OpenSharing, Model Serving, AI Functions, Genie, Photon, serverless compute and Predictive Optimization could not be run; those lessons are built from the Databricks documentation as of October 2026 and say so, and where a small Python or Spark program models documented behaviour, it is labelled as a model and not as Databricks code. The cost lesson uses invented mock billing rows. Where a local experiment failed or showed nothing (a caching micro-benchmark, a hung Python UDF timing), the lesson reports that instead of inventing results.

Databricks renames and changes things often: Delta Live Tables became Lakeflow Spark Declarative Pipelines, Asset Bundles became Declarative Automation Bundles, Delta Sharing is now documented as OpenSharing, Genie Spaces became Genie Agents and Vector Search became AI Search. The lessons say which name is current. Re-check anything marked "as of October 2026" against your own workspace.

docs.text:
Level Focus Modules What you can do after 1 · Lakehouse & Spark Foundations Architecture, compute, Spark, files, Delta, the log, time travel, tables and volumes 10 Build, change and recover a small Delta lakehouse 2 · Delta Lake & Data Engineering MERGE, schema, clustering, partitioning, execution and skew, streaming, Auto Loader, medallion 10 Build incremental, idempotent pipelines and make them fast 3 · Unity Catalog, Pipelines & Sharing Governance, privileges, storage, masks, lineage, declarative pipelines, jobs, sharing, SQL 10 Design and operate a governed, orchestrated platform 4 · Development, ML & Operations Bundles, testing, MLflow, serving, AI features, cost, performance, maintenance, migration 10 Ship, test, monitor and afford it, and plan the whole thing

Each level has 9 teaching modules plus a hands-on project (module 10), for 40 lessons total.

docs.title: How to use this site
docs.text:
• Run the local labs. You need Python 3.12 and Java 17 or newer. pip install pyspark delta-spark is enough for Levels 1 and 2. Set PYSPARK_PYTHON to the same interpreter, or Spark will stop with a version-mismatch error (one of the things that happened while writing this course).
  • Get a Free Edition workspace for the platform-only lessons. It's a serverless, quota-limited, no-cost workspace for learning; check its current limitations before relying on a feature.
  • Read the "what was run" note at the top of each lesson. It tells you whether the output you see is observed, modelled or documented.
  • Do the exercises, especially those that say "predict, then run". The surprises are the point.
  • Do the projects. Each combines its level into something you could adapt, and each states what it doesn't cover.

docs.title: Level 1 · Lakehouse & Spark Foundations
docs.text:
Level 1 takes you from "Databricks is a Spark platform" to building and recovering a small Delta lakehouse. Most of it runs on your own laptop with open-source Spark and Delta Lake, which means the code is real and the outputs in these lessons are observed, not paraphrased. Along the way it shows the quiet failures that cost people days: inferSchema turning a numeric column into strings, a CASE expression labelling missing amounts "small", a window function that returns different running totals for tied rows, and a VACUUM that makes a rollback impossible.

What was run, and what wasn't

This course was written without access to a Databricks workspace. Spark 4.2.0 and Delta Lake 4.4.1 (open source, from PyPI) were run locally for everything that doesn't need the platform; those outputs are labelled "local". Platform-only features (Unity Catalog, serverless compute, SQL warehouses, Auto Loader, Lakeflow, MLflow serving) are described from the Databricks documentation as of October 2026 and are marked as not run. A Databricks Free Edition workspace is enough to try the platform-only exercises.

Prerequisites: basic Python and SQL. Java 17+ and Python 3.12 to run the local labs. If SQL is new, start with the SQL Mastery Path; for Spark in more depth see the PySpark Mastery Path.

docs.title: Modules
docs.text:
1. The Lakehouse: Control Plane, Compute Plane & Storage: what a lakehouse is, the two planes, accounts, workspaces and metastores.
  2. Workspaces, Compute Types & Notebooks: serverless vs classic vs SQL warehouses, notebooks, dbutils, the CLI.
  3. Spark DataFrames: Transformations & Actions: lazy plans, explain, null semantics, joins.
  4. Spark SQL, Built-in Functions & Window Functions: GROUP BY ALL, windows and ties, QUALIFY, ANSI mode.
  5. Reading & Writing Files: CSV/JSON/Parquet, parse modes, partition pruning, save modes.
  6. Delta Lake Tables: create, update, delete, inspect, managed vs external.
  7. Inside the Delta Log: actions, statistics, checkpoints, a real write conflict.
  8. Time Travel, RESTORE & VACUUM: what you can recover and when it's gone.
  9. Tables, Views & Volumes: the object model and where files belong.
  10. Project: A Sales Lakehouse You Can Run Locally: bronze/silver/gold with a quarantine table and a rollback.

docs.title: After Level 1
docs.text: Level 2 makes tables fast and pipelines continuous: MERGE, schema enforcement, OPTIMIZE and clustering, how Spark executes queries, joins and skew, Structured Streaming, Auto Loader and the medallion architecture.

docs.title: 01 · The Lakehouse: Control Plane, Compute Plane & Storage
docs.text:
Databricks sells a simple idea with a lot of machinery behind it: keep your data in open files in cheap cloud object storage, and put a transactional layer, a catalog and several compute engines on top, so that the same copy of the data serves SQL dashboards, data-engineering pipelines and machine learning. That combination is called a lakehouse, because it tries to give a data lake's cost and openness the reliability and governance that used to be the warehouse's selling point.

This lesson builds the mental map you'll use for the rest of the course: what sits in your cloud account, what sits in Databricks', and which piece does what.

About this course and what was run

Databricks has no free local edition, and this course was written without access to a Databricks workspace. So no output here is presented as coming from Databricks. What was run, and where:

  • Apache Spark 4.2.0 and Delta Lake 4.4.1 (open-source builds, pyspark and delta-spark from PyPI) on a laptop with Python 3.12. Spark and Delta are the engine and table format underneath Databricks, so Spark code, Delta behaviour and the on-disk layout shown in Levels 1 and 2 are real observed output. Output blocks are labelled "local Spark" when they come from these runs.
  • Features that exist only on the platform (Unity Catalog governance, serverless compute, Photon, Auto Loader cloudFiles, Lakeflow pipelines, Jobs, SQL warehouses, MLflow serving, Genie) can't be run locally. Those lessons explain the documented behaviour, show configuration and code written against the documentation, and say plainly when nothing was executed. Docs were read on the Databricks documentation site in October 2026.
  • Product names, limits and defaults change quickly. Treat anything marked "as of October 2026" as something to re-check.

A free Databricks account (the Free Edition) or a trial lets you run the platform-only lessons yourself.

docs.title: What "lakehouse" means in practice
docs.text:
Three older ideas are being merged:

Idea Strength Weakness the lakehouse tries to fix Data warehouse ACID tables, fast SQL, governance Proprietary storage, expensive for raw/unstructured data, awkward for ML Data lake (files in object storage) Cheap, open, any file type No transactions, no schema enforcement, easy to corrupt, hard to govern Spark/ML clusters Flexible code, scales out Needs reliable tables underneath

The lakehouse answer is open file formats plus a transaction log. Data sits as Parquet files in object storage (S3, ADLS Gen2 or Google Cloud Storage). A table format called Delta Lake adds a log that records which files make up each version of a table, giving you transactions, schema checks and time travel (Lessons 06–08). A catalog, Unity Catalog, adds names, permissions and lineage on top (Level 3).

docs.title: Accounts, workspaces and metastores
docs.text:
Databricks account  (billing, identity, which regions, which metastores)
 ├── Unity Catalog metastore  (one per region)  ── catalogs ── schemas ── tables/volumes/models
 ├── Workspace "dev"   ─┐
 ├── Workspace "prod"  ─┼─ attached to the regional metastore, see the same governed data
 └── Workspace "ml"    ─┘
  • The account is the top-level entity: users and groups, billing, and the list of workspaces.
  • A workspace is the collaboration environment: notebooks, jobs, compute, dashboards. Companies commonly run several (dev/test/prod, or per business unit).
  • A metastore is the Unity Catalog governance container. One metastore can be attached to many workspaces in the same region, so every workspace sees the same catalogs and the same permissions.

docs.title: The two planes
docs.text:
Databricks describes its architecture as a control plane and a compute plane.

        ┌────────────── Databricks control plane ──────────────┐
        │ web UI · REST API · notebooks & job definitions ·    │
        │ cluster manager · Unity Catalog service · query UI   │
        └───────────────▲──────────────────────┬───────────────┘
                        │ commands/metadata    │ launch/stop
        ┌───────────────┴──────────────────────▼───────────────┐
        │                     compute plane                    │
        │  classic: VMs in YOUR cloud account (your VPC)       │
        │  serverless: capacity managed in Databricks' account │
        │       Spark driver + executors read/write data ──────┼──► object storage
        └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘     (S3 / ADLS / GCS)
  • The control plane is the managed backend that Databricks runs in its own account: the web app, the REST API, job scheduling and the cluster manager.
  • The compute plane is where data is actually processed. With classic compute, the virtual machines are launched in your cloud account, inside your own network. With serverless compute, Databricks runs and manages the capacity in its account within a network boundary for your workspace.
  • Your data stays in object storage. Databricks does not need to ingest it into a proprietary store: tables are folders of Parquet files plus a _delta_log directory (you'll open one in Lesson 07).

This split has practical effects. Cloud networking, firewalls and IAM roles matter for classic compute because the VMs are yours. Costs have two parts for classic compute: Databricks Units (DBUs) to Databricks and VM/storage charges to your cloud provider (Level 4 · 06). And a notebook you open in the browser is not "running on your laptop" or "in the browser": it's a client of a driver process in the compute plane.

docs.title: The runtime stack
docs.text:
Databricks compute runs the Databricks Runtime (DBR): a versioned image that bundles Apache Spark, Delta Lake, Python/Scala/R, common libraries, and Databricks-specific optimizations such as the Photon vectorized engine. A cluster picks a runtime version when it's created, and runtimes are released in LTS (long-term support) and non-LTS variants. Because the runtime is pinned per compute resource, upgrading a pipeline's Spark/Delta version is a configuration change you can test, not a platform-wide event.

Open-source Spark and Delta are what you can run locally. DBR layers extras on top, so code that works locally generally runs on Databricks, but not every Databricks-only behaviour (Photon, Predictive Optimization, some Delta features gated by runtime) exists in the open-source builds.

docs.title: A first look: the same code, two places
docs.text:
A notebook cell in a workspace and a script on your laptop look identical:

from pyspark.sql import functions as F

df = spark.createDataFrame(
    [(1, "alice", "DE", 120.5), (2, "bob", "US", 80.0), (3, "cara", "US", 45.25), (4, "dev", "IN", 300.0)],
    ["id", "name", "country", "amount"],
)
(df.filter(F.col("amount") > 60)
   .groupBy("country")
   .agg(F.sum("amount").alias("total"), F.count("*").alias("n"))
   .orderBy("country")
   .show())

In a Databricks notebook, spark already exists. Locally you build it:

from pyspark.sql import SparkSession
spark = SparkSession.builder.master("local[2]").appName("lab").getOrCreate()

Output from the local run (Spark 4.2.0):

+-------+-----+---+
|country|total|  n|
+-------+-----+---+
|     DE|120.5|  1|
|     IN|300.0|  1|
|     US| 80.0|  1|
+-------+-----+---+

The only difference is where the driver and executors live: one JVM on your laptop versus VMs managed by the platform.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
When you press Run on a cell, the browser talks to the control plane, which routes your command to the driver of the attached compute resource. The driver is a JVM (plus a Python process for PySpark) that holds your SparkSession. It turns your DataFrame operations into a plan, splits the plan into tasks, and hands tasks to executors: worker processes on the other VMs. Each executor reads its slice of Parquet files directly from object storage using cloud credentials attached to the compute resource, and processes it in memory. Results come back to the driver, which returns the displayed rows to the control plane and then your browser.

Two consequences follow. First, data does not flow through the control plane; only commands, metadata and small result sets do. Second, compute and storage are decoupled: you can stop every cluster and the data and tables are untouched in object storage, and you can point many different clusters, jobs and SQL warehouses at the same tables at once. Everything else in the course (Delta's log, Unity Catalog, serverless) elaborates one of those two facts.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Treating the lakehouse as "a warehouse with a different name". Tables are files you own in your storage; deleting the files, or writing to the same folder from a tool that ignores the Delta log, can corrupt a table.
  • Mixing up workspace and metastore. Permissions on tables live in the metastore and apply in every attached workspace; notebooks and job definitions live in one workspace.
  • Assuming classic and serverless behave the same. Serverless removes cluster configuration but has its own limits on libraries, languages and settings. Check the documentation for your feature.
  • Expecting the cloud bill to be one number. On classic compute you pay Databricks (DBUs) and your cloud provider separately.
  • Believing local Spark proves performance. A two-core laptop run proves logic, not scale or speed.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Draw your own version of the two-plane diagram for a company with a dev and a prod workspace in one region. Mark where the metastore, the object storage buckets and the classic compute VMs sit.
  2. Install the local stack (python3.12 -m venv .venv && .venv/bin/pip install pyspark delta-spark), run the example above, and confirm you get the same table.
  3. Explain in two sentences why stopping all clusters does not delete any table. (Hint: where do the files live?)
  4. In the Databricks architecture documentation, find what is stored in the workspace storage bucket and say which of those items is not your table data.

docs.title: 02 · Workspaces, Compute Types & Notebooks
docs.text:
You can't run anything on Databricks without compute, and choosing the wrong kind is the most common cause of both slow work and surprise bills. This lesson maps the compute options, then covers the notebook environment you'll spend most of your time in.

What was run

Compute creation, notebooks and the CLI talk to a live workspace, so nothing in this lesson was executed against Databricks. The compute descriptions follow the Databricks documentation (October 2026). The one thing run locally is the Python that mimics notebook widgets and parameter handling, shown at the end. See Lesson 01 for the full note on what this course ran.

docs.title: The compute menu
docs.text:
Compute Who manages it Best for Notes Serverless compute (notebooks, jobs, pipelines) Databricks Most interactive work and scheduled jobs with spiky demand No cluster to configure; starts quickly; has documented limitations on libraries, languages and some configs All-purpose (interactive) classic compute You Exploration, development, custom libraries/init scripts Stays up until you stop it or auto-termination fires; billed at the higher all-purpose rate Job compute (classic) You define, the platform creates per run Production batch jobs Created for a run, terminated after; priced lower than all-purpose SQL warehouse (serverless, pro, classic) Databricks BI, SQL analytics, dashboards, JDBC/ODBC SQL (and SQL-based) workloads only; sized in T-shirt sizes

Classic compute also has two access modes worth knowing. Standard (multi-user) compute lets several people share a cluster, with Lakeguard isolating each user's code. Dedicated compute is assigned to a single user or group and is used when you need features that need full machine access. Pick the access mode before anything else, since it determines which libraries and languages are allowed.

Free Edition

Databricks Free Edition is a no-cost, serverless-only, quota-limited workspace meant for learning. It replaced the older Community Edition, which was retired in 2025. It's the cheapest way to run the platform-only lessons in this course. Check its current limitations page before relying on a feature.

docs.title: What you configure on classic compute
docs.text:
• Runtime version (e.g. an LTS release): the bundled Spark, Delta, Python and library versions.
  • Node types for the driver and workers: general-purpose, memory-optimized or compute-optimized instances.
  • Autoscaling (min and max workers) or a fixed worker count, and single-node mode for small work.
  • Auto-termination minutes: the single most useful cost control on all-purpose compute.
  • Photon acceleration (a vectorized engine; availability and pricing multipliers depend on the cloud and plan).
  • Policies: admin-defined rules that limit what users may choose (max size, allowed runtimes, tags).
  • Tags for cost attribution (Level 4 · 06).

Because job compute is created per run and torn down afterwards, you never leave a forgotten job cluster running. That, plus a lower rate, is why production schedules use job compute or serverless, not an all-purpose cluster.

docs.title: Notebooks
docs.text:
A Databricks notebook is a sequence of cells attached to one compute resource and one language. Key behaviours:

  • Default language per notebook (Python, SQL, Scala or R). Override per cell with a magic on the first line.
  • Shared state within a notebook session: variables set in one cell exist in the next. Detaching or restarting the compute clears that state; Delta tables you saved survive.
  • spark, sc, dbutils, display are predefined in notebooks.
# Cell 1 (Python)
df = spark.range(5)
display(df)            # rich table/chart renderer; not available outside notebooks

%sql
-- Cell 2: magic switches this cell to SQL
SELECT id, id * id AS square FROM range(5)

%md
Cell 3 renders **Markdown** for documentation inside the notebook.

Other magics: %sh runs a shell command on the driver only, %pip install ... installs notebook-scoped Python libraries, and %run ./other_notebook executes another notebook in the same session.

docs.title: dbutils: the notebook utility belt
docs.text:
dbutils.widgets.text("run_date", "2026-10-21", "Run date")   # parameter input shown at top of notebook
run_date = dbutils.widgets.get("run_date")                    # read it (always a string)

dbutils.fs.ls("/Volumes/main/raw/landing/")                  # list files in a Unity Catalog volume
dbutils.notebook.exit("ok")                                   # return a value to a calling job/notebook

Widgets are how a notebook receives parameters from a job: a Jobs task passes run_date=2026-10-22 and the widget with the same name picks it up. (Lakeflow Jobs also supports job parameters; Level 3 · 07 covers them.)

docs.title: Try the widget pattern locally
docs.text:
dbutils does not exist outside Databricks, so production-bound code should keep parameter handling separate and testable. A pattern that runs anywhere:

import argparse, datetime

def parse_run_date(value: str) -> datetime.date:
    return datetime.date.fromisoformat(value)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    p = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    p.add_argument("--run_date", default="2026-10-21")
    args = p.parse_args()
    print(parse_run_date(args.run_date))

Run locally with python job.py --run_date 2026-10-22; local output: 2026-10-22. In a notebook you'd replace the argparse lines with dbutils.widgets.get("run_date") and keep parse_run_date unchanged, which is what makes it unit-testable (Level 4 · 02).

docs.title: The Databricks CLI and other clients
docs.text:
You aren't limited to the browser. The Databricks CLI (a Go binary installed separately, not a PyPI package of the same name) authenticates with a profile in ~/.databrickscfg and wraps the REST API:

databricks auth login --host https://<your-workspace-host>     # OAuth browser login
databricks clusters list
databricks workspace export /Users/me@example.com/etl --format SOURCE

Other ways in: the Databricks SDKs (Python, Java, Go), the SQL Connector for Python and JDBC/ODBC drivers for SQL warehouses, and Databricks Connect which lets an IDE run Spark code against remote compute. The commands above were written from the documentation and weren't run (no workspace was available).

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
A classic all-purpose cluster is a set of cloud VMs. When it starts, the control plane asks the cloud provider for instances, installs the chosen runtime image, starts a Spark driver on one node and executors on the others, and registers them. That is why starting takes minutes and why instance pools (idle pre-warmed VMs) exist.

A notebook attaches to the driver. Each cell is sent to a long-lived interpreter on the driver, so variables persist between cells; your spark object is a client of the Spark session in that same process. Because the driver is one machine, %sh and plain Python (pandas, open()) operate on the driver's local disk, not on the distributed filesystem. Distributed work only happens when you call Spark APIs.

Serverless removes the VM lifecycle from your view: Databricks keeps capacity ready in its own compute plane, hands your session an isolated environment and scales it for you. You trade configuration freedom (no custom init scripts, a managed runtime version, restrictions on some APIs) for fast start and no idle cluster to forget.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Developing on the production job's cluster type. Use a small all-purpose cluster or serverless for development, and let production run on job compute or serverless jobs.
  • No auto-termination on all-purpose compute. Idle clusters bill until stopped.
  • Doing heavy pandas work on the driver. df.toPandas() pulls all data to one machine; it works on a sample and fails or crawls on a large table.
  • Storing results in notebook variables. State disappears when compute restarts. Save to a table or volume.
  • Assuming %sh runs on workers. It runs only on the driver.
  • Hard-coding secrets in cells. Use secret scopes or a secrets manager (Level 4 · 01).

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. A team runs a nightly 40-minute ETL and 6 analysts run ad-hoc queries during the day. Pick a compute type for each and justify it in one sentence.
  2. Write parse_run_date tests (valid date, invalid date) that run with pytest and need no Spark.
  3. In the compute documentation, find the difference between standard and dedicated access mode, and list one thing you can do in dedicated mode that standard mode restricts.
  4. (Needs a workspace or Free Edition.) Create a notebook, run the three cells above, and observe that display(df) gives a table with chart controls while df.show() prints plain text.

docs.title: 03 · Spark DataFrames: Transformations & Actions
docs.text:
Almost everything on Databricks compiles down to Apache Spark, and the DataFrame is Spark's main abstraction: a distributed table with named, typed columns. If you understand two ideas, lazy evaluation and the plan, most Spark behaviour (including most performance problems) stops being mysterious.

What was run

All Spark output in this lesson is from local Spark 4.2.0 (pyspark from PyPI, Python 3.12, local[2]), not from a Databricks cluster. The API is identical; the execution environment, file locations and speed are not. Plan text (explain) can differ in small details, such as the extra operators Photon adds on Databricks.

docs.title: A DataFrame is a plan, not data
docs.text:
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession, functions as F

spark = SparkSession.builder.master("local[2]").appName("lab").getOrCreate()   # a notebook already has `spark`

orders = spark.createDataFrame(
    [(1, "2026-01-03", "DE", 120.5, "paid"),
     (2, "2026-01-03", "US",  80.0, "paid"),
     (3, "2026-01-04", "US",  None, "refunded"),
     (4, "2026-01-05", "IN", 300.0, "paid"),
     (5, "2026-01-05", "DE",  45.25, "paid")],
    "id INT, order_date STRING, country STRING, amount DOUBLE, status STRING",
)

paid = (orders
        .withColumn("order_date", F.to_date("order_date"))
        .filter(F.col("status") == "paid")
        .withColumn("amount_eur", F.round(F.col("amount") * 0.92, 2)))

print(type(paid).__name__)     # DataFrame

Nothing has been computed. Each call returned a new DataFrame describing "the previous one plus this step".

Transformations build the plan and return a DataFrame: select, filter/where, withColumn, groupBy().agg, join, orderBy, union, distinct. Actions force execution and return a result to the driver or write output: show, collect, count, first, take, write.save, toPandas.

paid.select("id", "order_date", "amount_eur").show()

+---+----------+----------+
| id|order_date|amount_eur|
+---+----------+----------+
|  1|2026-01-03|    110.86|
|  2|2026-01-03|      73.6|
|  4|2026-01-05|     276.0|
|  5|2026-01-05|     41.63|
+---+----------+----------+

docs.title: Reading the plan with explain
docs.text:
paid.explain(True) prints four stages of planning. The last two are the ones to watch (local Spark output, trimmed to the relevant parts):

== Optimized Logical Plan ==
Project [id#0, cast(order_date#1 as date) AS order_date#5, country#2, amount#3, status#4, round((amount#3 * 0.92), 2) AS amount_eur#6]
+- Filter (isnotnull(status#4) AND (status#4 = paid))
   +- LogicalRDD [id#0, order_date#1, country#2, amount#3, status#4], false

== Physical Plan ==
*(1) Project [id#0, cast(order_date#1 as date) AS order_date#5, ...]
+- *(1) Filter (isnotnull(status#4) AND (status#4 = paid))
   +- *(1) Scan ExistingRDD[id#0,order_date#1,country#2,amount#3,status#4]

Read plans bottom to top: data enters at the scan, flows through the filter, then the projection. Notice that the optimizer added isnotnull(status) (an equality can never be true for NULL, so it's a free extra filter) and replaced to_date(...) with a plain cast because the string was already in yyyy-MM-dd form. Those rewrites are Catalyst, Spark's optimizer, at work. The *(1) marks operators fused into one code-generated stage.

docs.title: Null semantics: the quiet source of wrong numbers
docs.text:
SQL's three-valued logic applies to DataFrames. Row 3 has a NULL amount:

orders.filter(F.col("amount") > 50).count()        # 3
orders.filter(~(F.col("amount") > 50)).count()     # 1  -> the 45.25 row only
orders.filter(F.col("amount").isNull()).count()    # 1

The first two counts add up to 4, not 5: the NULL row is in neither > 50 nor its negation, because NULL > 50 is NULL, not false. Equality has the same trap, and the null-safe operator <=> (eqNullSafe) fixes it:

orders.select(F.col("amount") == None, F.col("amount").eqNullSafe(None)).limit(3).show()

+---------------+-----------------+
|(amount = NULL)|(amount <=> NULL)|
+---------------+-----------------+
|           NULL|            false|
|           NULL|            false|
|           NULL|             true|
+---------------+-----------------+

Aggregates skip NULLs, and count("*") differs from count("col"):

orders.groupBy("country").agg(
    F.count("*").alias("rows"), F.count("amount").alias("non_null"),
    F.sum("amount").alias("sum"), F.avg("amount").alias("avg")).orderBy("country").show()

+-------+----+--------+------+------+
|country|rows|non_null|   sum|   avg|
+-------+----+--------+------+------+
|     DE|   2|       2|165.75|82.875|
|     IN|   1|       1| 300.0| 300.0|
|     US|   2|       1|  80.0|  80.0|
+-------+----+--------+------+------+

For US, the average is 80.0, not 40.0: the refunded row's missing amount is excluded from both numerator and denominator. Whether that's what the business wants is a modelling question you have to ask on purpose.

docs.title: Conditionals and the NULL fall-through
docs.text:
orders.select("id",
    F.when(F.col("amount") >= 100, "large")
     .when(F.col("amount") >= 50, "medium")
     .otherwise("small").alias("size")).show()

+---+------+
| id|  size|
+---+------+
|  1| large|
|  2|medium|
|  3| small|
|  4| large|
|  5| small|
+---+------+

Order 3 has no amount, yet it is labelled small: both when conditions evaluated to NULL, which isn't true, so otherwise fired. Handle NULL explicitly (F.when(F.col("amount").isNull(), "unknown") first) whenever a missing value must not be bucketed with real ones.

docs.title: Joins
docs.text:
countries = spark.createDataFrame([("DE", "Germany"), ("US", "United States"), ("FR", "France")],
                                  "code STRING, name STRING")
orders.join(countries, orders.country == countries.code, "left")     # keep every order
orders.join(countries, orders.country == countries.code, "left_anti")  # orders with NO matching country
orders.join(countries, orders.country == countries.code, "full")     # everything from both sides

Local output for the left_anti join is a single row, order 4 (country IN, which the lookup table lacks). The full join returns all five orders, with NULL in code/name for order 4, plus a sixth row for FR with NULL order columns. left_anti is the cleanest way to find orphan keys; left_semi is its mirror (keep rows that do match, without adding the other table's columns).

docs.title: Window functions in the DataFrame API
docs.text:
from pyspark.sql import Window
w = Window.partitionBy("country").orderBy(F.col("amount").desc())
orders.withColumn("rk", F.row_number().over(w)).filter("rk = 1").select("country", "id", "amount").orderBy("country").show()

+-------+---+------+
|country| id|amount|
+-------+---+------+
|     DE|  1| 120.5|
|     IN|  4| 300.0|
|     US|  2|  80.0|
+-------+---+------+

"Top row per group" is a window plus a filter, the Spark equivalent of Snowflake's QUALIFY. Note that for US, row_number puts the NULL amount last in a descending sort by default in Spark (nulls are the smallest values), so the 80.0 order wins as intended. Lesson 04 covers windows in SQL.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
When you call an action, Spark runs a pipeline:

  1. Parse your DataFrame calls into an unresolved logical plan.
  2. Analyze: resolve column names and types against the schema (this is why a typo'd column fails at the action or the next transformation, not at import time).
  3. Optimize (Catalyst): push filters toward the scan, prune unused columns, fold constants, reorder joins, simplify expressions.
  4. Physical planning: pick concrete operators (broadcast vs sort-merge join, hash vs sort aggregate).
  5. Execution: split the plan into stages at shuffle boundaries, split each stage into tasks (one per data partition), and run tasks on executor cores. Adaptive Query Execution can re-plan between stages (Level 2 · 05).

Laziness is what lets step 3 exist: because Spark sees the whole chain before running it, it can drop columns you never use and apply filters before expensive joins. It also means that calling an action twice runs the plan twice unless you cache() or save an intermediate result.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• collect() on a large DataFrame. It brings every row to the driver. Use limit, take or write the result.
  • Row-by-row Python loops over collect() output, or Python UDFs where a built-in function exists. Built-ins stay inside the optimized engine; Python UDFs serialize every row out to a Python worker.
  • Forgetting NULL handling in filters, when chains and averages, as shown above.
  • Expecting show() to be cheap. It's an action. df.count() followed by df.show() computes the plan twice.
  • withColumn in a loop for dozens of columns builds an enormous plan. Use one select with a list of expressions, or withColumns({...}).
  • Comparing with == None instead of isNull() or eqNullSafe.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Using the orders DataFrame, compute revenue per country for paid orders only, rounded to one decimal. Predict the output, then run it locally.
  2. Add a column size that labels missing amounts unknown. Verify order 3 no longer says small.
  3. Run .explain(True) on orders.filter(F.col("country") == "US").select("id"). Compare the analyzed and optimized plans: what extra predicate appears on country, and which operator order differs from how you wrote the code? (Lesson 05 shows column pruning on a real file scan, which an in-memory DataFrame like this one can't demonstrate.)
  4. Join orders to countries so that every order appears exactly once, with Unknown for missing country names. (Use coalesce.)

docs.title: 04 · Spark SQL, Built-in Functions & Window Functions
docs.text:
SQL is a first-class citizen on Databricks. Notebooks can mix SQL and Python, SQL warehouses speak only SQL, and DataFrame code is compiled by the same optimizer. This lesson covers the SQL you'll write daily plus the traps that produce wrong-but-plausible numbers.

What was run

Queries below ran on local Spark 4.2.0 against a small temp view, and output blocks are copied from those runs. Databricks SQL adds platform-specific syntax and functions on top of Spark's, and some statements shown elsewhere in the course (for example Unity Catalog GRANT) need a workspace. Where I say "Databricks also supports...", that comes from the documentation, not a run.

Setup used throughout (the same data works as a table in a workspace):

CREATE OR REPLACE TEMP VIEW sales AS SELECT * FROM VALUES
  (1,'2026-01-01','DE','book',12.0), (2,'2026-01-01','US','pen',3.0),  (3,'2026-01-02','DE','pen',3.5),
  (4,'2026-01-02','US','book',15.0), (5,'2026-01-03','DE','book',11.0), (6,'2026-01-03','DE','lamp',40.0),
  (7,'2026-01-04','US','lamp',42.0)
AS t(id, day, country, item, amount);

docs.title: Aggregation conveniences
docs.text:
SELECT country, item, SUM(amount) AS total FROM sales GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY 1, 2;

GROUP BY ALL groups by every non-aggregate expression in SELECT, so you don't repeat the list.

|DE     |book|23.0 |
|DE     |lamp|40.0 |
|DE     |pen |3.5  |
|US     |book|15.0 |
|US     |lamp|42.0 |
|US     |pen |3.0  |

FILTER restricts one aggregate without a CASE:

SELECT country, COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE item = 'book') AS books, COUNT(*) AS n
FROM sales GROUP BY country ORDER BY 1;

|DE     |2    |4  |
|US     |1    |3  |

PIVOT turns row values into columns (the list of values must be written out):

SELECT * FROM (SELECT country, item, amount FROM sales)
PIVOT (SUM(amount) FOR item IN ('book', 'pen', 'lamp')) ORDER BY country;

|country|book|pen|lamp|
|DE     |23.0|3.5|40.0|
|US     |15.0|3.0|42.0|

docs.title: Window functions
docs.text:
A window function computes a value per row using related rows, without collapsing them the way GROUP BY does.

SELECT day, country, amount,
       SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY country ORDER BY day
                         ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS running,
       LAG(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY country ORDER BY day)                AS prev,
       RANK()      OVER (PARTITION BY country ORDER BY amount DESC)        AS rk
FROM sales ORDER BY country, day;

Local output:

|day       |country|amount|running|prev|rk |
|2026-01-01|DE     |12.0  |12.0   |NULL|2  |
|2026-01-02|DE     |3.5   |15.5   |12.0|4  |
|2026-01-03|DE     |40.0  |66.5   |11.0|1  |
|2026-01-03|DE     |11.0  |26.5   |3.5 |3  |
|2026-01-01|US     |3.0   |3.0    |NULL|3  |
|2026-01-02|US     |15.0  |18.0   |3.0 |2  |
|2026-01-04|US     |42.0  |60.0   |15.0|1  |

Look at the two DE rows on 2026-01-03. Their running values (66.5 and 26.5) and prev values (11.0 and 3.5) depend on which of the two tied rows Spark happened to sort first. Here the 11.0 row came first for the window calculation (it shows running 26.5), even though the final ORDER BY country, day listed the 40.0 row first. If you need deterministic results, add a tie-breaker to the window's ORDER BY (ORDER BY day, id). A running total or LAG over a sort key with ties is one of the most common silent bugs in analytics SQL.

Two more details visible in the output: RANK() leaves gaps after ties while DENSE_RANK() doesn't, and an explicit ROWS frame states exactly which rows are summed. Without a frame, a window with ORDER BY defaults to a range frame, which treats tied rows as peers and gives all of them the same running value. Writing the frame removes the ambiguity.

docs.title: Top row per group: QUALIFY
docs.text:
Databricks SQL and Spark 4 support QUALIFY, which filters on window results without a subquery (this ran on local Spark 4.2.0):

SELECT country, item, amount FROM sales
QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY country ORDER BY amount DESC) = 1
ORDER BY country;

|DE     |lamp|40.0  |
|US     |lamp|42.0  |

If you must support an engine without QUALIFY, wrap the window in a subquery and filter in the outer WHERE.

docs.title: Arrays, structs and higher-order functions
docs.text:
Lakehouse data is often nested. Spark SQL has first-class array/map/struct types:

SELECT country, collect_list(item) AS items, array_distinct(collect_list(item)) AS uniq
FROM sales GROUP BY country ORDER BY 1;
-- DE  [book, pen, book, lamp]   [book, pen, lamp]

SELECT transform(array(1,2,3), a -> a * 10) AS scaled;       -- [10, 20, 30]
SELECT explode(sequence(1, 3)) AS n;                          -- one row each for 1, 2, 3
SELECT from_json('{"a":1,"b":[1,2]}', 'a INT, b ARRAY<INT>') AS j;   -- {1, [1, 2]}

(Those values were produced by the local run; for the first query the order inside collect_list is not guaranteed and can change between runs because it depends on partition order.) Higher-order functions such as transform, filter, exists and aggregate apply a lambda to each array element inside the engine, avoiding an explode and re-aggregate.

Dates and strings:

SELECT date_trunc('MONTH', DATE'2026-01-17')                   AS m,    -- 2026-01-01 00:00:00
       date_add(DATE'2026-01-31', 1)                           AS d,    -- 2026-02-01
       datediff(DATE'2026-03-01', DATE'2026-02-01')            AS dd,   -- 28
       to_date('03/04/2026', 'dd/MM/yyyy')                     AS p;    -- 2026-04-03
SELECT regexp_extract('order-4821-DE', '(\\d+)', 1)            AS n,    -- 4821
       concat_ws('-', 'a', NULL, 'c')                          AS c,    -- a-c
       lpad('7', 3, '0')                                       AS z;    -- 007

Always pass an explicit format to to_date: 03/04/2026 is 3 April or 4 March depending on the pattern you give.

docs.title: ANSI mode: errors instead of silent NULLs
docs.text:
Spark 4 enables ANSI SQL semantics by default (spark.sql.ansi.enabled printed true in the local run). Invalid operations then fail loudly:

SELECT 1/0;                    -- [DIVIDE_BY_ZERO] Division by zero. Use `try_divide` to tolerate ...
SELECT CAST('abc' AS INT);     -- [CAST_INVALID_INPUT] The value 'abc' ... cannot be cast to "INT" ...
SELECT try_cast('abc' AS INT); -- NULL
SELECT try_divide(1, 0);       -- NULL

Older Spark versions (3.x) returned NULL for both, so migrating code can start raising errors it never raised before. Databricks Runtime behaviour depends on the runtime version and workspace/compute settings, so check the setting on your compute with SET spark.sql.ansi.enabled rather than assuming. Use try_cast and try_divide where bad data is expected, and let errors surface where it isn't.

docs.title: Parameters and pipe syntax
docs.text:
Never build SQL by string concatenation. Spark supports named parameter markers when you pass args:

spark.sql("SELECT * FROM sales WHERE country = :c AND amount > :min", args={"c": "DE", "min": 10})

(Running SELECT :x + 1 without supplying args fails with [UNBOUND_SQL_PARAMETER], as the local run showed.) Spark 4 also accepts SQL pipe syntax, which reads top to bottom:

FROM sales |> WHERE country = 'DE' |> AGGREGATE SUM(amount) AS t GROUP BY item |> ORDER BY item

|book|23.0|
|lamp|40.0|
|pen |3.5 |

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
spark.sql(...) and the DataFrame API produce the same kind of logical plan, so there is no inherent speed difference between them. A window function becomes a plan node that first shuffles rows so each PARTITION BY key lands on one task, then sorts within each partition by the ORDER BY, then streams through the sorted rows applying the frame. That is why a window with no PARTITION BY is dangerous: all rows go to one task. And it explains the tie problem above: sorting is stable only with respect to the keys you gave it, so tied rows come out in whatever order the shuffle delivered them.

GROUP BY works differently: a hash aggregate computes partial results per task, shuffles by group key, and merges the partials. FILTER clauses and PIVOT are rewritten into conditional aggregates before execution.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Window ORDER BY with ties and no tie-breaker (see above).
  • ROW_NUMBER vs RANK for "top N": RANK returns more than N rows when there are ties.
  • A window with no PARTITION BY on a big table: single-task bottleneck.
  • Assuming collect_list preserves order. It doesn't, unless you sort afterward (sort_array).
  • Relying on implicit casts. ANSI mode turns bad casts into errors; decide between CAST and try_cast on purpose.
  • Ambiguous date parsing without an explicit pattern.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Write a query returning each country's best-selling item by revenue using QUALIFY, then rewrite it with a subquery. Check they match.
  2. Change the running-total query's window ORDER BY to day, id and confirm the two tied DE rows now give a stable answer on repeated runs.
  3. Compute each country's revenue share of the total with a window over the whole result set (SUM(...) OVER ()), rounded to 2 decimals.
  4. Predict what SELECT 5 / 0 and SELECT try_divide(5, 0) do on your compute, then check them. If the first returns NULL instead of an error, find which setting explains it.

docs.title: 05 · Reading & Writing Files: Formats, Schemas & Modes
docs.text:
Before Delta, every lakehouse pipeline starts with files: CSV exports, JSON events, Parquet from another system. How you read them decides whether bad data fails loudly, gets quietly nulled, or silently changes your column types.

What was run

Everything below ran on local Spark 4.2.0 against files on a laptop disk, and output is copied from those runs. On Databricks the same code reads from Unity Catalog volumes or cloud storage paths instead (/Volumes/..., s3://..., abfss://...); that part wasn't run here.

docs.title: Reading CSV: schema inference is a trap
docs.text:
Here is a small CSV with three planted problems (an empty amount, a bad date, a non-numeric amount):

id,order_date,country,amount
1,2026-01-03,DE,120.50
2,2026-01-03,US,80
3,2026-01-04,US,
4,not-a-date,IN,300
5,2026-01-05,DE,abc

d = spark.read.option("header", True).option("inferSchema", True).csv("orders.csv")
d.printSchema()

root
 |-- id: integer (nullable = true)
 |-- order_date: string (nullable = true)
 |-- country: string (nullable = true)
 |-- amount: string (nullable = true)

Inference scanned the data, found not-a-date and abc, and silently fell back to string for those two columns. Nothing failed, but every downstream amount > 100 is now a string comparison. Inference also costs an extra pass over the file, and on a different batch with no bad rows the same code would infer double: the schema depends on the data. Production reads should declare the schema.

docs.title: Declare a schema and capture the bad rows
docs.text:
schema = "id INT, order_date DATE, country STRING, amount DOUBLE, _bad STRING"
d = (spark.read.option("header", True)
       .schema(schema)
       .option("columnNameOfCorruptRecord", "_bad")     # PERMISSIVE mode (the default) keeps bad lines here
       .csv("orders.csv"))
d.cache()      # Spark requires materializing before querying only the corrupt column
d.show(truncate=False)

|id |order_date|country|amount|_bad               |
|1  |2026-01-03|DE     |120.5 |NULL               |
|2  |2026-01-03|US     |80.0  |NULL               |
|3  |2026-01-04|US     |NULL  |NULL               |
|4  |NULL      |IN     |300.0 |4,not-a-date,IN,300|
|5  |2026-01-05|DE     |NULL  |5,2026-01-05,DE,abc|

Three parse modes exist:

Mode Bad record behaviour PERMISSIVE (default) Unparseable fields become NULL; the raw line goes to the corrupt-record column if you defined one DROPMALFORMED The row is discarded without a trace (dangerous: rows vanish) FAILFAST The read raises an error on the first bad record

Notice what PERMISSIVE did with row 3: the empty amount became NULL but wasn't flagged as corrupt, because an empty string is a valid "missing" CSV value. Only rows 4 and 5 are quarantined. A common pattern is to write rows with a non-NULL _bad to a quarantine table and continue with the rest. With FAILFAST the same read raised an exception when collected (the local run's top-level message was just "An error occurred while calling collectToPython", with the parse error deeper in the stack trace).

Other CSV options you'll use: sep, quote, escape, multiLine (quoted fields containing newlines), encoding, nullValue, dateFormat, timestampFormat.

docs.title: Reading JSON: schemas with nesting
docs.text:
{"id":1,"user":{"name":"a","tags":["x","y"]}}
{"id":2,"user":{"name":"b"},"extra":true}

j = spark.read.json("e.json")        # JSON Lines: one object per line
j.printSchema()

root
 |-- extra: boolean (nullable = true)
 |-- id: long (nullable = true)
 |-- user: struct (nullable = true)
 |    |-- name: string (nullable = true)
 |    |-- tags: array (nullable = true)
 |    |    |-- element: string (containsNull = true)

Spark inferred a schema that is the union of both records (hence extra appears, nullable), and sorted the top-level fields alphabetically. Nested fields use dot paths; arrays are exploded one row per element:

j.select("id", "user.name", F.explode_outer("user.tags").alias("tag")).show()
# id=1 a x | id=1 a y | id=2 b NULL    (explode_outer keeps the row with no tags; plain explode would drop it)

For files that are a single JSON array or pretty-printed, use option("multiLine", True). As with CSV, inference reads the data; for large feeds supply a schema (or a sample-based schema you then freeze).

docs.title: Parquet: the default for a reason
docs.text:
Parquet is a columnar, compressed, typed format; the schema travels inside the file. For 200,000 generated rows with a string and a double column, the local run wrote:

CSV (with header):   3,446,684 bytes
Parquet (snappy):    1,598,600 bytes

Besides being smaller, Parquet lets Spark read only the columns a query needs and skip row groups using min/max statistics. Delta tables (Lesson 06) are Parquet files plus a log.

docs.title: Partitioned layout and partition pruning
docs.text:
data.write.mode("overwrite").partitionBy("day").parquet("pq")

['_SUCCESS', 'day=2026-01-01', 'day=2026-01-02', 'day=2026-01-03']

Each distinct day becomes a directory (day=2026-01-02/part-....parquet). A filter on the partition column reads only the matching directories. The physical plan from the local run shows it:

spark.read.parquet("pq").filter("day = '2026-01-02'").select("id").explain()

*(1) Project [id#230]
+- *(1) ColumnarToRow
   +- FileScan parquet [id#230,day#233] ... PartitionFilters: [isnotnull(day#233), (day#233 = 2026-01-02)], ...

PartitionFilters means whole directories were skipped, and the scan lists only [id, day], which is column pruning: the amount and country columns are never decoded. Partition columns are stored in the path, not inside the files, which is why they reappear on read. Level 2 · 04 covers choosing partition columns (spoiler: most tables shouldn't be partitioned at all).

docs.title: Save modes
docs.text:
df.write.mode("append").parquet(p)      # add files
df.write.mode("overwrite").parquet(p)   # replace everything at the path
df.write.mode("errorifexists").parquet(p)   # default: fail if the path exists
df.write.mode("ignore").parquet(p)      # do nothing if it exists

Appending the same 30-row DataFrame twice gave a count of 60; overwriting once brought it back to 30; and errorifexists on an existing path raised [PATH_ALREADY_EXISTS] Path ... already exists. Set mode as "overwrite" to overwrite the existing path. Plain Parquet append is not idempotent: re-running a job after a partial failure duplicates data. Delta's transactions and MERGE (Level 2) are the fix.

docs.title: File counts follow partition counts
docs.text: One output file is written per task. With repartition(5) the local write produced 5 Parquet files; with coalesce(1) it produced 1. Many tiny files slow down every later read (each file costs a metadata lookup and task), and one giant file can't be read in parallel. Lesson 04 of Level 2 returns to this as the "small files problem".

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
A read is lazy: spark.read... only lists the files and (if inferring) samples them. Spark divides the files into input splits of roughly spark.sql.files.maxPartitionBytes (128 MB by default), and each split becomes a task. For Parquet each task reads the footer to find column chunks, decodes only requested columns, and tests row-group min/max statistics against pushed-down filters to skip data. For CSV/JSON there is no such metadata, so every byte is parsed as text every time, which is much slower.

A write is a distributed commit: each task writes its output into a temporary directory, and a commit protocol renames the files into place when the job succeeds, writing _SUCCESS last. This is safe against a job crashing on its own, but plain file commits aren't truly atomic on cloud object stores: a reader listing the directory mid-commit may see a partial result. That gap is one of the problems the Delta log solves.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Using inferSchema in production and finding types change when the data does.
  • DROPMALFORMED hiding data loss. Prefer PERMISSIVE plus a quarantine, or FAILFAST for strict feeds.
  • Partitioning by a high-cardinality column (user id) and creating millions of tiny directories.
  • Overwriting a path you are also reading from in the same job.
  • Treating empty CSV fields and the literal text NULL as the same. Set nullValue / emptyValue deliberately.
  • Writing CSV for internal pipelines. Use Parquet or Delta; keep CSV for exchange with other people.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Run the CSV example yourself. Add a sixth row with an amount of 1e3 and see what the declared schema does with it.
  2. Modify the pipeline to write rows with a non-NULL _bad to quarantine/ as JSON and the rest to clean/ as Parquet. Check the row counts add up to 5 (careful: drop _bad from the clean output).
  3. Write the data DataFrame partitioned by country instead of day. Run explain() for country = 'DE' and point at the PartitionFilters line.
  4. Generate 200,000 rows and compare file sizes for CSV, JSON and Parquet on your machine. Your numbers will differ from the ones above; what ordering do you expect, and do you get it?

docs.title: 06 · Delta Lake Tables: Create, Read, Update, Delete
docs.text:
Delta Lake is the table format at the heart of Databricks. A Delta table looks like any SQL table (you can INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE and MERGE), but underneath it's a directory of Parquet files plus a transaction log. This lesson is the day-to-day SQL and Python; Lesson 07 opens the log.

What was run

All statements and outputs below come from open-source Delta Lake 4.4.1 on local Spark 4.2.0, writing to a laptop folder. Databricks runs a superset of this engine, so the statements work there too, but table properties, defaults (for example which table features are enabled for new tables) and the metadata shown by DESCRIBE differ between the open-source build and a Databricks runtime. On Databricks you'd normally address tables by a three-level Unity Catalog name (main.sales.emp), which wasn't run here.

docs.title: Create a table
docs.text:
CREATE TABLE emp (
  id     INT NOT NULL,
  name   STRING,
  dept   STRING,
  salary DOUBLE
) USING delta
COMMENT 'employees';

INSERT INTO emp VALUES (1,'Ann','eng',100), (2,'Bo','eng',90), (3,'Cy','ops',70);
UPDATE emp SET salary = salary * 1.1 WHERE dept = 'eng';
DELETE FROM emp WHERE id = 3;
SELECT * FROM emp ORDER BY id;

Locally (I added LOCATION '<folder>' so the files land somewhere I could inspect), the final query gave:

+---+----+----+------------------+
| id|name|dept|            salary|
+---+----+----+------------------+
|  1| Ann| eng|110.00000000000001|
|  2|  Bo| eng| 99.00000000000001|
+---+----+----+------------------+

That 110.00000000000001 is not a Delta bug: DOUBLE is binary floating point, and 100 * 1.1 isn't exactly 110. Use DECIMAL(p,s) for money. (The same applies to FLOAT.)

On Databricks, USING delta is the default format for managed tables, so CREATE TABLE t (...) alone is enough. Locally you must have the Delta extension configured, as in the Lesson 01 setup:

from delta import configure_spark_with_delta_pip
builder = (SparkSession.builder.master("local[2]")
    .config("spark.sql.extensions", "io.delta.sql.DeltaSparkSessionExtension")
    .config("spark.sql.catalog.spark_catalog", "org.apache.spark.sql.delta.catalog.DeltaCatalog"))
spark = configure_spark_with_delta_pip(builder).getOrCreate()

docs.title: Create from a query, and from a DataFrame
docs.text:
CREATE TABLE dept_pay USING delta AS
SELECT dept, avg(salary) AS avg_sal FROM emp GROUP BY dept;      -- CTAS: schema comes from the query

(df.write.format("delta")
   .mode("overwrite")                      # also "append", "errorifexists", "ignore"
   .saveAsTable("emp_copy"))               # or .save("/path") for a path-based table

Reading is spark.table("emp") or spark.read.format("delta").load("/path"); the SQL equivalent for a path is SELECT * FROM delta.`/path`.

docs.title: Row-level changes with the Python API
docs.text:
from delta.tables import DeltaTable

dt = DeltaTable.forName(spark, "emp")            # or DeltaTable.forPath(spark, "/path")
dt.update("dept = 'ops'", {"salary": "1"})       # condition and assignments are SQL strings
dt.delete("id = 3")
dt.toDF().show()                                  # current snapshot as a DataFrame

The condition dept = 'ops' matched no rows in the local run (Cy had already been deleted), and the table was unchanged. An UPDATE or DELETE that matches nothing succeeds without error, so check row counts when it matters.

docs.title: Inspecting a table
docs.text:
DESCRIBE DETAIL emp;      -- one row: format, location, numFiles, sizeInBytes, partitionColumns, properties, protocol versions
DESCRIBE HISTORY emp;     -- one row per commit
DESCRIBE EXTENDED emp;    -- columns plus catalog metadata

Local DESCRIBE DETAIL (selected columns):

|format|numFiles|properties|minReaderVersion|minWriterVersion|partitionColumns|
|delta |2       |{}        |1               |2               |[]              |

and DESCRIBE HISTORY:

|version|operation   |operationParameters                                  |
|3      |DELETE      |{predicate -> ["(id#1783 = 3)"]}                     |
|2      |UPDATE      |{predicate -> ["(dept#468 = eng)"]}                  |
|1      |WRITE       |{mode -> Append, partitionBy -> []}                  |
|0      |CREATE TABLE|{partitionBy -> [], clusterBy -> [], description -> employees, ...}|

Every statement was a separate commit and a separate version. The INSERT appears as WRITE. Notice that the predicate shows Spark's internal attribute ids (id#1783), a reminder that operationParameters are diagnostic text, not a stable API to parse.

Constraints are enforced at write time. Inserting a NULL into the NOT NULL column failed (the local run raised an exception from spark.sql; the full [DELTA_NOT_NULL_CONSTRAINT_VIOLATED]-style message was buried under a generic Python error, so inspect the exception's cause when you see one). Level 2 · 02 covers CHECK constraints and schema enforcement properly.

docs.title: Managed vs external, and what DROP TABLE does
docs.text: Because I created these tables with a LOCATION, they are external tables, and DESCRIBE EXTENDED showed Type EXTERNAL. After dropping a CTAS table that had been created with a LOCATION (it was named emp2 in my run) in the local run the table name disappeared, but the folder, its _delta_log and its Parquet file were all still on disk. For a managed table (no LOCATION) the catalog owns the files, and dropping the table deletes data too (on Databricks with Unity Catalog, managed-table data is retained for a recovery window and can be undropped; Lesson 08 and Level 3 · 03). Know which kind you have before you run DROP.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
Each SQL statement above becomes one Delta commit: Spark runs the query to produce new Parquet files, then atomically adds one JSON file to _delta_log/ listing which data files were added and which were removed. Parquet files are immutable, so UPDATE and DELETE don't edit files: they find the files containing matching rows, rewrite those files without (or with changed) rows, and commit "remove old file, add new file".

You can see this in the operationMetrics of the history (Lesson 07 prints them): the UPDATE removed two files (numRemovedFiles -> 2) and rewrote their rows, even though it changed only some of them. Newer Delta versions can avoid some rewrites with deletion vectors, small side files that mark rows as deleted without rewriting the data file; they're a table feature you opt into or that a platform enables by default. Which behaviour you get depends on the table's features, not just the SQL you write.

Reads never lock anything. A query takes the table's latest committed version at the start and reads exactly the files that version lists, so a writer committing mid-query can't change what you see.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Using DOUBLE for currency. Use DECIMAL.
  • Treating INSERT OVERWRITE/mode("overwrite") as an append. It replaces the table contents (as a new version).
  • Writing to the table's folder with plain spark.write.parquet. Files not recorded in the log are invisible to Delta readers, and VACUUM may delete them.
  • Dropping an external table and expecting the data to go away (or dropping a managed one and expecting it to stay).
  • No-op UPDATEs/DELETEs passing silently when the predicate is wrong. Check operationMetrics or row counts.
  • Parsing operationParameters as stable structured data.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Create emp as above with a LOCATION. After each statement run DESCRIBE DETAIL emp and write down numFiles. Explain the changes.
  2. Change salary to DECIMAL(10,2) in a new table, repeat the 10% raise, and compare the displayed results.
  3. Create emp as a managed table (no LOCATION) and find where Spark put its files (DESCRIBE EXTENDED). Drop it and check whether the folder is gone.
  4. Run an UPDATE whose predicate matches no row. Compare DESCRIBE HISTORY before and after; does it add a version? (Run it and write down what you observe rather than guessing.)

docs.title: 07 · Inside the Delta Log: Transactions & ACID
docs.text:
A Delta table is a folder with two kinds of content: Parquet data files and a _delta_log/ directory of small JSON files. The log is the table: the data files are only meaningful as far as the log mentions them. Reading the log once removes most of the mystery from Delta behaviour, from time travel to why concurrent writers sometimes fail.

What was run

The log contents, checkpoint and conflict below were produced with open-source Delta Lake 4.4.1 on local Spark 4.2.0. Databricks tables follow the same log protocol, but Databricks may enable extra table features (so protocol versions, extra properties and file layout can differ), and cloud storage makes commit atomicity depend on the storage service's guarantees. File names are shortened in the output for readability.

docs.title: Anatomy of a table folder
docs.text:
spark.createDataFrame([(1, "a"), (2, "b")], "id INT, v STRING").coalesce(1).write.format("delta").save(p)

p/
├── part-00000-bd3c7a7e-....snappy.parquet      # data
└── _delta_log/
    └── 00000000000000000000.json               # commit 0

(The local run also had .crc helper files, which are Hadoop checksum artifacts of the local filesystem, and a _staged_commits folder used by newer Delta versions for commit coordination.) Each commit is one file named with a 20-digit version number. The log is append-only: commits are never edited.

docs.title: What a commit contains
docs.text:
Each line of a commit file is one JSON action. Here is version 0, as printed by a small script that reads the file (file names shortened):

== v0
commitInfo WRITE isBlindAppend True readVersion None
metaData   {"type":"struct","fields":[{"name":"id","type":"integer","nullable":true,...
protocol   {"minReaderVersion": 1, "minWriterVersion": 2}
add        part-00000-bd3c7a7e-81b3.. size 669 stats {"numRecords":2,"minValues":{"id":1,"v":"a"},"maxValues":{"id":2,"v":"b"},"nullCount":{"id":0,"v":0}}

The action types you need to know:

Action Meaning metaData The table's schema, partition columns, and configuration (written at creation or when they change) protocol Minimum reader/writer versions (and table features) a client must support to use the table safely add A data file is part of the table from this version; carries size and statistics remove A data file is no longer part of the table (it stays on disk until VACUUM) commitInfo Operation name, parameters, metrics, isolation level, isBlindAppend, readVersion

Now an append (v1) and an update (v2):

== v1
commitInfo WRITE isBlindAppend True readVersion 0
add        part-00001-be08c006-7112.. size 666 stats {"numRecords":1,"minValues":{"id":3,"v":"c"},...}

== v2
commitInfo UPDATE isBlindAppend False readVersion 1
add        part-00000-910a0e7d-40da.. size 668 stats {"numRecords":2,"minValues":{"id":1,"v":"B"},"maxValues":{"id":2,"v":"a"},...}
remove     part-00000-bd3c7a7e-81b3.. dataChange True

The update didn't touch the file added in v1. It found the one file that contained id = 2 (the v0 file), wrote a replacement file with the changed row, and committed add new + remove old. Note readVersion 1: the writer records which version it read, which is how conflicts are detected (below). Also note the statistics in v2: "minValues":{"v":"B"},"maxValues":{"v":"a"}. Uppercase B sorts before lowercase a in a byte-wise string ordering, a reminder that min/max for strings isn't alphabetical in the human sense.

docs.title: The table's state = replaying the log
docs.text: To know what's in the table at version N, a reader applies actions from version 0 to N: start with an empty set of files, add inserts, remove deletes. The result is the snapshot. Time travel (Lesson 08) is just "stop replay at version N".

docs.title: Checkpoints
docs.text:
Replaying thousands of JSON files would be slow, so every 10 commits Delta writes a checkpoint: a Parquet file holding the complete state (the live add files plus protocol and metadata) as of that version. After 12 commits in the local run, the log folder contained:

00000000000000000000.json … 00000000000000000009.json
00000000000000000010.checkpoint.parquet
_last_checkpoint        ->  {"version":10,"size":13,"sizeInBytes":20891,"numOfAddFiles":10,...}

A reader first reads _last_checkpoint, loads the checkpoint, then applies only the JSON commits after it. (Old JSON files are cleaned up after delta.logRetentionDuration, 30 days by default; Lesson 08.)

docs.title: ACID, concretely
docs.text:
• Atomicity. A commit is one file being created. Either …0002.json exists and the whole transaction is visible, or it doesn't and none of it is. A job that crashes after writing Parquet files but before the commit leaves orphan data files that no snapshot references; VACUUM removes them later.
  • Consistency. Before committing, Delta checks the new schema, NOT NULL and CHECK constraints against the data (Level 2 · 02).
  • Isolation. Readers use a fixed snapshot, so they never see half a commit. Writers use optimistic concurrency control: do the work, then try to create the next version number; if someone else got there first, check whether the two transactions conflict.
  • Durability. Once the commit file is in object storage, it's as durable as the storage.

docs.title: A real conflict
docs.text:
Two threads ran UPDATE ... WHERE g = 0 on the same table at the same time (one adding 100 to id, the other adding 200). The local result:

{'u2': '[DELTA_CONCURRENT_APPEND.WITHOUT_HINT] Transaction conflict detected. a concurrent UPDATE added data to table ...', 'u1': 'ok'}
count = 10, sum(id) = 545
history: version 1 UPDATE, version 0 WRITE

One writer won version 1; the other read version 0, planned to rewrite the same files, found at commit time that version 1 had changed them, and raised DELTA_CONCURRENT_APPEND. The table holds exactly one writer's change (sum 545 = the +100 update on five rows), with no lost or doubled rows. The loser must retry, which re-reads the new snapshot. Delta's rule of thumb: writes to disjoint data (different partitions, or files that don't overlap) can both succeed; writes that touch the same files conflict. That's why partitioning and clustering choices affect concurrency (Level 2).

Databricks documents isolation levels (WriteSerializable is the default for tables; Serializable is stricter) and row-level concurrency features that can reduce conflicts on tables with deletion vectors or liquid clustering. Those platform behaviours weren't exercised here.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
Atomic commit is the one primitive everything depends on: "create file N.json only if it doesn't exist." On storage systems that offer conditional put or atomic rename (HDFS, ADLS, GCS, and S3 with conditional writes), that is the whole story. Where the store lacked it (older S3), Delta needed an external coordination service (such as a DynamoDB table) to guarantee a single winner. Databricks manages this for you, and the protocol also has a catalog-managed commits feature where the catalog arbitrates commits; its availability depends on platform and version, so check the docs before relying on it.

The stats in each add action is what makes data skipping possible: when you query WHERE id > 1000, the engine reads the log (not the data), drops every file whose maxValues.id is at most 1000, and opens only the rest. By default Delta collects statistics for the first 32 columns. That number, and which columns have stats, is why column order in a wide table can matter (Level 2 · 04).

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Editing or deleting log files by hand. You can make the table unreadable; there is no undo for a corrupted log.
  • Deleting data files with a file-system tool instead of DELETE + VACUUM. The log still references them.
  • Treating a conflict error as a bug. It's the design working; add retries (and idempotent logic) around writes.
  • Sharing one table between engines that don't support the table's protocol features; upgrading the protocol can lock out older readers and can't easily be undone.
  • Many tiny commits (a streaming job committing every second) create lots of small files and a long log.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Reproduce the walk-through: write a table, append, update, then write a ~15-line script that prints each action type and path for every commit. Explain which file each remove refers to.
  2. Make 12 more commits and list the _delta_log folder. Find the checkpoint and read _last_checkpoint.
  3. Provoke a conflict yourself with two threads (or two terminals), first updating the same rows, then rows in different partitions of a partitioned table. Report which combination fails on your setup.
  4. In the log, find the numRecords stat for each file and verify it by spark.read.parquet(<file>).count().

docs.title: 08 · Time Travel, RESTORE & VACUUM
docs.text:
Because Delta never edits data files in place, the files for previous versions stay around until something deletes them. Time travel exposes that history for queries, RESTORE rolls a table back, and VACUUM is the thing that finally erases it. Knowing how those three interact tells you what you can and can't recover.

What was run

The queries and errors below are from open-source Delta Lake 4.4.1 on local Spark 4.2.0. VACUUM options such as LITE/FULL, Unity Catalog UNDROP, and automatic maintenance by Predictive Optimization are Databricks features described from the documentation (October 2026) and weren't executed.

docs.title: A table with some history
docs.text:
CREATE TABLE tt (id INT, v STRING) USING delta;
INSERT INTO tt VALUES (1,'a'), (2,'b');      -- version 1
UPDATE tt SET v = 'z';                       -- version 2
DELETE FROM tt WHERE id = 1;                 -- version 3
DESCRIBE HISTORY tt;

|version|timestamp              |operation   |
|3      |2026-10-21 23:33:30.772|DELETE      |
|2      |2026-10-21 23:33:27.522|UPDATE      |
|1      |2026-10-21 23:33:20.723|WRITE       |
|0      |2026-10-21 23:33:18.46 |CREATE TABLE|

docs.title: Querying the past
docs.text:
SELECT * FROM tt VERSION AS OF 1;                         -- by version number
SELECT * FROM tt TIMESTAMP AS OF '2026-10-21 23:33:20.723';  -- by time

Both returned the original two rows (1,a) and (2,b) in the local run. In Python:

spark.read.format("delta").option("versionAsOf", 1).load(path)
spark.read.format("delta").option("timestampAsOf", "2026-10-21 23:33:20.723").load(path)

A timestamp query returns the latest version committed at or before that time. A timestamp earlier than the first commit (or beyond the retained log) is an error, not an empty table. There is also a path shorthand, delta.`/path@v1`; on that local table @v0 returned 0 rows because version 0 was the empty CREATE TABLE.

Time travel is a handy diff tool:

SELECT * FROM tt VERSION AS OF 1
EXCEPT
SELECT * FROM tt;          -- rows present at version 1 that are not in the current table

This returned both original rows, since UPDATE changed v for every row and DELETE removed row 1. (Spark's EXCEPT compares whole rows; it is a set operation and removes duplicates, so use EXCEPT ALL when duplicates matter.)

docs.title: RESTORE: roll back
docs.text:
RESTORE TABLE tt TO VERSION AS OF 1;
-- or: RESTORE TABLE tt TO TIMESTAMP AS OF '...';

RESTORE is itself a new commit, not a deletion of history: it adds back the files that were live at version 1 and removes the ones added since. In the earlier 12-commit local table (Lesson 07), restoring to version 1 reported:

|table_size_after_restore|num_of_files_after_restore|num_removed_files|num_restored_files|removed_files_size|restored_files_size|
|1335                    |2                         |10               |1                 |6662              |669                |

and DESCRIBE HISTORY then listed version 12 RESTORE on top of the earlier versions. That's an important safety property: a rollback can be rolled back.

RESTORE needs the old files to still exist

After VACUUM removed them, the local run's RESTORE TABLE tt TO VERSION AS OF 1 failed with: Not all files from version 1 are available in file system.

docs.title: VACUUM: the point of no return
docs.text:
VACUUM tt DRY RUN;                 -- lists files that would be deleted (up to 1000)
VACUUM tt RETAIN 168 HOURS;        -- default: 7 days

VACUUM deletes files that are (a) not referenced by the current snapshot and (b) were logically removed longer ago than the retention threshold, plus files in the table folder that Delta doesn't track at all. It never touches _delta_log. Retention is measured from when the remove was committed, not the file's modification time.

Delta guards against dangerously short retention:

VACUUM tt RETAIN 0 HOURS;
-- [DELTA_VACUUM_RETENTION_PERIOD_TOO_SHORT] The specified VACUUM retention period is too low and may corrupt this Delta table if any writes are in progress.

For the demo I disabled the check with SET spark.databricks.delta.retentionDurationCheck.enabled = false. Then:

VACUUM tt RETAIN 0 HOURS DRY RUN   -> 4 files to delete
files in folder before / after VACUUM:  5 -> 1
SELECT * FROM tt VERSION AS OF 1   -> error (the data files are gone)
RESTORE TABLE tt TO VERSION AS OF 1 -> Not all files from version 1 are available in file system.

(The VERSION AS OF 1 failure surfaced locally as a generic Python "error occurred while calling showString"; the underlying cause is the missing Parquet files. Don't copy RETAIN 0 anywhere that matters: it can also delete files that an in-flight write has produced but not yet committed.)

docs.title: Two retention knobs
docs.text:
Property Default Controls delta.logRetentionDuration 30 days How long commit history (JSON/checkpoints) is kept; bounds time travel by metadata delta.deletedFileRetentionDuration 7 days How long removed data files are kept; VACUUM uses it as its default threshold

Time travel needs both: the log entry and the data files. So the effective window is the shorter of the two, which by default is the 7-day file retention. To keep 30 days of travel you must raise both:

ALTER TABLE tt SET TBLPROPERTIES (
  'delta.logRetentionDuration' = 'interval 30 days',
  'delta.deletedFileRetentionDuration' = 'interval 30 days');

Longer retention means more storage: every old file you keep is paid for. And it is not a backup: it lives in the same storage, deleted by the same VACUUM, and the retention is a cleanup default, not a guarantee. Use deep clones or cross-region copies for real backups (Level 4 · 09).

docs.title: Dropped tables and Unity Catalog
docs.text: Time travel does nothing for a dropped table. In Unity Catalog, the Databricks documentation says dropped managed or external tables can be recovered with UNDROP TABLE within a recovery period (7 days by default, configurable at catalog or schema level), restoring metadata such as privileges and properties but not primary/foreign key constraints. SHOW TABLES DROPPED lists candidates. (Documented, not run here.)

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
Time travel is log replay stopped early (Lesson 07). VERSION AS OF 1 loads the newest checkpoint at or before version 1, applies commits up to version 1, and gets a file list. The reader then simply opens those Parquet files. If a file in that list has been vacuumed, the open fails, which is exactly the error you saw.

TIMESTAMP AS OF first maps the timestamp to a version using the commit timestamps (taken from the log files' modification times or recorded commit timestamps), then proceeds the same way.

VACUUM works by listing the table directory, subtracting the set of files referenced by versions inside the retention window, and deleting the remainder. That listing is why VACUUM on a huge table is slow and why Databricks added LITE mode (uses the log instead of listing the directory) and runs maintenance automatically with Predictive Optimization (Level 4 · 08).

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Treating time travel as a backup. VACUUM ends it; a dropped, non-UC table has no history at all.
  • Setting RETAIN 0 HOURS to "reclaim space now" and breaking concurrent writers or all rollback.
  • Raising only one retention property. You need both for longer travel.
  • Using time travel in pipelines to read "yesterday's data" with a hard-coded timestamp: a vacuum breaks the job. Persist what you need as its own table or use the change data feed (Level 2 · 01).
  • Forgetting that RESTORE is a write that creates new data-change events for downstream streams.
