  • Expecting VACUUM to shrink the log. The log is cleaned by logRetentionDuration at checkpoint time.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Build the tt table, then use time travel to produce a diff of rows deleted between versions 2 and 3.
  2. Wrong delete: run DELETE FROM tt (no predicate), then recover with RESTORE. Check DESCRIBE HISTORY.
  3. Run VACUUM tt DRY RUN right after your changes. Why does it list nothing with the default retention?
  4. Disable the retention check locally, vacuum with RETAIN 0 HOURS, and confirm that both VERSION AS OF and RESTORE fail. Write down which files were deleted (use the DRY RUN output first).

docs.title: 09 · Tables, Views & Volumes: Where Data Lives
docs.text:
"Where is my data?" has four answers on Databricks: in a table, behind a view, in a volume (files), or in a legacy location you should be migrating away from. Choosing correctly decides who can see the data, what DROP deletes, and whether your code still works after a platform change.

What was run

Table and view behaviour below was run on local Spark 4.2.0 with Delta 4.4.1, using Spark's built-in catalog (a local warehouse folder and a sales database). That catalog has two-level names (schema.table). Databricks with Unity Catalog adds a top level (catalog.schema.table), volumes, and governance; those parts are described from the Databricks documentation (October 2026) and weren't executed.

docs.title: The object model
docs.text:
catalog                      (Unity Catalog: a top-level container, e.g. main, prod, dev)
 └── schema (database)       (a grouping: sales, finance)
      ├── tables             (Delta by default; managed or external)
      ├── views              (stored queries) / materialized views
      ├── volumes            (governed file storage: managed or external)
      ├── functions
      └── registered models

Names resolve as catalog.schema.object. Locally we only had sales.orders; on Databricks it would be main.sales.orders. You can set defaults with USE CATALOG main; USE SCHEMA sales; so short names work.

docs.title: Managed vs external tables
docs.text:
CREATE TABLE sales.orders (id INT, amt DOUBLE) USING delta;       -- managed: the catalog picks the location
CREATE TABLE sales.orders_ext (id INT, amt DOUBLE) USING delta
  LOCATION 's3://bucket/path/orders_ext';                         -- external: you pick the location

DESCRIBE TABLE EXTENDED sales.orders locally reported:

|Type    |MANAGED                                            |
|Location|file:/private/tmp/claude-501/exp/wh/sales.db/orders|
|Provider|delta                                              |
Managed External Location Chosen and organized by the catalog Any path you register DROP TABLE Removes metadata and data (Unity Catalog keeps managed-table data recoverable for a while) Removes metadata only; files stay Good for Default for tables owned by the lakehouse Data shared with other systems, or already existing in cloud storage Governance Unity Catalog controls access end to end Needs an external location and storage credential (Level 3 · 03)

Databricks recommends managed tables for most uses; Unity Catalog managed tables also get platform optimizations such as automatic maintenance via Predictive Optimization (Level 4 · 08). Use external tables when something outside Databricks must read or write the same files directly.

In Lesson 06 a locally created external table (with LOCATION) kept its folder after DROP TABLE, as the table above predicts.

docs.title: Views
docs.text:
A view is a stored query, not stored data:

CREATE VIEW sales.big AS SELECT * FROM sales.orders WHERE amt > 5;
SELECT * FROM sales.big;          -- (2, 7.0)

DESCRIBE EXTENDED sales.big shows Type VIEW and the View Text (SELECT * FROM sales.orders WHERE amt>5). Three behaviours worth seeing for yourself (all from the local run):

  1. After ALTER TABLE sales.orders ADD COLUMN note STRING, SELECT * FROM sales.big still worked and returned only the original two columns. A view captures its column list when it is created, so SELECT * inside it does not pick up later columns. Recreate (or ALTER VIEW ... AS) the view to include them.
  2. After DROP TABLE sales.orders, the view still existed in the catalog, but querying it failed with [TABLE_OR_VIEW_NOT_FOUND] The table or view sales.orders cannot be found. Views don't protect against dropped dependencies, and don't track them for you.
  3. SHOW TABLES IN sales lists tables and views together; isTemporary distinguishes session-scoped ones.

Other view flavours:

Kind Lifetime Use CREATE VIEW Persisted in the catalog Reusable, shareable logic; basis for access control (expose a subset of columns/rows) CREATE TEMP VIEW This Spark session only Name an intermediate DataFrame for SQL (df.createOrReplaceTempView("t")) CREATE GLOBAL TEMP VIEW Application lifetime, in global_temp Share between sessions of one application; rarely needed CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW (Databricks SQL/pipelines) Stored result, refreshed Precomputed aggregates; covered with Lakeflow pipelines in Level 3 · 06

docs.title: Volumes: governed files
docs.text:
Not everything is a table. Raw CSV drops, images, PDFs, model artifacts and checkpoint files need a home with permissions too. In Unity Catalog that home is a volume, a governed logical volume of cloud storage. Per the documentation:

  • Managed volumes store files in storage that Unity Catalog manages for the schema.
  • External volumes register an existing cloud storage path; dropping the volume leaves the files.
  • You access them by path: /Volumes/<catalog>/<schema>/<volume>/<path>.
  • Files in a volume cannot be registered as tables: volumes are for path-based access. Load the data into a Delta table to govern it as tabular data.
# Needs a workspace; not run locally
df = spark.read.format("csv").option("header", True).load("/Volumes/main/raw/landing/orders/2026-10-21/")
dbutils.fs.ls("/Volumes/main/raw/landing/")

CREATE VOLUME main.raw.landing;
GRANT READ VOLUME ON VOLUME main.raw.landing TO `data-engineers`;

The GRANT statement above follows the documented syntax; it couldn't be executed here. Volumes are the recommended landing zone for Auto Loader and COPY INTO (Level 2 · 08).

docs.title: Legacy locations you will still meet
docs.text:
The documentation marks the DBFS root (dbfs:/, with folders such as /FileStore and /user/hive/warehouse) and DBFS mounts as deprecated and not recommended; new accounts are provisioned without access to them. Their replacements are Unity Catalog volumes and external locations (governed), and workspace files (for code, configs and small files). The dbfs:/ scheme itself still works as an optional prefix when addressing volumes. When you inherit older notebooks, expect dbfs:/mnt/... paths and hive_metastore.default.table names; migration is covered in Level 4 · 09.

Also remember driver-local storage: /tmp or ./file from %sh or plain Python is a disk on the driver node, visible only there and gone when compute stops.

Need Put it in Tabular data used by many Managed Delta table Existing files other tools also write External table, or external volume if non-tabular Raw drops, images, documents Volume Notebooks, small config, .py modules Workspace files / Git folders Scratch for a single run Driver-local disk (not durable)

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
A catalog is a metadata service: a row says "table main.sales.orders is a Delta table at location X, owned by Y, with these grants". The data files exist independently in object storage. Managed means the catalog chose X and is responsible for its lifecycle; external means you chose X and the catalog merely points at it. That's why DROP differs: it removes the catalog row, and for managed tables also schedules deletion of X.

A view is another catalog row holding SQL text and the resolved column list. The query is re-planned against the underlying tables on every read, so you always see current data, but a missing or changed dependency only surfaces at query time (the failure above).

Volumes add a path-translation layer: a /Volumes/... path is resolved by Unity Catalog to a cloud storage location after a permission check, and compute reads the files with credentials that the catalog vends, so users don't need cloud keys.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Dropping a managed table you thought was external (or the reverse).
  • Hard-coding hive_metastore. or dbfs:/mnt/ paths in new work.
  • Relying on SELECT * views to follow schema changes.
  • Using a temp view across notebooks or jobs. It exists only in its Spark session.
  • Writing files into a volume and expecting a table. Volumes aren't tables.
  • Storing durable results in /tmp on the driver.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Locally, create a managed table and an external table (LOCATION) in a sales database. Drop both and list the folders. Which data remained?
  2. Recreate the "view that stops working": create the view, add a column to the base table, and check which columns the view returns. Then fix the view.
  3. Look up DESCRIBE EXTENDED output for a view on your platform. Which field tells you its defining SQL?
  4. On a workspace (or from the documentation), list the three differences between a managed and an external volume.

docs.title: 10 · Project — A Sales Lakehouse You Can Run Locally
docs.text:
You'll build a miniature lakehouse end to end on your laptop: ingest a messy CSV, quarantine bad rows, clean the rest into a typed Delta table, build an aggregate, answer questions in SQL, then make a mistake and recover from it with time travel. It uses only what Level 1 taught: explicit schemas, parse modes, Delta tables, SQL windows and RESTORE.

What was run

The script below was run exactly as shown on local Spark 4.2.0 + Delta Lake 4.4.1 (Python 3.12), and every output block in this lesson is copied from that run. The data is generated with a fixed random seed, so you should get the same counts; the revenue figures depend on Python's seeded generator and are not meant to represent any real business. On Databricks you'd swap the local folder for a Unity Catalog schema and the landing file for a volume.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
python3.12 -m venv .venv && .venv/bin/pip install pyspark delta-spark
export PYSPARK_PYTHON=$PWD/.venv/bin/python      # workers must use the same Python as the driver
mkdir lab && cd lab

(Java 17 or newer must be installed. Without PYSPARK_PYTHON, a mismatch between the driver's and the workers' Python minor version stops the job with PYTHON_VERSION_MISMATCH, which happened during development on a machine with two Pythons.)

docs.title: The task
docs.text:
The landing file has 200 orders plus four deliberate problems:

Problem Planted as Missing price order 10 has an empty unit_price Impossible date order 20 has date 2026-13-45 Exact duplicate order 5 appears twice Unknown country order 999 has country XX

Requirements: (1) corrupt rows go to a quarantine table, never silently dropped; (2) the silver table has no duplicates, no missing prices and only known countries; (3) a gold table gives revenue per country; (4) answer three questions; (5) delete a country by mistake and restore it.

docs.title: The script
docs.text:
"""Level 1 project: a small sales lakehouse, runnable locally with pyspark + delta-spark."""
import csv, random, shutil, pathlib
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession, functions as F
from delta import configure_spark_with_delta_pip

ROOT = pathlib.Path("lakehouse"); shutil.rmtree(ROOT, ignore_errors=True); (ROOT / "landing").mkdir(parents=True)

# 1. Generate a landing file with planted problems (seeded, so everyone gets the same data)
random.seed(7)
countries = ["DE", "US", "IN", "BR"]
rows = []
for i in range(1, 201):
    rows.append([i, f"2026-03-{1 + i % 28:02d}", f"C{random.randint(1, 40):03d}", random.choice(countries),
                 random.choice(["book", "pen", "lamp", "desk"]), random.randint(1, 5), round(random.uniform(3, 120), 2)])
rows[9][6] = ""                    # missing price
rows[19][1] = "2026-13-45"         # impossible date
rows.append(rows[4][:])            # exact duplicate order
rows.append([999, "2026-03-05", "C001", "XX", "pen", 2, 4.0])   # unknown country code
with open(ROOT / "landing/orders.csv", "w", newline="") as f:
    w = csv.writer(f); w.writerow(["order_id", "order_date", "customer", "country", "item", "qty", "unit_price"]); w.writerows(rows)

builder = (SparkSession.builder.master("local[2]").appName("proj1")
           .config("spark.sql.extensions", "io.delta.sql.DeltaSparkSessionExtension")
           .config("spark.sql.catalog.spark_catalog", "org.apache.spark.sql.delta.catalog.DeltaCatalog")
           .config("spark.sql.shuffle.partitions", "4").config("spark.ui.enabled", "false")
           .config("spark.sql.warehouse.dir", str(ROOT / "warehouse")))
spark = configure_spark_with_delta_pip(builder).getOrCreate(); spark.sparkContext.setLogLevel("ERROR")

# 2. Raw -> bronze: explicit schema, keep bad rows
schema = ("order_id INT, order_date DATE, customer STRING, country STRING, item STRING, qty INT, "
          "unit_price DOUBLE, _bad STRING")
raw = (spark.read.option("header", True).schema(schema).option("columnNameOfCorruptRecord", "_bad")
       .csv(str(ROOT / "landing/orders.csv")).cache())
print("raw rows:", raw.count())
raw.filter("_bad IS NOT NULL").select("_bad").show(truncate=False)
raw.filter("_bad IS NULL").drop("_bad").write.format("delta").mode("overwrite").saveAsTable("bronze_orders")
raw.filter("_bad IS NOT NULL").select("_bad").write.format("delta").mode("overwrite").saveAsTable("quarantine_orders")

# 3. Silver: dedupe, validate, enrich
countries_df = spark.createDataFrame([("DE", "Germany"), ("US", "United States"), ("IN", "India"), ("BR", "Brazil")],
                                     "code STRING, country_name STRING")
silver = (spark.table("bronze_orders").dropDuplicates()
          .filter(F.col("unit_price").isNotNull() & (F.col("qty") > 0))
          .join(countries_df, F.col("country") == F.col("code"), "inner").drop("code")
          .withColumn("revenue", F.round(F.col("qty") * F.col("unit_price"), 2)))
silver.write.format("delta").mode("overwrite").saveAsTable("silver_orders")
print("bronze:", spark.table("bronze_orders").count(), "silver:", spark.table("silver_orders").count(),
      "quarantine:", spark.table("quarantine_orders").count())

# 4. Gold + analytics
spark.sql("""CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE gold_revenue_by_country USING delta AS
  SELECT country_name, COUNT(*) AS orders, ROUND(SUM(revenue),2) AS revenue FROM silver_orders GROUP BY country_name""")
spark.sql("SELECT * FROM gold_revenue_by_country ORDER BY revenue DESC").show()
spark.sql("""SELECT item, SUM(qty) units FROM silver_orders GROUP BY item ORDER BY units DESC""").show()
# top customer per country
spark.sql("""WITH spend AS (SELECT country_name, customer, ROUND(SUM(revenue),2) AS spend FROM silver_orders GROUP BY country_name, customer)
  SELECT * FROM spend QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY country_name ORDER BY spend DESC, customer) = 1
  ORDER BY country_name""").show()

# 5. History + time travel
spark.sql("DESCRIBE HISTORY silver_orders").select("version", "operation").show()
spark.sql("DELETE FROM silver_orders WHERE country_name = 'Brazil'")
print("after delete:", spark.table("silver_orders").count(),
      "| version 0:", spark.sql("SELECT * FROM silver_orders VERSION AS OF 0").count())
spark.sql("RESTORE TABLE silver_orders TO VERSION AS OF 0")
print("after restore:", spark.table("silver_orders").count())

# 6. Self-check
assert spark.table("silver_orders").groupBy("order_id").count().filter("count > 1").count() == 0
assert spark.table("silver_orders").count() == 198
assert spark.table("quarantine_orders").count() == 1
print("checks passed")

docs.text:
The counts are the key check. 202 raw lines were read (200 orders + the duplicate + order 999), and exactly one was unparseable:

|_bad                             |
|20,2026-13-45,C029,IN,desk,3,5.64|

Reconcile them: 202 lines, minus 1 quarantined = 201 in bronze. Silver removes the duplicate (200), the missing-price order (199) and the XX country (198). Every row is accounted for. Note that the missing-price row wasn't quarantined: an empty field is a valid CSV null, so it reached bronze and was filtered in silver. Whether that row should be quarantined too is a design choice; write it down.

+-------------+------+--------+
|        India|    52|11121.09|
|       Brazil|    51|10171.84|
|United States|    49| 9544.12|
|      Germany|    46| 8515.32|

|item|units|
+----+-----+
|lamp|  166|
| pen|  149|

And the recovery:

docs.title: Things the project is quietly teaching
docs.text:
1. Explicit schema + corrupt-record column is what made the quarantine possible. With inferSchema, order 20's date would have turned the whole column into strings.
  2. Window + QUALIFY needs a tie-breaker. The top-customer query orders by spend DESC, customer so ties can't change the answer between runs. My first attempt put SUM(revenue) inside the window of a GROUP BY query and Spark raised UNRESOLVED_COLUMN; computing the sums in a CTE first is the portable pattern.
  3. A plain CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE ... AS SELECT on local Spark failed with UNSUPPORTED_FEATURE.TABLE_OPERATION until I added USING delta: the local default table provider isn't Delta. Databricks defaults to Delta, so you can usually omit it there, but being explicit never hurts.
  4. Reconciliation is a test. Row counts at every layer, adding up, is the cheapest data-quality check there is.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: Each saveAsTable or CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE above is a Delta commit (a WRITE or CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE AS SELECT action in the log), and each table has its own folder under the local warehouse directory with Parquet files and a _delta_log. dropDuplicates() triggers a shuffle (rows are hashed by all columns so duplicates land on one task); the join to the tiny countries DataFrame is a candidate for a broadcast join, which Spark chooses for small inputs; I did not inspect this run's plan, and Level 2 · 06 shows how to check. RESTORE didn't copy data back: it re-added the file entries that the DELETE had removed from the snapshot, which is possible only because the files hadn't been vacuumed.

docs.title: Extensions
docs.text:
• Add a silver_customers dimension and a gold "revenue by month" table. Which columns need DECIMAL?
  • Re-run the script twice. What happens to row counts? (mode("overwrite") makes this one idempotent. Would append?)
  • Write a check.py that asserts the reconciliation identity and the absence of duplicates, and exits non-zero on failure.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Running without PYSPARK_PYTHON and getting PYTHON_VERSION_MISMATCH from the workers.
  • Using inferSchema so a bad date silently turns a whole column into strings.
  • Dropping bad rows instead of quarantining them, so the counts can no longer be reconciled.
  • CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE ... AS without USING delta on a local Spark whose default provider isn't Delta.
  • Putting an aggregate inside a window in the same GROUP BY query instead of aggregating in a CTE first.
  • Restoring after a VACUUM: RESTORE needs the old files to still exist.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Run the project and confirm your counts equal 202 / 201 / 198 / 1.
  2. Quarantine missing-price rows as well, so quarantine becomes 2 and silver stays 198. What changes in the script?
  3. Change the seed to 8. Which numbers must stay the same (and why), and which change?
  4. Add a second planted problem (a negative quantity) and make the pipeline handle it without losing track of the row.

docs.title: Level 2 · Delta Lake & Data Engineering
docs.text:
Level 2 is about making tables correct, fast and continuously updated. It leans on measurements you can repeat on a laptop: a partition key that turned 2 MB of data into 86,665 files, a Z-order that cut the files read for a filter from 16 to 2, a hot key that put 329,083 rows into one shuffle partition, a deleted checkpoint that duplicated every row, and an ALTER TABLE ... CLUSTER BY that silently rewrote nothing.

What was run, and what wasn't

As in Level 1, Spark 4.2.0 and Delta Lake 4.4.1 (open source) were run locally and those outputs are labelled. Auto Loader, Photon, Predictive Optimization and other platform-only features are described from the Databricks documentation (October 2026) and are marked as not run. Where a local experiment gave a negative or surprising result (for example AQE skew handling not triggering on a tiny dataset), the lesson says so.

Prerequisites: Level 1, especially Delta tables, the Delta log and time travel.

docs.title: Modules
docs.text:
1. MERGE, Upserts & the Change Data Feed: upserts, the duplicate-source rule, SCD Type 2, row-level change events.
  2. Schema Enforcement, Evolution & Constraints: what Delta rejects, how to evolve, the INSERT * trap, column mapping, CHECK.
  3. OPTIMIZE, Z-Order & Liquid Clustering: compaction vs clustering, with measured data skipping.
  4. Partitioning, File Sizes & Data Skipping: when not to partition, and which columns get statistics.
  5. How Spark Executes: Stages, Shuffles & AQE: reading plans, join strategies, adaptive execution.
  6. Joins, Broadcast & Data Skew: hints, detecting skew, salting.
  7. Structured Streaming & Checkpoints: triggers, exactly-once, watermarks, foreachBatch.
  8. Auto Loader: Incremental File Ingestion: cloudFiles, detection modes, schema evolution.
  9. The Medallion Architecture: what each layer guarantees.
  10. Project: A Bronze/Silver/Gold Pipeline: incremental, idempotent, reconciled.

docs.title: After Level 2
docs.text: Level 3 moves from "can I build the pipeline" to "can the organization trust and operate it": Unity Catalog governance, privileges, storage credentials and volumes, row filters and masks, lineage and system tables, Lakeflow declarative pipelines and jobs, Delta Sharing and SQL warehouses.

docs.title: 01 · MERGE, Upserts & the Change Data Feed
docs.text:
Real pipelines don't just append: yesterday's customer changes city, an order gets corrected, a record must be deleted. MERGE INTO applies a batch of changes to a Delta table in one atomic transaction, and the Change Data Feed (CDF) records exactly what changed so downstream tables can follow along.

What was run

All statements and outputs are from open-source Delta Lake 4.4.1 on local Spark 4.2.0. MERGE, CDF and table_changes behave the same on Databricks; performance features that only exist there (for example Photon, deletion-vector-based merges, low-shuffle merge) change speed, not results, and weren't measured.

docs.title: The basic upsert
docs.text:
Target table cust (CDF enabled so we can look at it later), and a batch of incoming changes:

CREATE TABLE cust (id INT, name STRING, city STRING) USING delta
TBLPROPERTIES (delta.enableChangeDataFeed = true);
INSERT INTO cust VALUES (1,'Ann','Pune'), (2,'Bo','Oslo'), (3,'Cy','Lima');

-- incoming batch as a view `upd`: (2,'Bo','Bergen'), (3,'Cy','Lima'), (4,'Di','Rome')

MERGE INTO cust t USING upd u ON t.id = u.id
WHEN MATCHED AND t.city <> u.city THEN UPDATE SET *
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT *
WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE THEN DELETE;

The merge returns a one-row summary (local run):

|num_affected_rows|num_updated_rows|num_deleted_rows|num_inserted_rows|
|3                |1               |1               |1                |

and the table now holds:

|id|name|city  |
|2 |Bo  |Bergen|
|3 |Cy  |Lima  |
|4 |Di  |Rome  |

Walk through each clause:

  • Row 2 matched and the city differs → updated.
  • Row 3 matched but nothing changed → the extra condition t.city <> u.city made it skip, so it wasn't rewritten (num_updated_rows is 1, not 2). Always add a change condition to avoid rewriting identical rows.
  • Row 4 is only in the source → inserted.
  • Row 1 is only in the target → deleted by WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE. That clause treats the source as the complete truth, so use it only for full snapshots, never for incremental batches (where "not in the batch" just means "unchanged").

UPDATE SET * and INSERT * map columns by name. Clauses are evaluated in order, and the first one whose condition is true for a row wins.

docs.title: The rule MERGE enforces: one source row per target row
docs.text:
-- source `dup` has two rows for id 2
MERGE INTO cust t USING dup u ON t.id = u.id WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET *;

[DELTA_MULTIPLE_SOURCE_ROW_MATCHING_TARGET_ROW_IN_MERGE] Cannot perform Merge as multiple source rows matched and
attempted to modify the same target row in the Delta table in possibly conflicting ways. ...

Delta refuses rather than guessing which row wins. Deduplicate the source first, usually keeping the latest by a sequence or timestamp:

SELECT * FROM events QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY id ORDER BY seq DESC) = 1

(On a small test set with ids 7 and 8 this kept (7,'b',2) and (8,'c',1).) Note that the error only fires when the duplicate would modify the same target row with a matched clause; duplicates that only reach INSERT aren't caught, and silently insert twice. Deduplicate the source regardless.

docs.title: Slowly changing dimension (Type 2)
docs.text:
To keep history instead of overwriting, close the old row and insert a new one. The standard trick unions the source twice: once with the real key (to find the current row) and once with a NULL key (to force an insert):

MERGE INTO dim d
USING (SELECT c.id AS mk, c.* FROM chg c
       UNION ALL
       SELECT NULL AS mk, c.* FROM chg c JOIN dim x ON x.id = c.id AND x.is_current AND x.city <> c.city) u
ON d.id = u.mk AND d.is_current
WHEN MATCHED AND d.city <> u.city THEN UPDATE SET is_current = false, valid_to = DATE'2026-02-01'
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT (id, city, valid_from, valid_to, is_current)
     VALUES (u.id, u.city, DATE'2026-02-01', NULL, true);

With dim starting as (1,Pune) and (2,Oslo) both current, and a change feed of (1,Mumbai) and (3,Rome), the local result was:

|id|city  |valid_from|valid_to  |is_current|
|1 |Pune  |2026-01-01|2026-02-01|false     |
|1 |Mumbai|2026-02-01|NULL      |true      |
|2 |Oslo  |2026-01-01|NULL      |true      |
|3 |Rome  |2026-02-01|NULL      |true      |

Running the same merge again reported num_affected_rows = 0 and left the table unchanged: the change conditions make it idempotent. That matters because jobs retry. (The hard-coded date is for the demo; use the batch's effective date.)

docs.title: The Python API
docs.text:
from delta.tables import DeltaTable
(DeltaTable.forName(spark, "cust").alias("t")
   .merge(updates.alias("u"), "t.id = u.id")
   .whenMatchedUpdateAll(condition="t.city <> u.city")
   .whenNotMatchedInsertAll()
   .execute())

It is the same operation as the SQL; use whichever fits your codebase. Remember to put an equality on the key in the ON condition, ideally also on a partition or clustering column (below).

docs.title: Change Data Feed
docs.text:
With delta.enableChangeDataFeed = true, every change to the table is also recorded as row-level change events in a hidden _change_data folder (for updates, deletes and merges; pure appends are derivable from the added files).

SELECT id, city, _change_type, _commit_version FROM table_changes('cust', 1)
ORDER BY _commit_version, id, _change_type;

|id|city  |_change_type    |_commit_version|
|1 |Pune  |insert          |1              |
|2 |Oslo  |insert          |1              |
|3 |Lima  |insert          |1              |
|1 |Pune  |delete          |2              |
|2 |Bergen|update_postimage|2              |
|2 |Oslo  |update_preimage |2              |
|4 |Rome  |insert          |2              |

Version 1 is the initial insert; version 2 is the merge: row 1 deleted, row 2 changed (both the old pre-image and the new post-image), row 4 inserted, and row 3 absent because it wasn't touched. Downstream jobs read the feed (spark.read.option("readChangeFeed", "true").option("startingVersion", n), or as a stream) and apply only the delta. Caveats: the feed only exists from the version you enabled it; it uses extra storage; and it's subject to the same VACUUM/log retention as the table.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
A merge runs in (at least) two phases inside one commit:

  1. Find touched files. Join source to target on the ON condition, using file-level statistics to prune files that can't match, and collect the names of target files that contain matching rows. In the local metrics: scanTimeMs and numTargetFilesRemoved -> 2.
  2. Rewrite. Join again, this time producing the new contents of those files: rows updated, rows kept (the numTargetRowsCopied -> 1 in the metrics are untouched rows that lived in a rewritten file), plus inserted rows. Write new files, then commit remove for the old files and add for the new.

Because the whole file is rewritten for one changed row, merges get expensive when the matching rows are scattered across the whole table. The fixes are all about making the first phase prune well: put the clustering or partition column in the ON clause, keep source batches focused, and use deletion vectors where your platform enables them. A merge that sees changes land mid-run fails with the concurrent-write errors from Level 1 · 07, so design for retries.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Duplicate source keys (error, or silent double inserts).
  • No change condition on WHEN MATCHED, rewriting identical rows, producing noise in CDF, and slowing everything.
  • WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE THEN DELETE on incremental batches, deleting everything not in this batch.
  • ON clause without the partition/cluster key, forcing a scan of the whole table.
  • Treating CDF as free history. It must be enabled before the changes happen.
  • Non-deterministic source (random values, current_timestamp() recomputed during rewrite phases) producing inconsistent results; materialize the source first.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Reproduce the first merge. Then change WHEN MATCHED AND t.city <> u.city to plain WHEN MATCHED and compare num_updated_rows, and the CDF output, for row 3.
  2. Insert a second source row for id 4 and run an insert-only merge. What happens? Fix it with a QUALIFY dedupe.
  3. Make the SCD2 merge handle a deleted customer by closing the current row. What extra clause do you need?
  4. Read CDF from version 2 as a DataFrame in Python and use it to keep a second table cust_copy in sync with a second merge.

docs.title: 02 · Schema Enforcement, Evolution & Constraints
docs.text:
A plain Parquet folder accepts any file you drop in. A Delta table doesn't: on every write it checks that the incoming data fits the table's schema and constraints, and rejects the whole commit if it doesn't. That's schema enforcement. Sometimes the schema should change, and Delta supports explicit schema evolution. The edge between the two is where pipelines break or, worse, silently lose data.

What was run

Every error and result here came from open-source Delta Lake 4.4.1 on local Spark 4.2.0. Error text is quoted from the first line of the exception. Databricks adds platform behaviour on top (for example, schema-evolution defaults in pipelines and Auto Loader, and different table features enabled by default), which isn't covered by these runs.

docs.title: Enforcement on write
docs.text:
Target table: tgt (id INT, v STRING). Here is what the local run did to each attempt:

Write Result INSERT ... SELECT 9 AS id, 'z' AS v, 'extra' AS w (extra column) Rejected: [DELTA_METADATA_MISMATCH] A metadata mismatch was detected when writing to the Delta table. INSERT INTO tgt (id) VALUES (10) (missing column) Allowed; v is NULL INSERT INTO tgt VALUES ('abc', 'q') (wrong type, by position) Rejected: [CAST_INVALID_INPUT] The value 'abc' of the type "STRING" cannot be cast to "INT" DataFrame .write.mode("append") with columns (v, id) in a different order Allowed: the DataFrame writer matched by name; row (11, 'm') landed correctly df.write.insertInto("tgt") with columns (v, id) Rejected: insertInto matches by position, so 'n' was cast to INT and failed Append a BIGINT id to an INT column Rejected: [DELTA_FAILED_TO_MERGE_FIELDS] Failed to merge fields 'id' and 'id'

Three rules fall out. Extra columns are rejected; missing columns become NULL (unless NOT NULL); and by-name vs by-position depends on the API. With ANSI mode on (Spark 4's default) the by-position mix-up above fails loudly, but with ANSI off and two columns of the same type it would silently put values in the wrong columns. Prefer by-name APIs (write.saveAsTable/append, INSERT INTO t BY NAME where available) and always name columns.

docs.title: Per write: mergeSchema
docs.text:
(df_with_new_column.write.format("delta").mode("append")
   .option("mergeSchema", "true").save(path))

In the local run, appending (9,'Zed','Rio','gold') with a new tier column added the column to the table; existing rows read back with tier = NULL:

|id|name|city  |tier|
|2 |Bo  |Bergen|NULL|
|3 |Cy  |Lima  |NULL|
|4 |Di  |Rome  |NULL|
|9 |Zed |Rio   |gold|

Schema evolution is itself a commit (the history shows the schema change as part of the WRITE). Older readers that pin an old schema can still read old files; new columns read as NULL for old data.

docs.title: Session-wide: autoMerge
docs.text:
SET spark.databricks.delta.schema.autoMerge.enabled = true;

This makes MERGE (and UPDATE SET */INSERT *) evolve the schema. Use it carefully: it applies to the whole session.

docs.title: The MERGE trap
docs.text:
Without autoMerge, this merge succeeded and silently dropped the new column:

-- source has (id, v, tier); target has (id, v)
MERGE INTO tgt t USING nsrc u ON t.id = u.id WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT *;
-- num_inserted_rows = 1, and the target still has only (id, v)

INSERT * means "insert the target's columns, taken from the source by name", so the extra source column tier was ignored without an error. The data in tier was never written anywhere. If you rely on * clauses and a source gains a column, nothing alerts you unless you compare schemas yourself. A pipeline guard that checks set(source.columns) - set(target.columns) before merging is cheap insurance.

docs.title: Replacing the schema
docs.text:
For a deliberate breaking change (a column's type must change), overwrite with overwriteSchema:

(df.write.format("delta").mode("overwrite").option("overwriteSchema", "true").save(path))

The local run turned id from INT to STRING this way, as a new version of the same table. DESCRIBE HISTORY showed it as an ordinary WRITE. Older versions are expected to keep their old schema when read with time travel (I did not test this), but anything reading the current table now sees strings, so treat it as a breaking change for consumers. Databricks also offers a type widening table feature for safe widenings such as INT to BIGINT without rewriting data; the plain append above failed because that feature wasn't on, and I did not test the feature itself.

docs.title: Renaming and dropping columns: column mapping
docs.text:
ALTER TABLE tgt RENAME COLUMN v TO val;
-- [DELTA_UNSUPPORTED_RENAME_COLUMN] Column rename is not supported for your Delta table.

By default, Delta stores column names inside the Parquet files, so renaming would orphan them. Turn on column mapping, which gives each column a stable physical id:

ALTER TABLE tgt SET TBLPROPERTIES (
  'delta.columnMapping.mode' = 'name',
  'delta.minReaderVersion' = '2', 'delta.minWriterVersion' = '5');
ALTER TABLE tgt RENAME COLUMN v TO val;     -- now succeeds, no data rewritten
ALTER TABLE tgt DROP COLUMN val;            -- also a metadata-only change

Locally both statements worked, and DESCRIBE DETAIL showed the table at reader version 2 / writer version 5 with delta.columnMapping.mode -> name. That protocol bump means older clients can no longer read the table. Check what reads your tables (other engines, old runtimes) before enabling it.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
NOT NULL and CHECK constraints are enforced at write time:

ALTER TABLE chk ADD CONSTRAINT qty_pos CHECK (qty > 0);

If existing rows violate it, Delta refuses to add it (local run: [DELTA_NEW_CHECK_CONSTRAINT_VIOLATION] 1 rows in chk violate the new CHECK constraint (qty > 0)); after deleting the bad row it was accepted, and a later INSERT VALUES (3, 0) was rejected by Delta's invariant check. The constraint shows up as a table property (delta.constraints.qty_pos -> qty > 0). Adding a CHECK also raised the table's writer protocol (to version 3 in the open-source build), another example of constraints being protocol features.

Note: PRIMARY KEY, FOREIGN KEY and UNIQUE constraints on Databricks are informational and not enforced, per the Databricks constraints documentation; only NOT NULL and CHECK stop writes.

Generated columns (GENERATED ALWAYS AS (...)) are a related feature: the value derives from other columns, and a write that provides a conflicting value is rejected. They're handy for deriving a partition or clustering column such as day from a timestamp, so queries that filter on the timestamp still benefit.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
Before committing, a Delta writer compares the incoming DataFrame's schema with the metaData action of the table's current snapshot. If they match, it writes files. If not, it raises unless an evolution option is set, in which case it computes the merged schema and includes a new metaData action in the same commit as the new add files. The check occurs in the writer, not the storage layer, so tools that write Parquet directly into the table folder bypass it, and that is exactly how people corrupt tables.

Constraint checks work similarly: the writer adds a filter expression to the write plan that fails the job if any row evaluates false. NOT NULL is stored in the schema; CHECK constraints are stored as properties in the same metaData action. For the ALTER TABLE ADD CONSTRAINT case, Delta first scans the table to validate existing data, which is why a violation blocked the statement.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Enabling mergeSchema everywhere so that a typo'd column name creates a new column.
  • INSERT * merges that quietly ignore new source columns.
  • Positional inserts (insertInto, INSERT INTO t SELECT ... without column names) reordered by a refactor.
  • Writing Parquet files straight into the Delta folder.
  • Upgrading the protocol (column mapping, new features) without checking all readers.
  • Assuming primary, foreign or unique keys are enforced on Databricks tables.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Reproduce the table above. Try each write, predict the outcome first, and compare with the local run.
  2. Make the MERGE trap fail loudly: write a function that compares source and target columns and raises when the source has extras, then enable autoMerge and watch the column appear.
  3. Enable column mapping on a table with data, rename a column, then use time travel to read an old version. Which column name do you see?
  4. Add a CHECK (amount >= 0) constraint to a table, then attempt a write containing a negative value in a batch of a thousand good rows. Is the good data written? Confirm with the history.

docs.title: 03 · OPTIMIZE, Z-Order & Liquid Clustering
docs.text:
Delta can skip files whose min/max statistics rule out a query's filter, but only if the data is arranged so that each file covers a narrow value range. Random loading order, streaming trickles and many small commits ruin that. OPTIMIZE compacts files, and ZORDER or liquid clustering rearrange rows so skipping works.

What was run, and a caveat about the numbers

The experiments use open-source Delta Lake 4.4.1 on local Spark 4.2.0 with 400,000 synthetic rows. To get multiple files from a small dataset I lowered spark.databricks.delta.optimize.maxFileSize to 200 KB, so absolute file counts (like 143) reflect that artificial setting and would be tiny on real data. The pattern (how many files a filter must read before and after) is what to take away. I measured "candidate files" via DataFrame.inputFiles() after a filtered read, which reports files remaining after file-level skipping on stats, not wall-clock time. Databricks-only behaviour (Photon, Predictive Optimization, automatic liquid-clustering key selection) is from the documentation and wasn't run.

docs.title: Small files and OPTIMIZE
docs.text:
Twenty tiny appends each wrote one small Parquet file. Local result:

files before: 20
OPTIMIZE -> numFilesAdded 1, numFilesRemoved 20
active files after: 1       (but 21 Parquet files still on disk until VACUUM)
after VACUUM RETAIN 0 HOURS: 1 file on disk

OPTIMIZE bin-packs small files into larger ones (target around 1 GB by default for the setting delta.targetFileSize; Databricks can autotune it based on table size and workload). It writes the combined files, then commits add new + remove old as ordinary Delta actions: the old files stay on disk (and travel-able) until VACUUM. It's safe to run while readers and writers are active, because it only rearranges existing data (dataChange = false on its actions, so streaming readers ignore it).

OPTIMIZE sales.orders;                          -- whole table
OPTIMIZE sales.orders WHERE order_date >= '2026-10-01';    -- partition/predicate-limited

docs.title: Data skipping in practice
docs.text:
Test table: 400,000 rows in random order, columns a and b (both uniform 0–999) and a padding column. Query filters: a BETWEEN 10 AND 20 (about 1% of rows) and b BETWEEN 10 AND 20. Count of files that survive skipping:

Layout Total files Files read for filter on a …on b …on a and b Written randomly (16 files) 16 16 16 n/a OPTIMIZE only (no zorder) 16 16 16 n/a OPTIMIZE ... ZORDER BY (a) 143 2 143 n/a OPTIMIZE ... ZORDER BY (a, b) 143 14 18 1

Reading it:

  • Random layout: every file contains values from the whole range 0–999, so its min/max for a is about 0–999 and can never be excluded. Skipping did nothing; statistics only help when files are narrow.
  • Compaction alone didn't help either: the 16 files were already at the (lowered) target size, so there was nothing to merge, and compaction never reorders rows.
  • Z-order by a: each file now covers a thin band of a. The file stats of the last commit showed ranges such as 0–7, 7–14, 14–21, so the filter 10..20 touches two files out of 143.
  • Z-order by (a, b) interleaves both columns. Neither is as good as a dedicated single-column sort (14 and 18 files vs 2), but both filters now skip most of the table, and the combined filter reads just one file. The more columns you Z-order by, the less each one helps, so use a handful at most.

Z-order is a physical clustering technique: it orders rows along a space-filling curve (a Z-curve) so that rows close in all the chosen dimensions land in the same file.

OPTIMIZE sales.events ZORDER BY (customer_id, event_date);

Z-order is not incremental in the simple sense: each OPTIMIZE ZORDER BY run rewrites files that aren't already Z-ordered, and rows you append later are unsorted until the next run. It also needs statistics on the columns chosen (by default only the first 32 columns have statistics; Level 2 · 04), so don't Z-order by a column beyond that, or a long string.

docs.title: Liquid clustering
docs.text:
Liquid clustering is the newer replacement: you declare clustering keys on the table, and OPTIMIZE incrementally clusters data to match. It can't be combined with partitioning or ZORDER on the same table.

CREATE TABLE lc_t (id BIGINT, a INT, b INT, pad STRING) USING delta CLUSTER BY (a);
-- ...loads...
OPTIMIZE lc_t;

Local results, same data and filters:

before OPTIMIZE:   16 files, filter on a reads 16
after OPTIMIZE:    143 files, filter on a reads 3 (of 143), filter on b reads all 143
ALTER TABLE lc_t CLUSTER BY (b);   -- history shows version 'CLUSTER BY'
OPTIMIZE lc_t:     0 files added, 0 removed -> a still 2, b still 143   (nothing re-clustered!)
OPTIMIZE lc_t FULL: 145 added, 143 removed -> a reads 145 (of 145), b reads 3

Two lessons:

  1. CLUSTER BY only declares intent. Until OPTIMIZE runs, newly written files aren't clustered.
  2. Changing the clustering keys does not rewrite existing data. A plain OPTIMIZE after ALTER TABLE ... CLUSTER BY (b) did nothing in my run (0 files added, filters on b still read all files). Only OPTIMIZE ... FULL re-clustered everything. The Databricks documentation says the default behaviour does not cluster previously written data and to use OPTIMIZE ... FULL to force reclustering; this run shows the open-source build behaves the same way. On Databricks, with Predictive Optimization or automatic clustering, parts of this are automated, but check the table's history to see whether it actually happened.

You can change keys at any time without rewriting the table, which is the point of the feature: no re-partitioning migration when query patterns change. CLUSTER BY AUTO (Databricks, Unity Catalog managed tables, per the docs) lets the platform choose keys from query history; that isn't available locally and wasn't tested.

Hive-style partitioning ZORDER Liquid clustering Declared At creation Per OPTIMIZE run On the table (CLUSTER BY) Change later Rewrite table Choose different columns next run ALTER TABLE ... CLUSTER BY (+ OPTIMIZE FULL to apply to old data) High-cardinality columns Bad (too many directories) OK OK Incremental n/a Rewrites unsorted files Yes (clusters new data) Combine with partitions n/a Yes No

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
Skipping is a log operation. Each add action carries minValues/maxValues/nullCount per column (Level 1 · 07). For a filter a BETWEEN 10 AND 20, the reader evaluates "could any row in this file satisfy it?" from the stats and discards files where max < 10 or min > 20 before opening any Parquet. Everything above is therefore about making those ranges narrow.

Z-ordering computes, for each row, a single integer by bit-interleaving the (ranked) values of the chosen columns, sorts rows by that integer, and cuts the sorted stream into files. Rows close in the sort are close in every dimension, so each file covers a small box rather than a whole range. Liquid clustering applies the same idea with a different clustering algorithm (the exact curve is an implementation detail I haven't verified) and tracks per-file clustering state in the log so that each OPTIMIZE only touches files that aren't yet clustered by the current keys, which explains why a changed key doesn't trigger a rewrite until you ask for a full one.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Expecting OPTIMIZE alone to speed up selective filters. Compaction fixes file count; clustering fixes ranges.
  • Z-ordering by many columns or by a low-value column, diluting the benefit.
  • Never re-running OPTIMIZE ZORDER on a table that keeps receiving appends.
  • Changing liquid clustering keys and assuming old data followed.
  • Optimizing a tiny table: the overhead exceeds any benefit.
  • Forgetting VACUUM: OPTIMIZE adds storage until old files are removed.
  • Choosing keys with no statistics (beyond the first 32 columns, or very long strings).

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Re-run the data-skipping experiment with maxFileSize left at the default. What happens to the file counts, and can you still show a difference? (Hint: you may need more rows.)
  2. Z-order by b instead of a and fill in the table row.
  3. Create a liquid-clustered table, change its keys twice, and record numFilesAdded for OPTIMIZE vs OPTIMIZE FULL each time.
  4. For your own largest table, list the top three filter columns in the last month's queries. Which would you cluster on, and why not all three?

docs.title: 04 · Partitioning, File Sizes & Data Skipping
docs.text:
Partitioning is the first performance idea most people learn, and for Delta it's the one most often misused. This lesson measures what partitioning does to file counts and write time, shows when it prunes, and explains which columns get data-skipping statistics.

What was run

All numbers come from open-source Delta Lake 4.4.1 on local Spark 4.2.0 (two cores, shuffle.partitions = 4, 200,000 synthetic rows), writing to a laptop SSD. Sizes and file counts are deterministic enough to trust; write times are laptop-specific and only the ratios mean anything. Databricks' recommendation, per its documentation, is liquid clustering instead of partitioning for most new tables; the platform behaviour wasn't run here.

docs.title: The experiment
docs.text:
The same 200,000 rows (columns id, user_id with about 50,000 distinct values, day with 30 distinct values, and amount) were written three ways:

base.write.format("delta").save(p)                          # no partitioning
base.write.format("delta").partitionBy("day").save(p)       # 30 partitions
base.write.format("delta").partitionBy("user_id").save(p)   # ~50,000 partitions
Layout Data files Total size Average file Write time (this laptop) No partitioning 2 2,125 KB 1,063 KB 5.9 s partitionBy("day") 60 2,580 KB 43 KB 1.0 s partitionBy("user_id") 86,665 105,606 KB 1.2 KB 467 s

Partitioning by the high-cardinality user_id turned 2 MB of data into 50 times more bytes, spread over 86,665 files (about 1.7 files per partition directory, each ~1 KB), and the write took almost eight minutes. Each tiny file carries Parquet footer and metadata overhead that dwarfs its few rows. Every later query now has to list, open and plan around 86,000 files. (The none row's 5.9 s probably includes one-time JVM and Delta warm-up (I didn't isolate it), which would explain why by_day looks faster. Don't read anything into that comparison.)

partitionBy("day") also yielded 60 files for 30 partitions: two shuffle tasks wrote a file into each. That's already tiny (43 KB average). On a real table you'd choose a partition column so each partition holds gigabytes, not kilobytes.

docs.title: What partitioning buys: pruning
docs.text:
Filter on the partition column, and the engine reads only matching directories. For day = '2026-01-05', the plan shows PartitionFilters: [isnotnull(day), (day = 2026-01-05)], and the file count surviving the filter was:

candidate files with day filter:   2 of 60
candidate files with user filter:  59 of 60   (the table is partitioned by day, not user)

So partitioning helps queries on the partition key and does nothing for others, and the second case is worth noticing: data skipping on user_id statistics couldn't exclude files because users are scattered randomly in each day.

docs.title: Generated partition columns
docs.text:
Users filter on timestamps, not on your derived day column. A generated column lets Delta translate one into the other:

CREATE TABLE gp (ts TIMESTAMP, v INT, d DATE GENERATED ALWAYS AS (CAST(ts AS DATE)))
USING delta PARTITIONED BY (d);
-- SELECT ... WHERE ts >= '2026-01-02' AND ts < '2026-01-03'   -> reads partition d = 2026-01-02

In the local run, the timestamp range filter read 1 file of 3: Delta inferred the partition predicate from the generation expression. (This works for expressions Delta knows how to invert, like casts to date and date-part functions.)

docs.title: When to partition at all
docs.text:
Guidance from the numbers above and the Databricks documentation's general direction:

  • Most tables under about a terabyte shouldn't be partitioned. Without partitions you still get data skipping from statistics; with the wrong partitioning you get the small-files blow-up.
  • If you do partition, use a low-cardinality column that is filtered on constantly (typically a date or day), where each partition would hold roughly a gigabyte or more.
  • Never partition by an ID, a free-text field or a timestamp with sub-day precision.
  • Prefer liquid clustering (Lesson 03) for new tables: it handles high-cardinality columns and changing patterns, and can't be mixed with partitioning.
  • Partitioning is also an operational tool (drop a whole partition by deleting a directory's worth of data; limit maintenance to recent partitions), so "date partition for retention" remains a legitimate reason.

docs.title: Statistics: which columns can skip?
docs.text:
Delta stores min/max/null-count for the first 32 columns by default (delta.dataSkippingNumIndexedCols). Local test with the limit set to 2 on a 4-column table:

indexed stats columns:            ['c1', 'c2']
filter c2 > 100  (indexed)      -> 0 files read  (stats prove nothing matches)
filter c4 > 100  (not indexed)  -> 2 files read  (no stats, so it can't exclude anything)

Both queries match zero rows. The difference is whether Delta could prove it from statistics. Practical rules:

  1. Put the columns you filter on within the first 32, or set delta.dataSkippingNumIndexedCols / delta.dataSkippingStatsColumns (Databricks documents the latter for naming specific columns) deliberately.
  2. Move long strings and blobs out of the leading columns: computing stats on them is expensive and rarely useful.
  3. Nested struct fields count as columns for this limit.
  4. Changing the setting only affects files written afterward; recompute stats for old files if needed (Databricks provides a command for this; check the current docs).

docs.title: File sizes
docs.text:
Aim for files of hundreds of MB to about a gigabyte for large tables: big enough to amortize metadata and open costs, small enough to parallelize and to rewrite cheaply in MERGE. Three levers:

Lever Effect OPTIMIZE (Lesson 03) Compacts existing small files Optimized writes / auto compaction (Databricks table properties) Reduce small files at write time. Their availability and defaults differ between Databricks and open-source Delta versions, so check the docs for yours; they weren't run here repartition(n) / coalesce(n) before a write Controls the number of output files from a job you own

Databricks' documentation also describes autotuned target file sizes based on table size, so the "ideal" number moves with the platform; treat the figures here as orders of magnitude.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
A partition column is encoded in the path (day=2026-01-05/part-...parquet), recorded in each add action as partitionValues, and removed from the Parquet file itself. Query planning evaluates partition predicates against the partitionValues in the log (no storage listing needed) and discards non-matching files immediately.

Each partition value requires at least one file per writing task. With many partition values and many tasks, a write of N rows fans out to up to tasks × distinct values files. That's why the user_id write exploded: each of the 4 shuffle tasks wrote a separate file into most of the ~50,000 directories. Skew in the other direction (one giant partition) creates the opposite problem: a single huge task.

Statistics are column-level aggregates stored in the same add action as JSON, computed while the file is written. That is why they cost nothing to read at query time, and why a column without them can't help.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Partitioning by a high-cardinality or ID column. (86,665 files in the experiment.)
  • Over-partitioning on two or three columns "to be safe": the partition count multiplies.
  • Filtering on a timestamp while the table is partitioned by a derived date, with no generated column linking them.
  • Wide tables with filter columns past position 32 and no stats configuration.
  • Compacting without clustering and expecting faster selective queries.
  • Expecting a partition column to behave like an index for other columns.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Reproduce the three layouts with 20,000 rows and 5,000 distinct users (so it finishes quickly). Record file counts and total sizes.
  2. Write the day-partitioned version with repartition("day") first. How many files do you get now, and why?
  3. Create a 40-column table with the filter column in position 35. Show that a selective filter reads all files, then fix it with the table property.
  4. For a table you own, decide: partition, cluster, or neither? Justify with row count, size, and top filter columns.

docs.title: 05 · How Spark Executes: Stages, Shuffles & AQE
docs.text:
You can write Spark for years without looking inside it, until a job runs for six hours and nobody knows why. The vocabulary of the Spark UI and of explain() (job, stage, task, shuffle, Exchange) is the toolkit for finding out. This lesson builds it from real plans.

What was run

Plans and partition counts are from local Spark 4.2.0 + Delta 4.4.1, reading Delta tables of 100,000 and 1,000 rows. Plan operator names are standard Spark; on Databricks with Photon you'll see Photon operators in their place (documented, not run here), and the Spark UI looks different from a local one.

docs.title: The execution hierarchy
docs.text:
• A job is triggered by an action (count, show, a write).
  • A job is divided into stages at every shuffle boundary.
  • A stage is a set of identical tasks, one per data partition, run in parallel on executor cores.
  • A shuffle redistributes rows across the cluster so that rows with the same key end up together (needed for joins, groupings, distinct, repartition, global sorts and window functions).

Narrow operations (filter, select, withColumn, map-style) process each partition independently and are pipelined into one stage. Wide operations require a shuffle: write every partition's output to local disk, then fetch the right slice from every other node. Shuffles are where Spark spends most of its time and fails most often.

docs.title: Reading a physical plan
docs.text:
A.groupBy("k").agg(F.sum("v")).explain()    # A: 100,000 rows read from a Delta table

Local output (AQE disabled for clarity, shortened):

*(2) HashAggregate(keys=[k], functions=[sum(v)])
+- Exchange hashpartitioning(k, 8), ENSURE_REQUIREMENTS
   +- *(1) HashAggregate(keys=[k], functions=[partial_sum(v)])
      +- *(1) ColumnarToRow
         +- FileScan parquet [k,v] ... PartitionFilters: [], PushedFilters: [], ReadSchema: ...

Read bottom to top. The scan reads only k and v (column pruning). Stage 1 (*(1)) does a partial aggregation inside each scan task, so each task pre-sums its own rows. Then Exchange hashpartitioning(k, 8) is the shuffle: rows are routed into 8 partitions by hash of k. Stage 2 (*(2)) merges the partial sums. The partial aggregate before the shuffle is why grouping 100,000 rows into 1,000 groups shuffles roughly 1,000 rows per task, not 100,000. Anywhere you see Exchange, there's a stage boundary and a network/disk cost.

docs.title: Join strategies
docs.text:
Joining a 100,000-row table A to a 1,000-row B, with broadcasting disabled (spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold = -1):

SortMergeJoin [cast(k as bigint)], [k2], Inner
:- Sort [cast(k as bigint) ASC]
:  +- Exchange hashpartitioning(cast(k as bigint), 8)
:     +- Filter isnotnull(k) ... FileScan parquet [id,k,v]
+- Sort [k2 ASC]
   +- Exchange hashpartitioning(k2, 8)
      +- Filter isnotnull(k2) ... FileScan parquet [k2,name]

Both sides are shuffled by the join key (two Exchanges) and sorted, then merged. With the default threshold (10 MB) Spark chose a different plan, because B is tiny:

BroadcastHashJoin [cast(k as bigint)], [k2], Inner, BuildRight
:- Filter isnotnull(k) ... FileScan parquet [id,k,v]
+- BroadcastExchange HashedRelationBroadcastMode(...)
   +- Filter isnotnull(k2) ... FileScan parquet [k2,name]

Here the small side is collected, shipped to every executor, and held as a hash table; the large side is never shuffled. That is the biggest single win in most Spark tuning (Lesson 06 shows when and how to force it).

One more detail in these plans: cast(k as bigint). k is an INT and k2 is a BIGINT, so Spark cast the INT side to match. Mismatched key types force casts on every row, and can prevent the use of statistics or partitioning on the cast column. Join keys should have identical types.

docs.title: Adaptive Query Execution (AQE)
docs.text:
Static plans use guessed sizes. AQE (enabled by default in current Spark and, per its documentation, in Databricks) re-optimizes the plan at shuffle boundaries using the real sizes of the shuffle output. Three main behaviours:

  1. Coalescing shuffle partitions: many small post-shuffle partitions are merged.
  2. Switching join strategy: a sort-merge join becomes a broadcast join if one side turns out to be small.
  3. Skew-join handling: oversized partitions are split (Lesson 06).

Local demonstration: with spark.sql.shuffle.partitions = 200 and the same group-by on 1,000 distinct keys:

AQE off:  result has 200 partitions     (199 mostly empty tasks)
AQE on:   result has 1 partition        (plan shows: AQEShuffleRead coalesced)

The final plan printed AdaptiveSparkPlan isFinalPlan=true, with the Initial Plan (200 shuffle partitions) shown below the Final Plan (AQEShuffleRead coalesced). 200 tasks for a few kilobytes of data would have mostly been scheduling overhead. On Databricks, the documented default for spark.sql.shuffle.partitions is still 200, and setting it to auto enables auto-optimized shuffle, which chooses the number from the query plan and input size (per the AQE documentation).

docs.title: The Spark UI mental model
docs.text:
Whether it's the local UI or the Databricks Spark UI, the workflow is the same:

  1. Jobs tab / SQL tab: find the slow query. The SQL tab shows the plan with row counts and time per operator.
  2. Stage view: look at the task duration distribution. Roughly equal tasks mean healthy parallelism. A maximum far above the median means skew (one task has too much data).
  3. Shuffle read/write sizes: huge shuffle volume relative to input suggests a join or aggregation that could be reduced (filter earlier, broadcast, pre-aggregate).
  4. Spill (memory/disk): tasks that exceed memory write to disk and slow down; fix by more partitions, more memory per core, or less data per task.
  5. GC time high relative to run time: too many objects or too little memory.

I didn't capture UI screenshots because the local runs had the UI disabled; the numbers above come from explain() and partition counts.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
When a job is submitted, the DAG scheduler walks the physical plan backwards from the result, cutting at each shuffle to form stages. Stages are run in dependency order; each stage's tasks go to a task scheduler that places them on executor cores, preferring nodes that already hold the input data. A shuffle write puts each task's output into one file per reducer partition on local disk (or an external shuffle service); the downstream stage's tasks then fetch their partition from every upstream task. If an executor dies, lost shuffle files mean re-running the producing tasks.

AQE adds query stages as materialization points: at each shuffle it finishes the upstream stage, reads its statistics, then re-plans the rest of the query. That's why plans print as AdaptiveSparkPlan with an initial and a final version.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Tuning shuffle.partitions once for all jobs. The right number varies with data volume; prefer AQE and platform defaults over a hard-coded 200 or 2000.
  • Not knowing where the Exchanges are. Each is an opportunity to reduce data first.
  • Joining on mismatched types (INT vs BIGINT, string vs int).
  • Calling repartition(...) reflexively. It forces an extra shuffle.
  • Judging performance on tiny local data. The shape of the plan transfers; the timings don't.
  • Using collect()/toPandas() on a stage's output and blaming Spark for driver memory errors.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Run explain("formatted") on a query with a join, a filter and a group-by. Mark every Exchange and name the key.
  2. Turn AQE off and on for the 200-partition group-by and record the partition counts. Explain the difference in one sentence.
  3. Change the join key type on one side (cast k to string) and compare plans. What changed?
  4. Open the Spark UI of a local session (spark.ui.enabled=true, port 4040) while a join runs and find the stage whose Exchange feeds the join.

docs.title: 06 · Joins, Broadcast & Data Skew
docs.text:
Most slow Spark jobs are slow joins, and most slow joins are slow because of one of three things: a join that shuffles a table it didn't need to, a key that doesn't match well, or skew — one key owning so many rows that a single task does most of the work. This lesson measures each.

What was run

Plans and partition sizes are from local Spark 4.2.0, with a synthetic 400,000-row fact table where 80% of rows share one key, and a 1,001-row dimension. Row counts per partition are exact and reproducible; I didn't measure run times, since a two-core laptop can't show cluster stragglers faithfully. The AQE skew-join result below is a negative result on this tiny dataset and is reported as such.

docs.title: The strategies
docs.text:
Strategy When Spark picks it Cost Broadcast hash join One side is below spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold (10 MB default), or hinted Small side shipped to every executor; large side not shuffled. Fastest Shuffle hash join Hinted, or the planner estimates one side is much smaller Both sides shuffled; a hash table is built on the smaller side per partition Sort-merge join Default for large-large equi-joins Both sides shuffled and sorted; scales to huge inputs; sensitive to skew Broadcast nested loop / cartesian Non-equi joins without keys Quadratic; avoid

You can ask for a strategy with a hint, in SQL or DataFrame code:

from pyspark.sql.functions import broadcast
fact.join(broadcast(dim), "k")

SELECT /*+ BROADCAST(d) */ * FROM f JOIN d ON f.k = d.k;     -- also SHUFFLE_HASH(d), MERGE(d)

The local plans confirmed each hint: BROADCAST(d) produced a BroadcastHashJoin ... BuildRight with a BroadcastExchange over the dimension; SHUFFLE_HASH(d) produced ShuffledHashJoin ... BuildRight; the default with broadcasting disabled produced SortMergeJoin. Broadcasting is only safe for genuinely small tables: a hinted join whose "small" side is a few GB can crash executors with out-of-memory errors, since the whole table is held in memory on every one of them.

Databricks adds optimizer features (for example, dynamic file pruning and runtime filters that skip fact-table data using the dimension's matches) that aren't in plain Spark; they're documented but I couldn't run them.

docs.title: Detecting skew
docs.text:
Skew means the key distribution isn't uniform. First look at the key counts:

fact.groupBy("k").count().orderBy(F.desc("count")).limit(3).collect()
# [Row(k=0, count=319925), Row(k=100, count=109), Row(k=803, count=107)]

One key holds 319,925 of 400,000 rows (80%); the next hundred or so. Now see what that does to a shuffle on k, by counting rows per partition after repartition(8, "k"):

rows per shuffle partition (hash by k):
[8786, 9767, 9941, 10145, 10705, 10761, 10812, 329083]

Seven partitions hold roughly 10,000 rows each and one holds 329,083, about 32 times the others (the hot key plus its hash neighbours). Every row for key 0 must be processed by the same task. On a cluster that task is the straggler: the stage finishes only when it does, other cores sit idle, and it may spill to disk or run out of memory. In the Spark UI you'd see this as one task with a far longer duration and larger shuffle-read size than the median.

Typical sources of skew: NULL or default keys (-1, 'unknown') that pile up, popular entities (one huge customer, a viral product), and time-based keys when everything arrives "today".

docs.title: Fix 1: broadcast the small side
docs.text: If the other side is small enough to broadcast, the fact table isn't shuffled at all, so skew in its keys is irrelevant. This is the first thing to try.

docs.title: Fix 2: handle the hot key separately
docs.text: Filter the hot key out, join it differently (broadcast, or aggregate it directly), and union the results. This is explicit and often the clearest; it needs you to know which keys are hot.

docs.title: Fix 3: salting
docs.text:
Add a random suffix to the fact table's key, replicate the dimension rows across all suffixes, and join on (key, salt). The hot key is split across N partitions:

N = 4
salted = fact.withColumn("salt", (F.rand() * N).cast("int"))
dim_s  = dim.crossJoin(spark.range(0, N).withColumnRenamed("id", "salt"))
joined = salted.join(dim_s, ["k", "salt"])

Local measurement, rows per partition after repartition(8, "k", "salt"):

[9896, 10117, 10392, 10637, 89246, 89482, 89854, 90376]

The 329,083-row partition became four partitions of about 90,000 rows. It isn't perfectly flat (the hot key's four salted slices are still ~9× the others), but the worst task dropped to about 27% of its former size. The result was unchanged: the salted join returned 400,000 rows, the same as the plain join. Costs: the dimension is replicated N times (fine for 1,001 rows, expensive for big dimensions), and N is a tuning parameter. Use a bigger N for hotter keys, and apply salting only to the hot keys when you can.

docs.title: AQE skew handling
docs.text:
The Databricks documentation lists skew-join handling among AQE's features: it detects skewed shuffle partitions in sort-merge and shuffle-hash joins at runtime and splits them into smaller tasks, replicating the other side's matching partition. It's governed by settings including spark.sql.adaptive.skewJoin.enabled, the skewed-partition factor and threshold in bytes.

I tried it on the local data with thresholds lowered (skewedPartitionThresholdInBytes = 64KB, skewedPartitionFactor = 2). It did not trigger: the final plan was a SortMergeJoin without a skew-join marker (isSkew=true absent). A likely reason is that with AQE on and a tiny dataset, the shuffle outputs were too small for the byte thresholds and advisory sizing to classify anything as skewed, but I didn't confirm the cause. The lesson is practical: don't assume AQE fixed your skew; look for the skew marker in the final plan, or compare task durations in the Spark UI.

docs.title: Join correctness checklist
docs.text:
• Type-match keys. INT vs BIGINT created a cast(k as bigint) on every row in the plans above.
  • NULL keys never match in an equi-join (NULL = NULL is not true); use eqNullSafe or <=> if you need them to.
  • Duplicate keys multiply rows. Joining on a non-unique dimension key inflates fact counts silently. Check count before and after: here 400,000 before and 400,000 after.
  • Exploding intermediate joins: filter and aggregate early.
  • approx_count_distinct is a cheap guide for key cardinality: on the fact table it returned 1,026 vs the exact countDistinct of 1,001 (an approximation with about a few percent error by default), useful for deciding whether a key is safe to partition or salt on, and far cheaper than the exact count on big data.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
A shuffle partitions rows with hash(key) mod numPartitions. Equal keys always hash to the same partition, which is what makes joins and groupings possible and also what makes skew inevitable: no hash function can split one key. Salting works by making the effective key (k, salt), which hashes to different partitions.

A broadcast join avoids this by turning the join into a local lookup: the driver collects the small relation, serializes it as a hash table and sends it to every executor (a BroadcastExchange), and each task joins its slice of the large side against it. The cost is memory per executor and driver collection time, which is why Spark gates it with a size threshold.

AQE's skew handling is salting done automatically at runtime, using actual partition sizes: it splits a big shuffle partition into several by map-output ranges, and duplicates the matching partition from the other side for each piece.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Broadcasting a table that isn't small, causing executor OOM.
  • Disabling broadcast globally (-1) after one bad case.
  • Salting everything when only a handful of keys are hot.
  • Ignoring NULL/default keys as the true hot key.
  • Benchmarking skew fixes on tiny data and concluding they don't matter, or that AQE "didn't work".
  • Joining on a non-unique key and not noticing the row count increase.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Reproduce the skew measurement with your own data: generate a table where 50% of rows share one key and print rows per shuffle partition.
  2. Apply salting with N = 2, 4, 16. Record the largest partition for each. Where do returns diminish?
  3. Make the dimension 5 million rows (use spark.range) and decide whether salting or a hot-key-only split is better. Say why.
  4. Search the final plan of a join in your own session for isSkew. If absent, find the stage with the longest task in the Spark UI and compare it with the median.

docs.title: 07 · Structured Streaming & Checkpoints
docs.text:
Structured Streaming treats a stream as an unbounded table: you write the same DataFrame logic as for batch, and Spark runs it incrementally as new data arrives. On Databricks it's the engine under Auto Loader, Lakeflow pipelines and most incremental ETL. Delta is both a great source and a great sink for it.

What was run

Everything below ran on local Spark 4.2.0 + Delta 4.4.1, using a folder of JSON files as the source and Delta tables as sinks, with trigger(availableNow=True) so each run processes what's there and stops. That is deterministic and easy to demonstrate; continuous triggers, cluster restarts and cloud storage failure modes weren't exercised. Auto Loader and Lakeflow are covered in later lessons and were not run.

docs.title: Source → transform → sink
docs.text:
sch = "id INT, user STRING, amt DOUBLE, ts TIMESTAMP"

stream = spark.readStream.schema(sch).json("in/")            # a directory of JSON files, new files = new data
query = (stream.writeStream.format("delta")
         .option("checkpointLocation", "ckpt/")             # REQUIRED for restartable, exactly-once behaviour
         .trigger(availableNow=True)                          # process all available data, then stop
         .start("out/"))                                      # or .toTable("catalog.schema.table")
query.awaitTermination()

Streaming file sources need an explicit schema (or schema inference turned on explicitly), because a stream can't look ahead at data that hasn't arrived.

Triggers control cadence:

Trigger Behaviour default (unspecified) Start the next micro-batch as soon as the previous finishes processingTime="1 minute" Fixed-interval micro-batches availableNow=True Process everything available (possibly in several batches), then stop. Ideal for scheduled "incremental batch" jobs once=True Legacy single-batch version of the above (deprecated in favour of availableNow)

availableNow is the workhorse of cost-efficient pipelines: a job that wakes hourly, processes whatever arrived, and shuts the cluster down, with the checkpoint remembering where it stopped.

docs.title: Checkpoints give you exactly-once
docs.text:
First run, with two JSON rows in in/; second run with no new files; third run after dropping another file with one row. Local results:

run 1  numInputRows 2   batchId 0     -> output table has 2 rows
run 2  numInputRows 0                  -> (no new files: nothing to do)
run 3  numInputRows 1   batchId 1     -> output table has 3 rows

Each run picked up only files it hadn't seen. The checkpoint folder after these runs contained:

ckpt/
├── metadata          # query id
├── offsets/0, 1      # "about to process this range" - written BEFORE each batch
├── commits/0, 1      # "finished this batch"         - written AFTER each batch
└── sources/          # file-source bookkeeping

offsets/1 held the batch's timestamps and a long list of Spark configs (state store settings, for instance) plus the source offsets. Restart logic: if offsets/N exists but commits/N doesn't, the batch is replayed, and Delta's transaction (keyed by the checkpoint's query id and batch id) makes the re-run idempotent, so a crashed batch doesn't double-write. That's what "exactly-once" means here: at-least-once reading + idempotent Delta writes.

docs.title: What happens if you lose the checkpoint
docs.text:
I deleted ckpt/ and ran the same query again:

after deleting checkpoint, rows written again: 3     total rows in output: 6

 id | c
  1 | 2
  2 | 2
  3 | 2

Without its checkpoint the query has no memory, treats every file as new, and appends everything again: every id now appears twice. The checkpoint is state, as important as data. Treat it like a database file: store it durably, never share one between queries, never edit it, and don't delete it to "fix" a stuck stream without understanding the duplicate consequence. (Starting a fresh checkpoint on purpose, with a plan for the overlap, is how you replay.)

Changing a query's logic can also make the old checkpoint incompatible (for stateful operators especially), which forces the same choice between reprocessing and a migration plan.

docs.title: Time, windows and watermarks
docs.text:
An aggregation like "revenue per 10-minute window" must decide when a window is finished, otherwise it keeps state forever and can never emit a final result in append mode. A watermark says how late data may arrive:

agg = (stream.withWatermark("ts", "5 minutes")
             .groupBy(F.window("ts", "10 minutes"), "user")
             .agg(F.sum("amt").alias("t")))
agg.writeStream.format("delta").outputMode("append")...

The test data had events up to 10:09 in the first window, and one at 10:20. Output (window start, user, total):

2026-01-01 10:00:00   a   8.0     (5 + 1 + 2)
2026-01-01 10:00:00   b   7.0

The 10:00–10:10 window was emitted, but the window containing the 10:20 event was not: the watermark is the maximum event time seen minus 5 minutes (10:15), which has passed the end of 10:00–10:10 but not of the window containing 10:20, so that window is still open. That's correct behaviour, and surprises everyone once: the last window of a quiet stream may never appear until later events advance the watermark. Events arriving later than the watermark for a closed window are dropped from the aggregate. Pick the watermark by measuring real lateness, not by guessing.

Output modes: append (only finalized rows; needs a watermark for aggregations), update (changed rows), complete (whole result table every batch; small aggregates only).

docs.title: Upserts with foreachBatch
docs.text:
When the sink must be a MERGE (Lesson 01), use foreachBatch, which hands you each micro-batch as an ordinary DataFrame:

def upsert(batch_df, batch_id):
    d = batch_df.dropDuplicates(["id"])                       # MERGE needs one source row per key
    (DeltaTable.forPath(spark, "tgt").alias("t")
        .merge(d.alias("s"), "t.id = s.id")
        .whenMatchedUpdateAll().whenNotMatchedInsertAll().execute())

(stream.writeStream.foreachBatch(upsert)
       .option("checkpointLocation", "ck3/").trigger(availableNow=True).start())

Two runs over the same input gave tgt rows 5 both times: the merge is idempotent, so the second run (when the checkpoint said everything was processed anyway) added nothing. foreachBatch gives at-least-once delivery to your function, so the function itself must be idempotent (merge on a key, or use batch_id to deduplicate writes to non-Delta sinks).

docs.title: Reading a Delta table as a stream
docs.text:
spark.readStream.table("bronze_orders")                     # new commits become new micro-batches
spark.readStream.option("skipChangeCommits", "true").table("bronze_orders")   # tolerate updates/deletes upstream

A Delta streaming source reads appended data.
