If the upstream table is updated or deleted in place (a MERGE, DELETE or RESTORE), a plain stream fails when it meets a commit that changes existing data, since it would otherwise re-emit rewritten files as new rows. Options: skipChangeCommits (ignore those commits), or read the Change Data Feed (Lesson 01) to see deletes and updates properly. Compaction commits from OPTIMIZE are marked dataChange = false and are ignored.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
Each micro-batch is a normal Spark job. The driver asks every source for new offsets (new files, new Delta versions, Kafka offsets), records the planned range in offsets/N in the checkpoint, runs the incremental query plan over just that range (including state for aggregations and joins, stored in a state store such as RocksDB and snapshotted to the checkpoint), writes to the sink, then records commits/N. Failure between "planned" and "committed" means replay of the same range, which the idempotent sink absorbs.

The Delta sink achieves idempotence with transaction identifiers: each commit includes a txn action (query id, batch id), and before writing batch N the sink checks the log for an existing txn with that id.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Deleting or moving the checkpoint (duplicates, as shown).
  • Sharing one checkpoint between two queries.
  • No watermark on a stateful query, so state grows without bound.
  • Expecting the final window to emit while the stream is quiet.
  • Non-idempotent foreachBatch code (appending to a database without keys).
  • A continuous trigger on an all-purpose cluster that never terminates, billing around the clock for tiny volumes (consider availableNow on a schedule).
  • Reading an updated Delta table as a stream without skipChangeCommits or CDF.
  • Many tiny micro-batches producing many small files (compact and tune triggers).

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Reproduce the three runs and inspect offsets/ and commits/ after each. Delete only commits/1 and rerun. What happens, and why is the output still correct?
  2. Remove the watermark from the windowed query and try outputMode("append"). What error does Spark raise?
  3. Add a duplicate row to a new input file and show that the foreachBatch upsert collapses it, while the plain Delta sink would append it.
  4. Write a 10-line plan: a pipeline running hourly on availableNow, with checkpoint location, failure retry, and what you'd alert on.

docs.title: 08 · Auto Loader: Incremental File Ingestion
docs.text:
Data from outside the lakehouse mostly arrives as files: exports dropped by partners, logs shipped from applications, CDC dumps from databases. Auto Loader is Databricks' answer to "ingest each new file exactly once, without listing a million-file directory every minute, and without breaking when the source adds a column."

What was run, and what wasn't

Auto Loader (cloudFiles) exists only on Databricks, and was not run for this lesson. Everything about its options and behaviour comes from the Databricks documentation (October 2026). What I did run locally is (a) the plain Structured Streaming file source and checkpoint behaviour from Lesson 07, which is the mechanism Auto Loader builds on, and (b) a small Spark experiment, below, that is an analogue of the rescued-data column, with results that differ from Auto Loader in an instructive way. Code samples here follow the documentation but are untested.

docs.title: The basic pattern
docs.text:
(spark.readStream
   .format("cloudFiles")
   .option("cloudFiles.format", "json")
   .option("cloudFiles.schemaLocation", "/Volumes/main/raw/_schemas/orders")   # enables inference + evolution
   .load("/Volumes/main/raw/landing/orders/")
 .writeStream
   .option("checkpointLocation", "/Volumes/main/raw/_checkpoints/orders")
   .trigger(availableNow=True)
   .toTable("main.bronze.orders"))

cloudFiles is a Structured Streaming source. The checkpoint and trigger behave exactly as in Lesson 07, so the pipeline runs incrementally on a schedule (availableNow) or continuously. Per the documentation, Auto Loader supports S3, ADLS, GCS and Unity Catalog volumes as locations, and these formats: JSON, CSV, XML, Parquet, Avro, ORC, text and binary files. In a Lakeflow pipeline (Level 3 · 06) the schema and checkpoint locations are managed for you.

How progress is tracked: discovered files' metadata is persisted in a RocksDB key-value store in the checkpoint location, which is how a file already ingested is skipped even if the stream restarts. Auto Loader doesn't guarantee the order in which files are processed, so design downstream logic (like MERGE with sequence numbers) to cope with out-of-order arrival.

docs.title: Finding new files: two modes
docs.text:
Directory listing (default) File notification (recommended) How Lists the input directory each trigger Subscribes to storage events through a queue; reads the queue Setup None beyond read access Notification/queue services, or "file events" on a Unity Catalog external location Scales with Number of files in the directory Number of new files

The documentation recommends file notification mode with file events for most workloads, and states you can switch modes across restarts while keeping exactly-once guarantees. Directory listing is fine for small, slow landing zones, and has an optimization for lexically ordered file names (like date-prefixed paths).

docs.title: Schema inference and evolution
docs.text:
Pointing Auto Loader at a schemaLocation makes it infer the schema, store it in a _schemas folder, and evolve it. Facts from the documentation:

  • It samples the first 50 GB or 1,000 files, whichever limit is crossed first, to infer the schema.
  • For text formats that don't encode types (JSON, CSV, XML), it infers every column as string (including nested JSON fields) to avoid type-mismatch failures. Set cloudFiles.inferColumnTypes to true for Spark-style type inference. Parquet and Avro keep their encoded types.
  • You can fix types with schema hints (cloudFiles.schemaHints: "id BIGINT, amount DECIMAL(10,2)").
  • Rescue: unexpected data goes to a _rescued_data column.

When the source gains a column, what happens depends on cloudFiles.schemaEvolutionMode:

Mode Behaviour on a new column addNewColumns (default when no schema is given) Stream fails with UnknownFieldException after Auto Loader adds the column to the stored schema; restarting resumes with the new schema addNewColumnsWithTypeWidening As above, plus safe widenings (int to long); unsupported type changes go to the rescued column. Public Preview per the docs, on recent runtimes rescue Never evolves; the stream doesn't fail; new columns land in _rescued_data failOnNewColumns Fails and stays failed until you update the schema or remove the file none (default when you provide a schema) No evolution

The "fail then restart" design surprises people: a source schema change stops your job once on purpose, so the production recipe is a Lakeflow Job with automatic retries (the docs recommend this) that restarts the stream.

docs.title: A local analogue of the rescued data column (and where it differs)
docs.text:
The rescued-data idea is: never lose a value that didn't fit the schema. I tried the closest thing available in plain Spark: read three JSON lines with a typed schema and a corrupt-record column, on local Spark 4.2.0:

{"id":1,"amt":"12.5","city":"Pune"}
{"id":2,"amt":"abc","city":"Oslo","coupon":"X1"}
{"id":"three","amt":"7","city":"Rome"}

sch = "id INT, amt DOUBLE, city STRING, _rescued STRING"
spark.read.schema(sch).option("columnNameOfCorruptRecord", "_rescued").json(path).show(truncate=False)

|id  |amt |city|_rescued                                        |
|1   |NULL|Pune|{"id":1,"amt":"12.5","city":"Pune"}             |
|2   |NULL|Oslo|{"id":2,"amt":"abc","city":"Oslo","coupon":"X1"}|
|NULL|NULL|Rome|{"id":"three","amt":"7","city":"Rome"}          |

This is not Auto Loader behaviour, and the difference is the point. Plain Spark's JSON reader, given a DOUBLE column and a JSON string "12.5", treated the whole record as corrupt: amt became NULL even for the valid-looking "12.5", and the record was preserved only as raw text. Auto Loader's rescued data column, per the docs, captures the column(s) that didn't match (and any new/unexpected columns) in a JSON blob while the rest of the row parses normally. The lesson for a plain Spark pipeline: types in JSON are strict, so an upstream that sends numbers as strings can null whole rows. Ingest as strings first (what Auto Loader's default inference does), then cast deliberately in the silver layer with try_cast. A regular DataFrame way to find unexpected keys is from_json(value, "map<string,string>") and map_filter for keys outside the known list, which on the same data isolated {coupon -> X1}.

docs.title: Production configuration notes (from the docs)
docs.text:
• One checkpoint per ingestion workload. Two source locations loading into one table need two streams.
  • Source data retention: Auto Loader can archive or delete files after ingestion to keep listing fast and storage small. Use it or you'll have millions of files in the landing area.
  • Backfill vs incremental: the first run processes existing files too (cloudFiles.includeExistingFiles defaults to true per the documentation), so the first run of a large directory is a bulk load.
  • Monitoring: Auto Loader exposes file-level state you can query (the docs describe functions such as cloud_files_state) and stream metrics for backlog.
  • COPY INTO is the older SQL command for idempotent file loading; the docs generally recommend Auto Loader or pipelines for new work, but COPY INTO is simpler for small, one-off loads.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
Auto Loader is a Structured Streaming source that replaces "list the directory and diff" with a cheaper discovery mechanism. In listing mode it lists the path each micro-batch and compares with RocksDB state in the checkpoint; in notification mode it drains a queue of object-created events (with file events, via an event service tied to the Unity Catalog external location) and doesn't list at all. For each discovered file it records its path and modification metadata; the micro-batch's offset is then "the set of files" and the usual checkpoint/commit protocol from Lesson 07 makes the delivery exactly-once into Delta.

Schema inference runs before the first batch, over a sample, and then again on each micro-batch's data when new columns appear, which is when the stored schema (a versioned file in _schemas) is updated.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Assuming file order. Out-of-order arrival is normal.
  • Letting the landing directory grow forever (slow listing, large state).
  • Treating the evolution failure as an outage. It's by design; make the job restart itself.
  • Inferring types from a sample and being surprised later; prefer all-strings in bronze plus casts in silver, or explicit schema hints for critical columns.
  • Sharing a checkpoint between loads or deleting it (full re-ingestion, as Lesson 07's duplicate demo showed).
  • Forgetting the rescued column downstream; if you never look at _rescued_data, you never see bad data.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. (Local) Re-run the three-line JSON example. Change amt to STRING in the schema and see which rows now parse. What would you do downstream to convert safely?
  2. (Local) Using Lesson 07's pattern, build a "poor man's Auto Loader": a streaming file source with a checkpoint, availableNow, and an all-strings schema. Add a new column to a later file and see what the plain source does.
  3. (Workspace) Create an Auto Loader stream on a volume with schemaEvolutionMode = addNewColumns, add a new field to the JSON, and record the failure and the restart behaviour.
  4. Decide, for a landing zone receiving 50 files per hour versus 5 million per day, which detection mode you'd use and why.

docs.title: 09 · The Medallion Architecture
docs.text:
"Medallion" is Databricks' name for organizing a lakehouse into three quality layers: bronze (raw), silver (cleaned and conformed) and gold (business-ready). The names are marketing; the idea is old and sound — never overwrite the raw data, put validation in one place, and give consumers a stable, trustworthy layer. This lesson is about what each layer must guarantee, because that's what decides where a given piece of logic belongs.

What was run

The numbers in this lesson come from the Level 2 project (next lesson): an incremental pipeline on local Spark 4.2.0 + Delta 4.4.1 with synthetic events (seeded random data, so results are reproducible but not "real"). Platform features that automate medallion pipelines (Lakeflow pipelines with expectations, streaming tables, materialized views; Level 3 · 06) are described, not run.

docs.title: The three layers
docs.text: Bronze Silver Gold Purpose Faithful, replayable copy of the source Clean, typed, deduplicated, conformed entities Aggregates and models shaped for consumers Schema Source schema, usually all strings + lineage columns Declared, strongly typed Business terms, star schemas, KPIs Write pattern Append only (never update) Upsert (MERGE) / incremental Rebuild or incremental aggregate Quality rule Don't lose anything, don't fail on bad data Enforce types and keys; quarantine failures Reconcile to silver; stable definitions Audience Data engineers Engineers, analysts, data scientists BI, dashboards, ML features, executives

docs.title: Bronze: capture everything
docs.text: Bronze answers "what exactly did the source send, and when?" Keep fields as strings so no value can fail a type cast; add lineage columns such as _src_file and _ingested_at; append only. If anything downstream is wrong, you can rebuild silver and gold from bronze without going back to the source system (which may no longer have the data). In the project, bronze after day 1 held 43 rows from a file with 40 real events, 1 exact duplicate event and 2 malformed rows: all 43 were kept.

docs.title: Silver: where data becomes trustworthy
docs.text:
Silver does the cleaning that every consumer would otherwise redo differently:

  1. Type with try_cast so bad values become NULL instead of failing the batch.
  2. Validate (non-negative amount, parseable timestamp, key present).
  3. Quarantine rejects with a reason instead of dropping them.
  4. Deduplicate on the business key (latest ingestion wins).
  5. Upsert with MERGE, with a change condition so unchanged rows aren't rewritten.

In the project, day 1 produced silver 40 (43 − 1 duplicate − 2 quarantined), and quarantine holding the unparseable amount oops and the negative amount -5 with their raw values and a reason. Rejects are data too; someone has to look at them.

Day 2 added 20 new events, a correction to an earlier event (same id, new amount 99.99) and a late event timestamped on day 1. Bronze grew by 22 rows (65 total) and silver by 21 (61), because the correction updated the existing silver row rather than adding one: SELECT amount FROM silver_events WHERE event_id = 5 returned 99.99. Bronze still contains both versions, which is exactly the audit trail you want.

docs.title: Gold: shaped for questions
docs.text:
Gold tables are defined in business terms and kept small and fast: daily revenue per customer, active users per week, a fact table joined to its dimensions. In the project:

|day       |orders|revenue|
|2026-04-01|41    |1682.49|
|2026-04-02|20    |569.11 |

Day 1 shows 41 orders even though its file held 40 events: the late event arrived on day 2 but belongs to day 1, and gold, which is rebuilt from silver, put it where it belongs. A pipeline that aggregated only the newest file would have missed it. That is the practical reason gold is derived from silver state rather than from "today's batch".

docs.title: Reconciliation: the cheapest test you have
docs.text:
After each run, check that layers agree:

silver_total = spark.sql("SELECT SUM(amount) FROM silver_events").collect()[0][0]
gold_total   = spark.sql("SELECT SUM(revenue) + SUM(refunds) FROM gold_daily_revenue").collect()[0][0]
assert silver_total == gold_total          # local run: both 2688.03

And the row-count identity per run: bronze = silver + quarantine + duplicates removed. Day 1: 43 = 40 + 2 + 1. Checks like these catch dropped files, double loads, join explosions and filter mistakes before a dashboard does.

docs.title: Idempotence and replays
docs.text: Re-running every stage with no new files changed nothing (bronze 65, silver 61, quarantine 2, gold 12 before and after). Each stage is safe to retry because bronze uses a checkpoint (Lesson 07), silver uses MERGE on a key (Lesson 01) and only writes quarantine rows for batches it actually processes, and gold is rebuilt from scratch. If you can't re-run a stage safely, you'll eventually have a duplicate-data incident. One known gap in the project is worth naming: if the silver batch crashes after appending to quarantine but before its merge commits, the replay would append those quarantine rows again. A production design would give quarantine rows a deterministic key, or merge them too.

docs.title: Variations you'll see
docs.text:
• More layers. "Raw / base / curated / marts" is the same idea with more steps; don't add a layer without a rule it enforces.
  • Streaming vs batch per layer. Bronze often streams (availableNow or continuous); gold is often a materialized view or scheduled SQL.
  • Gold per team. Different consumers need different shapes; they all read the same silver.
  • Data products: in Unity Catalog each layer typically gets its own schema (or catalog) with different permissions: engineers write bronze, analysts only read gold (Level 3).
  • Materialized views and streaming tables (Databricks, Level 3 · 06) can implement silver/gold declaratively with expectations, instead of hand-written foreachBatch code.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
The pattern works because Delta gives each layer transactional tables and a change history. Each layer reads the previous one as a stream of committed changes (reading bronze with readStream.table(...), so only new commits are processed) or as a snapshot (gold reading silver). Because commits are atomic, a downstream reader never sees half of an upstream batch. And because bronze is immutable and append-only, the entire chain can be recomputed, which is the real safety net: fix the silver logic, truncate silver and gold, restart from bronze with a new checkpoint.

Backfills and corrections follow from this. A bug found after a month is fixed by changing the code and replaying; it's not fixed by hand-editing tables. That requires bronze retention longer than your longest plausible bug.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Cleaning in bronze, destroying the evidence of what the source sent.
  • Dropping bad rows silently instead of quarantining them with a reason.
  • Validating in gold or in dashboards, so each report invents its own rules.
  • Aggregating only the newest batch and missing late or corrected data.
  • Overwriting silver with each batch instead of merging.
  • No reconciliation checks, so a layer can silently drift from the one before it.
  • Treating the medallion as mandatory. A small, one-off analysis doesn't need three tables.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. For a data source you know, list the fields you would keep as strings in bronze and the cast and validation rule for each in silver.
  2. Design the quarantine table schema so that reprocessing the same bad record does not duplicate it.
  3. Explain what would go wrong if gold were computed as "sum of today's silver changes added to yesterday's gold" when a correction arrives for an old event. How would you handle it instead?
  4. Write the reconciliation checks you'd run after each pipeline execution, with the error you'd raise.

docs.title: 10 · Project — A Bronze/Silver/Gold Pipeline
docs.text:
This project pulls Level 2 together: files land in a folder, a stream ingests them to bronze, a foreachBatch merge maintains a typed and deduplicated silver table with a quarantine for rejects, and a gold table aggregates daily revenue. You'll run it across two "days" of data that include a duplicate, malformed rows, a correction and a late event, then re-run it with no new data to prove it is idempotent.

What was run

The script below was executed as shown on local Spark 4.2.0 + Delta Lake 4.4.1 (Python 3.12), and the outputs in this lesson are copied from that run. The data is synthetic (seeded random numbers). On Databricks you'd replace readStream.json(LAND) with Auto Loader on a volume (Lesson 08), local table names with Unity Catalog names, and the hand-written steps with a Lakeflow pipeline if you prefer declarative code (Level 3 · 06). Those substitutions were not run.

docs.title: The task
docs.text:
1. Bronze bronze_events: ingest JSON files incrementally; keep every field as a string; add _src_file and _ingested_at; append only.
  2. Silver silver_events: typed (INT, DECIMAL(10,2), TIMESTAMP), one row per event_id (latest ingestion wins), updated by MERGE. Rows that can't be typed or have negative amounts go to quarantine_events with a reason.
  3. Gold gold_daily_revenue: per day and customer: order count, revenue (status ok), refunds.
  4. Run day 1 (40 events + 1 duplicate + 1 non-numeric amount + 1 negative amount), then day 2 (20 new events + a correction of event 5 to 99.99 + a late event for day 1), then re-run with no new files.

docs.title: The script
docs.text:
"""Level 2 project: incremental medallion pipeline (local Spark + Delta). Run twice-over with new files to see incrementality."""
import json, pathlib, shutil, random
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession, functions as F
from pyspark.sql.window import Window
from delta import configure_spark_with_delta_pip, DeltaTable

ROOT = pathlib.Path("medallion"); shutil.rmtree(ROOT, ignore_errors=True); (ROOT / "landing").mkdir(parents=True)
b = (SparkSession.builder.master("local[2]").appName("proj2")
     .config("spark.sql.extensions", "io.delta.sql.DeltaSparkSessionExtension")
     .config("spark.sql.catalog.spark_catalog", "org.apache.spark.sql.delta.catalog.DeltaCatalog")
     .config("spark.sql.shuffle.partitions", "4").config("spark.ui.enabled", "false")
     .config("spark.sql.warehouse.dir", str(ROOT / "wh")))
spark = configure_spark_with_delta_pip(b).getOrCreate(); spark.sparkContext.setLogLevel("ERROR")
LAND = str(ROOT / "landing"); CK = ROOT / "checkpoints"

def drop_file(n, events):
    with open(f"{LAND}/events_{n}.json", "w") as f:
        for e in events: f.write(json.dumps(e) + "\n")

random.seed(11)
def make(first_id, n, day):
    out = []
    for i in range(first_id, first_id + n):
        out.append({"event_id": i, "customer": f"C{random.randint(1,6):02d}", "amount": str(round(random.uniform(5, 90), 2)),
                    "event_ts": f"{day}T{random.randint(0,23):02d}:{random.randint(0,59):02d}:00", "status": random.choice(["ok", "ok", "ok", "refund"])})
    return out

# --- BRONZE: raw, all strings, append-only, plus lineage columns
spark.sql("CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS bronze_events (event_id STRING, customer STRING, amount STRING, event_ts STRING, status STRING, _src_file STRING, _ingested_at TIMESTAMP) USING delta")
def run_bronze():
    s = (spark.readStream.schema("event_id STRING, customer STRING, amount STRING, event_ts STRING, status STRING").json(LAND)
         .withColumn("_src_file", F.input_file_name()).withColumn("_ingested_at", F.current_timestamp()))
    q = s.writeStream.format("delta").option("checkpointLocation", str(CK / "bronze")).trigger(availableNow=True).toTable("bronze_events")
    q.awaitTermination()

# --- SILVER: typed, deduplicated by event_id (latest ingest wins), bad rows quarantined
spark.sql("""CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS silver_events (event_id INT, customer STRING, amount DECIMAL(10,2), event_ts TIMESTAMP, status STRING) USING delta""")
spark.sql("CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS quarantine_events (event_id STRING, reason STRING, raw_amount STRING, raw_ts STRING) USING delta")
def silver_batch(df, batch_id):
    typed = (df.select("event_id", "customer", "status", "amount", "event_ts", "_ingested_at")
               .withColumn("e_id", F.expr("try_cast(event_id AS INT)")).withColumn("amt", F.expr("try_cast(amount AS DECIMAL(10,2))"))
               .withColumn("ts", F.expr("try_cast(event_ts AS TIMESTAMP)")))
    bad = typed.filter("e_id IS NULL OR amt IS NULL OR ts IS NULL OR amt < 0")
    bad.select("event_id", F.lit("unparseable or negative").alias("reason"), F.col("amount").alias("raw_amount"), F.col("event_ts").alias("raw_ts")) \
       .write.format("delta").mode("append").saveAsTable("quarantine_events")
    good = (typed.filter("e_id IS NOT NULL AND amt IS NOT NULL AND ts IS NOT NULL AND amt >= 0")
            .withColumn("rn", F.row_number().over(Window.partitionBy("e_id").orderBy(F.col("_ingested_at").desc())))
            .filter("rn = 1").select(F.col("e_id").alias("event_id"), "customer", F.col("amt").alias("amount"), F.col("ts").alias("event_ts"), "status"))
    (DeltaTable.forName(spark, "silver_events").alias("t").merge(good.alias("s"), "t.event_id = s.event_id")
        .whenMatchedUpdateAll(condition="t.amount <> s.amount OR t.status <> s.status OR t.customer <> s.customer OR t.event_ts <> s.event_ts")
        .whenNotMatchedInsertAll().execute())
def run_silver():
    q = (spark.readStream.option("skipChangeCommits", "true").table("bronze_events").writeStream.foreachBatch(silver_batch)
         .option("checkpointLocation", str(CK / "silver")).trigger(availableNow=True).start()); q.awaitTermination()

# --- GOLD: daily revenue by customer, recomputed from silver (small) as a table
def run_gold():
    spark.sql("""CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE gold_daily_revenue USING delta AS
      SELECT CAST(event_ts AS DATE) AS day, customer, COUNT(*) AS orders, SUM(CASE WHEN status='ok' THEN amount ELSE 0 END) AS revenue,
             SUM(CASE WHEN status='refund' THEN amount ELSE 0 END) AS refunds
      FROM silver_events GROUP BY ALL""")

def counts(label):
    c = {t: spark.table(t).count() for t in ["bronze_events", "silver_events", "quarantine_events", "gold_daily_revenue"] if spark.catalog.tableExists(t)}
    print(label, c)

# Day 1
ev = make(1, 40, "2026-04-01"); ev.append(dict(ev[3])); ev.append({"event_id": "x", "customer": "C01", "amount": "oops", "event_ts": "2026-04-01T09:00:00", "status": "ok"})
ev.append({"event_id": 41, "customer": "C02", "amount": "-5", "event_ts": "2026-04-01T09:00:00", "status": "ok"})
drop_file(1, ev); run_bronze(); run_silver(); run_gold(); counts("after day 1:")
# Day 2: 20 new events + a correction to event 5 (new amount) + a late event for day 1
ev2 = make(42, 20, "2026-04-02"); fix = dict(ev[4]); fix["amount"] = "99.99"; ev2.append(fix)
late = {"event_id": 62, "customer": "C03", "amount": "10.00", "event_ts": "2026-04-01T23:30:00", "status": "ok"}; ev2.append(late)
drop_file(2, ev2); run_bronze(); run_silver(); run_gold(); counts("after day 2:")
# idempotence: run everything again with no new files
run_bronze(); run_silver(); run_gold(); counts("re-run, no new data:")
spark.sql("SELECT event_id, amount FROM silver_events WHERE event_id = 5").show()
spark.sql("SELECT * FROM quarantine_events").show(truncate=False)
spark.sql("SELECT * FROM gold_daily_revenue ORDER BY day, customer LIMIT 4").show()
spark.sql("SELECT day, SUM(orders) orders, ROUND(SUM(revenue),2) revenue FROM gold_daily_revenue GROUP BY day ORDER BY day").show()
# reconciliation: silver sum == gold sum
a = spark.sql("SELECT SUM(amount) FROM silver_events").collect()[0][0]; g = spark.sql("SELECT SUM(revenue)+SUM(refunds) FROM gold_daily_revenue").collect()[0][0]
print("reconciles:", a == g, a, g)
spark.sql("DESCRIBE HISTORY silver_events").select("version", "operation").show()

Run it in an empty folder with the Level 1 environment (pip install pyspark delta-spark, PYSPARK_PYTHON set).

docs.title: Expected output
docs.text:
after day 1: {'bronze_events': 43, 'silver_events': 40, 'quarantine_events': 2, 'gold_daily_revenue': 6}
after day 2: {'bronze_events': 65, 'silver_events': 61, 'quarantine_events': 2, 'gold_daily_revenue': 12}
re-run, no new data: {'bronze_events': 65, 'silver_events': 61, 'quarantine_events': 2, 'gold_daily_revenue': 12}

Check the arithmetic: day 1 has 40 + 1 + 2 = 43 bronze rows; silver = 43 − 1 duplicate − 2 quarantined = 40. Day 2 adds 22 bronze rows (20 new, the correction, the late event); silver gains 21, because the correction updates a row instead of inserting one. The re-run changes nothing anywhere.

+--------+------+
|event_id|amount|
+--------+------+
|       5| 99.99|      <- the correction reached silver

+--------+-----------------------+----------+-------------------+
|event_id|reason                 |raw_amount|raw_ts             |
+--------+-----------------------+----------+-------------------+
|x       |unparseable or negative|oops      |2026-04-01T09:00:00|
|41      |unparseable or negative|-5        |2026-04-01T09:00:00|
+--------+-----------------------+----------+-------------------+

+----------+------+-------+
|       day|orders|revenue|
+----------+------+-------+
|2026-04-01|    41|1682.49|      <- 40 day-1 events + the late event that arrived on day 2
|2026-04-02|    20| 569.11|
+----------+------+-------+

reconciles: True 2688.03 2688.03

and the silver history shows two MERGE commits (one per day) after CREATE TABLE. Because the second silver run had no new bronze rows, it added no commit.

docs.title: What to notice
docs.text:
1. skipChangeCommits. Silver streams from bronze, which is append-only, so it isn't strictly needed here; it is included because the moment anyone runs a DELETE on bronze (for GDPR, say), a plain stream would fail.
  2. try_cast, not cast. With ANSI mode on (the default in Spark 4), cast('oops' AS DECIMAL) raises an error that would fail the whole batch. try_cast returns NULL so the row can be routed to quarantine.
  3. Dedupe inside the batch, then merge. MERGE rejects multiple source rows per key (Level 2 · 01). The window row_number() keeps the latest ingest per event_id.
  4. The change condition in whenMatchedUpdateAll. Without it every re-delivered duplicate would rewrite a file.
  5. Gold from silver, not from the batch. The late event landed in the right day because gold is rebuilt from silver state.
  6. A gap I left in on purpose. If the silver step crashes after writing quarantine rows but before the merge commits, a replay will append those quarantine rows a second time. Fix it as Exercise 2 asks.
  7. Development friction worth knowing about. My first run failed with The input source(parquet) is different from the table bronze_events's data source provider(delta): writeStream.toTable(...) defaults to Parquet unless you set .format("delta"). On Databricks, Delta is the default, but explicit is safer.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: Each stage is a separate availableNow stream with its own checkpoint. Stopping and restarting the script is safe because every stream's checkpoint records the last committed batch, and every sink is idempotent (Delta's txn bookkeeping for bronze, MERGE for silver, CREATE OR REPLACE for gold). The silver stream reads bronze as an incremental source by remembering the last bronze table version it processed; only commits after that version produce new rows. That is why the no-data re-run does zero work.

docs.title: Extensions
docs.text:
• Replace the gold rebuild with an incremental merge keyed on (day, customer) that recomputes only the days touched by the batch. What do you need to know about each batch to do that?
  • Add delta.enableChangeDataFeed on silver and drive gold from the change feed.
  • Add a data-quality table that records, per run, the counts of each layer and whether they reconcile.
  • Compact and cluster silver (Lesson 03) and check DESCRIBE DETAIL before and after.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• writeStream.toTable without .format("delta") against an existing Delta table (a provider mismatch error).
  • Using cast instead of try_cast under ANSI mode, so one bad value fails the whole batch.
  • Merging a source with duplicate keys (deduplicate inside the batch first).
  • Aggregating only the newest batch and missing late or corrected events.
  • Deleting a checkpoint to "fix" a stream, which re-ingests everything and duplicates rows in append-only layers.
  • Appending to quarantine in a non-idempotent step (the known gap in this project).

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Run the project and confirm your numbers match.
  2. Make quarantine idempotent: give each quarantine row a key (for example a hash of event_id and raw values) and write it with MERGE ... WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT. Prove it by replaying a batch.
  3. Add day 3 containing an event with status changed from ok to refund for an existing event. Verify silver and gold.
  4. Break the pipeline deliberately (delete silver's checkpoint) and predict what happens before running it. What does MERGE protect you from? Which table, if any, ends up with duplicates?

docs.title: Level 3 · Unity Catalog, Pipelines & Sharing
docs.text:
Levels 1 and 2 were about getting data in and making it fast. Level 3 is about operating it as a platform: who may see what, where the files live, how pipelines are declared and scheduled, how data leaves the organization, and how SQL users consume it.

What was run, and what wasn't

This level is the most platform-bound of the course. Unity Catalog, jobs, SQL warehouses, OpenSharing and Databricks dashboards cannot run locally, and nothing in Lessons 01 to 05 and 07 to 09 was executed on Databricks. Those lessons are built from the Databricks documentation (October 2026), and each one says what was and wasn't run. What was run: Lesson 06 uses the open-source Spark Declarative Pipelines runtime that ships with PySpark 4.2.0, running a real three-layer pipeline; Lessons 02, 03, 05, 07 and 10 include small local Python or Spark programs that model the documented rules (and are labelled as models, not Databricks code); Lesson 04 runs the filter and mask logic as ordinary SQL functions on local Spark. A Databricks Free Edition workspace is the way to try the platform parts.

Prerequisites: Levels 1 and 2.

docs.title: Modules
docs.text:
1. Unity Catalog: Metastore, Catalogs & Three-Level Names: the object hierarchy, managed storage precedence, and how to lay out catalogs.
  2. Privileges, Ownership & Grants: usage privileges, inheritance, ownership vs MANAGE, with a step-through model.
  3. Storage Credentials, External Locations & Volumes: how UC governs cloud storage and why locations can't overlap.
  4. Row Filters, Column Masks & ABAC: fine-grained access control and tag-based policies.
  5. Lineage, Audit & System Tables: impact analysis and access reviews, on mock tables.
  6. Lakeflow Spark Declarative Pipelines: streaming tables and materialized views, run locally with open-source Spark.
  7. Lakeflow Jobs: Orchestrating Workloads: DAGs, run-if conditions, retries and repair.
  8. OpenSharing (Formerly Delta Sharing): sharing live data outside your workspace.
  9. Databricks SQL, Warehouses & Dashboards: sizing, scaling, auto stop and the Python connector.
  10. Project: Design a Governed Data Platform: a spec, a generator and a tested linter.

docs.title: After Level 3
docs.text: Level 4 covers how teams build and ship all this: bundles and CI/CD, testing PySpark code, MLflow, model serving and AI features, cost management, performance, table maintenance, migration, and a capstone plan.

docs.title: 01 · Unity Catalog: Metastore, Catalogs & Three-Level Names
docs.text:
Level 1 and 2 treated "the catalog" as a place to put table names. Unity Catalog (UC) is much more: it is the governance layer that decides who can read what, records where every table's files live, tracks lineage and writes an audit log. This lesson is the object model; the following lessons are privileges, storage, fine-grained security and observability.

What was run

Unity Catalog cannot be run locally, and this lesson contains no executed output. Everything is taken from the Databricks documentation pages for Unity Catalog, managed storage, securable objects and the SQL reference, read in October 2026. SQL statements were parsed with sqlglot 30.24's Databricks dialect where possible; the dialect doesn't understand most Unity Catalog DDL (GRANT, CREATE CATALOG ... MANAGED LOCATION, CREATE VOLUME fall back to generic "command" parsing), so their syntax was checked by hand against the SQL reference pages instead. An open-source Unity Catalog project exists, but its behaviour isn't identical to the Databricks product and wasn't used here. A Free Edition workspace lets you run everything in this lesson.

docs.title: What Unity Catalog is
docs.text:
Per the documentation, Unity Catalog is the unified governance layer for data and AI built into Databricks. When enabled for a workspace it sits beneath data and AI interactions: it enforces access control when you query a table or call a model, tracks lineage, and logs activity for auditing. It is automatically enabled for workspaces created after 8 November 2023; older workspaces must be upgraded.

Governance belongs in a service rather than in each cluster's configuration because the alternative breaks down: with per-cluster settings and cloud-storage permissions, every new tool and every shared cluster is a new way around the rules.

docs.title: The object hierarchy
docs.text:
account
 └── metastore                       (one per region; attached to many workspaces)
      ├── catalog                    (top of the 3-level namespace: org unit or environment)
      │    └── schema                (a use case, project, team area)
      │         ├── table / view / materialized view
      │         ├── volume           (files)
      │         ├── function
      │         └── registered model
      ├── storage credential         (a cloud identity to access storage)
      ├── external location          (a storage path + credential)
      ├── connection                 (to external systems: Lakehouse Federation)
      ├── share / recipient / provider   (Delta Sharing)
      └── ...

Every object here is a securable: you can grant privileges on it to a principal (a user, a group or a service principal). Names resolve as catalog.schema.object:

SELECT * FROM prod.sales.orders;
USE CATALOG prod;
USE SCHEMA sales;
SELECT * FROM orders;             -- now resolves to prod.sales.orders
SELECT current_catalog(), current_schema();

docs.title: How people organize catalogs
docs.text:
The documentation describes catalogs as organizing data by organizational unit or software-development-lifecycle scope. Two common layouts, and the trade-offs:

Layout Example Strength Cost Per environment dev, test, prod Simple promotion; permissions per environment; workspace-catalog binding can pin each catalog to its workspace A business domain's data is split across catalogs Per domain/team finance, marketing Ownership is clear Environments become schemas or naming conventions Hybrid prod_finance, dev_finance Both Many catalogs to manage

Schemas then follow use cases, and medallion layers (Level 2 · 09) are commonly schemas (bronze, silver, gold) or name prefixes. Whatever you pick, decide it before the first tables exist: moving data between catalogs later means rewriting every reference.

docs.title: Creating the structure
docs.text:
CREATE CATALOG IF NOT EXISTS prod MANAGED LOCATION 's3://acme-prod/uc/prod' COMMENT 'Production data';
CREATE SCHEMA IF NOT EXISTS prod.sales COMMENT 'Sales domain';
CREATE TABLE prod.sales.orders (order_id BIGINT, customer_id BIGINT, amount DECIMAL(12,2), order_ts TIMESTAMP);
COMMENT ON TABLE prod.sales.orders IS 'One row per confirmed order';

The CREATE CATALOG syntax, from the SQL reference, includes MANAGED LOCATION, COMMENT, RETAIN DROPPED FOR n DAYS and DEFAULT COLLATION options; CREATE SCHEMA takes MANAGED LOCATION, COMMENT and RETAIN DROPPED FOR. To create a schema you need CREATE SCHEMA and USE CATALOG on the catalog (and, if you specify a managed location, CREATE MANAGED STORAGE on the external location backing it). The bucket path above is a made-up example.

docs.title: Where do managed tables go?
docs.text:
A managed storage location is cloud storage where UC keeps the data of managed tables and volumes. It can be set on the metastore, a catalog or a schema, and the most specific one wins. The documented rules:

  1. If the schema has a managed location, data goes there.
  2. Otherwise, if the catalog has one, data goes there.
  3. Otherwise it goes to the metastore's.

Databricks recommends setting managed storage at the catalog level for logical isolation (the data of prod and dev in different buckets, with different cloud permissions), with metastore-level and schema-level as options. Newly created UC workspaces get a workspace catalog with its own managed storage, without a metastore-level location. Three more documented properties: managed storage can't overlap external tables or volumes; a catalog or schema location must sit inside an external location (next lessons); and UC appends hashed subdirectories (like <root>/__unitystorage/schemas/<uuid>) so that every managed entity has a unique path.

You can see where things landed:

DESCRIBE CATALOG EXTENDED prod;
DESCRIBE SCHEMA EXTENDED prod.sales;
DESCRIBE DETAIL prod.sales.orders;         -- Delta: includes the table's storage location
DESCRIBE EXTENDED prod.sales.orders;

A practical consequence: the folder name of a managed table is a UUID path, not .../orders. You shouldn't read or write managed-table files by path; always use the table name, and let UC resolve the storage and vend the credentials.

docs.title: Metadata you get for free
docs.text:
• information_schema in every catalog: SQL views listing tables, columns, privileges, constraints, volumes, tags. A catalog's information_schema.tables lists its tables; information_schema.table_privileges lists grants.
  • The system catalog: Databricks-provided tables with audit logs, lineage, billing usage and more (Lesson 05 and Level 4 · 06).
  • Tags and comments on catalogs, schemas, tables and columns for discovery and classification (Lesson 05).
  • Discovery: Catalog Explorer lets people browse and search objects they have BROWSE on.

docs.title: Hive metastore, the legacy world
docs.text: Workspaces created before UC also have the legacy hive_metastore: a workspace-local, two-level (schema.table) catalog, with table access control that is weaker and per-workspace. In a UC workspace it shows up as a catalog named hive_metastore so old code keeps working. New work should go in UC catalogs; migration is covered in Level 4 · 09.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
UC is a metadata service in the Databricks control plane, plus enforcement points in compute. When a query names prod.sales.orders, the compute resource asks UC: who is this principal, does it hold USE CATALOG, USE SCHEMA and SELECT, and where are the files? If the answer is yes, UC returns the table's location and short-lived, scoped storage credentials for that path; the engine then reads the files directly from cloud storage using those credentials. If any check fails, the query fails before touching data. The user never holds cloud keys, which is why the same rules apply to notebooks, jobs, SQL warehouses and BI tools: the check happens in the platform, not in each tool.

On shared (standard) compute, user code is isolated so one user's code can't read another's credentials (the documentation describes this as Lakeguard). That is why some things behave differently on standard vs dedicated compute (Level 1 · 02).

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Putting everything in main.default. It works, and gives you no isolation or ownership story.
  • Mixing environments in one catalog and relying on naming conventions for access control.
  • Reading managed-table files by path and bypassing governance (it often just fails; the path is not stable).
  • Forgetting the managed location rules: a table "mysteriously" lands in the metastore root because the schema and catalog had none.
  • Using hive_metastore for new tables because old tutorials did.
  • Granting before designing the catalog/schema layout.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Sketch the catalog/schema layout for a company with two business domains and dev/prod environments. State which layout you chose and what you give up.
  2. For each of your catalogs, decide where managed storage lives, and write the three-line precedence rule that explains where a new table in prod.sales is stored.
  3. (Workspace) Run DESCRIBE CATALOG EXTENDED and SELECT * FROM system.information_schema.catalogs (or your own catalog's information_schema.tables), and list five columns you found useful.
  4. Find in the documentation what the RETAIN DROPPED FOR clause on CREATE SCHEMA does and link it to UNDROP from Level 1 · 08.

docs.title: 02 · Privileges, Ownership & Grants
docs.text:
Unity Catalog access control looks simple (GRANT SELECT ON TABLE ...) until the first time someone with SELECT gets "permission denied", or a catalog owner can't read a table they apparently own. The rules are consistent once you know three ideas: usage privileges are prerequisites, privileges inherit downward, and ownership does not.

What was run

Unity Catalog isn't available locally, so no GRANT below was executed. The rules are summarized from the Databricks documentation page on Unity Catalog permissions concepts, and the GRANT, REVOKE and SHOW GRANTS syntax from the SQL reference (October 2026); sqlglot can't validate this DDL (it falls back to treating it as an opaque command), so I checked it by hand against those pages. What I did run is a small Python model, written by me from the documented rules, that lets you step through access decisions on a laptop. It is a teaching aid, not Databricks code, and covers only the rules listed, so it can't tell you what a real workspace will do in edge cases.

docs.title: Principals and privileges
docs.text:
A principal is a user, a group or a service principal. Grant to groups, not individuals: membership changes without touching grants, and SHOW GRANTS stays readable.

GRANT USE CATALOG ON CATALOG prod TO `analysts`;
GRANT USE SCHEMA, SELECT ON SCHEMA prod.sales TO `analysts`;
GRANT MODIFY ON TABLE prod.sales.orders TO `etl-service`;
REVOKE SELECT ON TABLE prod.sales.orders FROM `interns`;
SHOW GRANTS ON TABLE prod.sales.orders;
SHOW GRANTS `analysts` ON SCHEMA prod.sales;

Syntax from the reference: GRANT privilege_types ON securable_object TO principal, the mirror REVOKE ... FROM, and SHOW GRANTS [principal] ON securable_object. The documentation notes that a REVOKE succeeds even if the privilege was never granted: it guarantees the privilege is absent, so it is safe in idempotent scripts.

Common privileges: SELECT (read tables/views), MODIFY (write; a composite whose children are INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE), USE CATALOG, USE SCHEMA, CREATE TABLE, CREATE SCHEMA, EXECUTE (functions), READ VOLUME and WRITE VOLUME, BROWSE, MANAGE, APPLY TAG. Use the privileges reference page for the full list: it changes.

docs.title: Rule 1: usage privileges are prerequisites
docs.text:
To read a table you need all three: USE CATALOG on its catalog, USE SCHEMA on its schema and SELECT on the table. The documentation states plainly that SELECT alone is not sufficient. The design lets catalog and schema owners draw boundaries: a table owner can't share data outside the area the parent owners approved, because only they can grant usage privileges.

Operation Needs Read a table or view USE CATALOG + USE SCHEMA + SELECT Write a table USE CATALOG + USE SCHEMA + MODIFY Create a table USE CATALOG + USE SCHEMA + CREATE TABLE (on the schema, or inherited from the catalog) Create a schema USE CATALOG + CREATE SCHEMA on the catalog Run a function USE CATALOG + USE SCHEMA + EXECUTE Read volume files USE CATALOG + USE SCHEMA + READ VOLUME

docs.title: Rule 2: privileges inherit downward
docs.text: A privilege granted on a catalog applies to every schema, table, view, volume and function in it, including ones created later. A privilege on a schema applies to everything in that schema. So GRANT SELECT ON CATALOG prod TO analysts means "read everything in prod, now and in the future", which is convenient and also the most common over-grant. Denials (from ABAC deny policies) inherit the same way. One exception: privileges granted on the metastore do not inherit to data objects (they control metastore-level operations such as CREATE CATALOG), except READ METADATA.

docs.title: Rule 3: ownership doesn't inherit, but gives control
docs.text:
Every securable has an owner, initially its creator. The owner can do everything on that object, grant and revoke privileges, transfer ownership and drop it, and automatically gets the ability to manage all child objects. But ownership does not make you the owner of children, and an owner of a catalog doesn't hold SELECT on the tables inside until it is granted (or the owner uses the manage ability to grant it to themselves). Databricks also doesn't list ALL PRIVILEGES for owners in SHOW GRANTS, so owners are easy to miss when auditing.

MANAGE is like ownership for permissions: it lets someone grant and revoke privileges, transfer ownership and drop the object, without being the owner. ALL PRIVILEGES deliberately excludes MANAGE (and READ METADATA, EXTERNAL USE SCHEMA, EXTERNAL USE LOCATION) to prevent accidental escalation.

BROWSE lets users discover that an object exists and request access, without access to data; the documentation recommends granting it on catalogs to all account users so data is discoverable.

Make owners groups or service principals, not individuals: when a person leaves, objects owned by their account become a problem.

docs.title: Step through the rules: a runnable model
docs.text:
This model encodes the rules above (usage prerequisites, inheritance from catalog/schema, ownership that does not inherit, ALL PRIVILEGES excluding MANAGE). Run it and watch each decision change as grants are added.

"""A teaching model of Unity Catalog's documented privilege rules (NOT Databricks code, no real API)."""
from dataclasses import dataclass, field

@dataclass
class Obj:
    kind: str; name: str; parent: "Obj|None" = None; owner: str = "admin"
    grants: dict = field(default_factory=dict)   # principal -> set(privileges)
    def path(self): return (self.parent.path() + "." if self.parent else "") + self.name
    def chain(self):  # object, then ancestors
        o, out = self, []
        while o: out.append(o); o = o.parent
        return out

def groups_of(user, membership): return {user} | membership.get(user, set())

def has(obj, principals, priv):
    """Explicit/inherited grant of `priv` on obj (grants on ancestors inherit down, except metastore)."""
    for o in obj.chain():
        if o.kind == "metastore" and o is not obj: continue
        for p in principals:
            gs = o.grants.get(p, set())
            if priv in gs or "ALL PRIVILEGES" in gs and priv not in ("MANAGE", "READ METADATA"): return True
    return False

def can_select(table, user, membership):
    pr = groups_of(user, membership); cat, sch = table.parent.parent, table.parent
    usage = (has(cat, pr, "USE CATALOG") or cat.owner in pr) and (has(sch, pr, "USE SCHEMA") or sch.owner in pr or cat.owner in pr)
    data = has(table, pr, "SELECT") or table.owner in pr
    return usage and data, dict(use_catalog=has(cat, pr, "USE CATALOG") or cat.owner in pr, use_schema=has(sch, pr, "USE SCHEMA") or sch.owner in pr or cat.owner in pr, select=data)

ms = Obj("metastore", "ms"); cat = Obj("catalog", "prod", ms, owner="platform"); sch = Obj("schema", "sales", cat, owner="platform")
orders = Obj("table", "orders", sch, owner="dana")
members = {"ana": {"analysts"}, "ben": {"analysts", "interns"}, "dana": set(), "platform": set()}
def show(label, user):
    ok, parts = can_select(orders, user, members); print(f"{label:<62} -> {'ALLOW' if ok else 'DENY '} {parts}")

show("1. nothing granted, user ana", "ana")
orders.grants["analysts"] = {"SELECT"}
show("2. SELECT on table only (no usage privileges)", "ana")
cat.grants["analysts"] = {"USE CATALOG"}
show("3. + USE CATALOG", "ana")
sch.grants["analysts"] = {"USE SCHEMA"}
show("4. + USE SCHEMA  (all three now present)", "ana")
orders.grants.clear(); cat.grants["analysts"] = {"USE CATALOG", "SELECT"}; sch.grants.clear()
show("5. SELECT + USE CATALOG on catalog, no USE SCHEMA", "ana")
sch.grants["analysts"] = {"USE SCHEMA"}
show("6. + USE SCHEMA: SELECT inherited from the catalog", "ana")
show("7. table owner dana (owner of table, no usage grants)", "dana")
cat.grants["dana"] = {"USE CATALOG"}; sch.grants["dana"] = {"USE SCHEMA"}
show("8. dana gets usage privileges", "dana")
show("9. platform (owner of catalog) reads the table", "platform")
cat.grants["analysts"] = {"USE CATALOG", "ALL PRIVILEGES"}
print("ALL PRIVILEGES includes MANAGE?", has(cat, {"analysts"}, "MANAGE"))

Output of running it:

1. nothing granted, user ana                                   -> DENY  {'use_catalog': False, 'use_schema': False, 'select': False}
2. SELECT on table only (no usage privileges)                  -> DENY  {'use_catalog': False, 'use_schema': False, 'select': True}
3. + USE CATALOG                                               -> DENY  {'use_catalog': True, 'use_schema': False, 'select': True}
4. + USE SCHEMA  (all three now present)                       -> ALLOW {'use_catalog': True, 'use_schema': True, 'select': True}
5. SELECT + USE CATALOG on catalog, no USE SCHEMA              -> DENY  {'use_catalog': True, 'use_schema': False, 'select': True}
6. + USE SCHEMA: SELECT inherited from the catalog             -> ALLOW {'use_catalog': True, 'use_schema': True, 'select': True}
7. table owner dana (owner of table, no usage grants)          -> DENY  {'use_catalog': False, 'use_schema': False, 'select': True}
8. dana gets usage privileges                                  -> ALLOW {'use_catalog': True, 'use_schema': True, 'select': True}
9. platform (owner of catalog) reads the table                 -> DENY  {'use_catalog': True, 'use_schema': True, 'select': False}
ALL PRIVILEGES includes MANAGE? False

Rows 7 and 9 are the surprising ones. In row 7 even the table's owner can't read it without usage privileges on the parents (the documentation says owners don't need usage privileges only for exercising MANAGE-type metadata abilities, not for reading data). In row 9 the catalog's owner has full control over the catalog and can manage its children, yet reading a table still needs SELECT, which they can grant themselves.

docs.title: A practical grant design
docs.text:
1. Create groups by role (analysts, data-engineers, finance-readers), synchronized from your identity provider.
  2. Grant USE CATALOG and BROWSE broadly; grant USE SCHEMA + SELECT at schema level for read-only roles; grant CREATE TABLE/MODIFY only to engineering and service principals.
  3. Keep grants at the highest sensible level to avoid thousands of table-level grants, but resist catalog-wide SELECT in catalogs that mix sensitive and non-sensitive schemas.
  4. Run pipelines as service principals, not people.
  5. Audit with SHOW GRANTS and the information_schema privilege views, plus the audit log (Lesson 05).

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: Each grant is a row in the metastore: (securable, principal, privilege). On a query, compute asks UC to resolve the principal's effective groups, walk from the table up to the metastore collecting grants and owners, and apply the rules: the three-part requirement for reads, inheritance from containers, and special cases such as ownership and MANAGE. Because evaluation happens in UC, one change takes effect for all compute immediately; there are no cached permissions to flush on clusters. Row filters, column masks and ABAC policies (Lesson 04) are evaluated after the basic privileges let the query through.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• GRANT SELECT on a table but no usage privileges on its parents.
  • Granting SELECT on a catalog that contains sensitive schemas.
  • Granting to individuals instead of groups.
  • Using ALL PRIVILEGES as a shortcut and assuming it covers MANAGE.
  • Individual owners, so access dies with the person.
  • Assuming ownership of a catalog gives data access to everything inside.
  • Not auditing: owners don't appear as ALL PRIVILEGES in SHOW GRANTS.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Add a new group interns to the model with SELECT on a second table and show it can't read the first table.
  2. Extend the model with BROWSE and show a user who can see the table's metadata but not read it.
  3. Design the grants for three roles (analyst, engineer, service principal) over catalog prod with schemas bronze, silver, gold. Write the exact GRANT statements.
  4. In the documentation, find what EXTERNAL USE SCHEMA protects against, and why ALL PRIVILEGES excludes it.

docs.title: 03 · Storage Credentials, External Locations & Volumes
docs.text:
Unity Catalog can govern tables and files only if it controls the door to the storage. That door is built from three objects: a storage credential (a cloud identity), an external location (a path plus a credential) and the privileges on them. Volumes then give governed, path-based access to files.

What was run

Nothing here touches a real cloud account or workspace. The facts come from the Databricks documentation pages on external locations, storage credentials, managed storage, volumes and "path overlap restrictions" (October 2026), for AWS; Azure and GCP use different credential types but the same ideas. The SQL statements couldn't be validated by sqlglot (it treats Unity Catalog DDL as opaque commands), so I checked their syntax against the SQL reference. The one program in this lesson is a small model I wrote of the documented no-overlap rule for external locations; it is a teaching aid, not Databricks code.

docs.title: The three objects
docs.text:
cloud IAM role / managed identity ──►  STORAGE CREDENTIAL        (who UC acts as when touching storage)
                  + a path           ►  EXTERNAL LOCATION         (where, and which credential)
                  + grants           ►  READ FILES / WRITE FILES / CREATE EXTERNAL TABLE / CREATE EXTERNAL VOLUME / CREATE MANAGED STORAGE
  • A storage credential wraps a cloud identity: on AWS an IAM role that Databricks can assume; on Azure a managed identity or service principal; on GCP a service account. Databricks recommends granting only CREATE EXTERNAL LOCATION on credentials, and no direct use.
  • An external location binds a storage path (like s3://acme-raw/landing) to a credential. It is the unit you grant access on.
  • On AWS you create the credential first, then the location. The documentation prerequisites include: the bucket must exist; its name can't contain dots; the path must use only standard ASCII characters; and the bucket cannot have an S3 ACL attached. You need CREATE STORAGE CREDENTIAL on the metastore for the first, and CREATE EXTERNAL LOCATION on both the metastore and the credential for the second (metastore admins have those on the metastore by default).
-- Credentials are normally created in Catalog Explorer or through the API (they need cloud-side IAM setup);
-- then, in SQL:
CREATE EXTERNAL LOCATION IF NOT EXISTS landing
  URL 's3://acme-raw/landing'
  WITH (STORAGE CREDENTIAL acme_raw_cred)
  COMMENT 'Raw drops from partners';

DESCRIBE EXTERNAL LOCATION landing;
GRANT READ FILES, WRITE FILES ON EXTERNAL LOCATION landing TO `ingest-service`;
GRANT CREATE EXTERNAL TABLE ON EXTERNAL LOCATION landing TO `data-engineers`;
SHOW STORAGE CREDENTIALS;
SHOW GRANTS ON EXTERNAL LOCATION landing;

(CREATE EXTERNAL LOCATION ... URL ... WITH (STORAGE CREDENTIAL ...), DESCRIBE EXTERNAL LOCATION, SHOW STORAGE CREDENTIALS and SHOW GRANTS ... ON EXTERNAL LOCATION match the reference pages; the bucket and credential names are invented.) One documented gotcha: WRITE FILES requires READ FILES on the same location, because writes involve metadata checks and path validation; a user with only WRITE FILES gets PERMISSION_DENIED. Grant both together. The documentation also recommends using volumes to govern file access, rather than granting READ FILES directly to many users.

docs.title: Path rules: no overlaps
docs.text:
Unity Catalog guarantees that two securables never govern the same bytes, via documented rules. External locations can't overlap other external locations; volumes can't overlap volumes; tables can't overlap tables; tables and volumes can't overlap each other; managed storage locations can't overlap each other, external tables or external volumes. Consequently you can't define an external location inside another one, can't register a table on files inside a volume, and can't define a volume on a directory inside a table. Files inside a volume can always be read and written by path (including Delta files), but they cannot be registered as tables.

Here is a tiny model of the first two rules. It registers locations (refusing overlaps in either direction) and finds which one governs a path:

"""Teaching model of one documented Unity Catalog rule: external locations can't overlap, and a path is
governed by the single external location that contains it. Not Databricks code."""
def contains(base, path):
    base = base.rstrip("/") + "/"; return (path.rstrip("/") + "/").startswith(base)

class Metastore:
    def __init__(self): self.locations = {}
    def create_external_location(self, name, url):
        clash = [n for n, u in self.locations.items() if contains(u, url) or contains(url, u)]
        if clash: raise ValueError(f"cannot register {url!r}: overlaps external location(s) {clash}")
        self.locations[name] = url
    def governing(self, path):
        hits = [n for n, u in self.locations.items() if contains(u, path)]
        return hits[0] if hits else None

ms = Metastore()
ms.create_external_location("landing", "s3://acme-raw/landing")
ms.create_external_location("curated", "s3://acme-curated")
for p in ["s3://acme-raw/landing/orders/2026-10-21/f.json", "s3://acme-raw/other/x.csv",
          "s3://acme-curated/sales/2026/part.parquet", "s3://acme-raw/landing-archive/x"]:
    print(f"{p:<50} -> {ms.governing(p) or 'no external location: access denied'}")
for name, url in [("sales", "s3://acme-curated/sales"), ("raw_all", "s3://acme-raw"), ("archive", "s3://acme-raw/landing-archive")]:
    try: ms.create_external_location(name, url); print(f"registered {name}: {url}")
    except ValueError as e: print("REJECTED:", e)

s3://acme-raw/landing/orders/2026-10-21/f.json     -> landing
s3://acme-raw/other/x.csv                          -> no external location: access denied
s3://acme-curated/sales/2026/part.parquet          -> curated
s3://acme-raw/landing-archive/x                    -> no external location: access denied
REJECTED: cannot register 's3://acme-curated/sales': overlaps external location(s) ['curated']
REJECTED: cannot register 's3://acme-raw': overlaps external location(s) ['landing']
registered archive: s3://acme-raw/landing-archive

Notice the string-prefix trap the model has to avoid: landing-archive starts with the characters landing but is a sibling folder, not a child. Comparing paths by startswith without the trailing / would wrongly treat them as overlapping; the first version of my model handled that by adding a separator before comparing. Overlap planning matters in practice: pick location boundaries before you create them (a bucket-wide location blocks every future per-folder location), and create external tables and volumes in sub-directories, not at the root of a location, as the docs advise.

docs.title: Volumes in depth
docs.text:
A volume is a governed directory in a schema. Managed volumes live in the schema's managed storage; external volumes point at a path in an external location.

CREATE VOLUME prod.raw.landing_managed COMMENT 'Staging area';
CREATE EXTERNAL VOLUME prod.raw.partner_drops
  LOCATION 's3://acme-raw/landing/partners' COMMENT 'Files delivered by partners';
GRANT READ VOLUME ON VOLUME prod.raw.partner_drops TO `analysts`;
GRANT WRITE VOLUME ON VOLUME prod.raw.partner_drops TO `ingest-service`;

Per the reference, CREATE VOLUME needs CREATE VOLUME on the schema, and creating an external volume also needs CREATE EXTERNAL VOLUME on the external location. Dropping an external volume leaves the files; dropping a managed volume deletes its data (with a 7-day retention per the volumes documentation).

Access paths:

From Path Spark, SQL, pandas, dbutils.fs, shell, %sh /Volumes/<catalog>/<schema>/<volume>/<path> Apps and REST Files API: /api/2.0/fs/files/Volumes/... Cloud URI Possible for external volumes with sufficient privileges; Unity Catalog privileges override those on the external location

docs.title: The cardinal rule: don't bypass UC
docs.text: The documentation is blunt: do not give non-UC identities storage-level access to managed tables or volumes. Anyone with direct bucket access bypasses UC's access control, escapes auditing and lineage, and can corrupt tables by writing files Delta doesn't know about. The only identity that should touch managed storage is the one UC uses. For external data that other systems also use, grant those systems access to their path through your cloud IAM, but make Databricks users go through UC.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
When compute needs s3://acme-raw/landing/orders/f.json, it presents the user's identity to UC. UC finds the governing external location (or the table/volume that maps to the path), checks the user's privileges on that object, then asks the cloud provider to assume the storage credential's role with a session policy narrowed to that path, and returns the resulting short-lived token to the compute. The engine reads with that token. Because credentials are minted per request, scoped and expiring, nothing long-lived is ever on a cluster, and revoking a grant takes effect at the next request.

A managed table path is a generated random directory (the docs say the name is randomly generated), which is why path-based access to managed tables isn't supported: use the table name.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Registering an external location at a bucket root, blocking every smaller location later.
  • Granting WRITE FILES without READ FILES and getting PERMISSION_DENIED.
  • Giving users direct S3/ADLS access to the buckets behind managed storage.
  • Trying to create a table on files inside a volume (not allowed; load them into a table).
  • Granting READ FILES on locations broadly instead of governing through volumes and tables.
  • Dots in S3 bucket names, or non-ASCII paths, which the AWS prerequisites exclude.
  • One credential for everything, so a compromise (or mistake) has maximum reach.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Add a method to the model that finds all objects a given path would overlap, and test it with a child, a parent and a sibling path (landing, landing/x, landing-archive).
  2. Plan the external locations for three buckets (raw, curated, sandbox) such that no overlap will block you later. Which privileges do the ingest job and the analysts need?
  3. Explain why granting analysts READ FILES on a location is weaker than giving them READ VOLUME on a volume.
  4. List three ways a person with direct bucket access could damage a managed table without Unity Catalog noticing.

docs.title: 04 · Row Filters, Column Masks & ABAC
docs.text:
Table privileges are all-or-nothing: a user either can SELECT the table or can't. Real requirements are finer: the EU team sees only EU customers; analysts see an email as a***@x.com; compliance sees it in full. Unity Catalog provides row filters and column masks, applied by the platform at query time, and ABAC policies that apply them across many tables by tag.

What was run, and what wasn't

The Unity Catalog features here (SET ROW FILTER, SET MASK, CREATE POLICY, governed tags) exist only on Databricks and were not run. Their syntax and rules come from the Databricks documentation (October 2026) and the SQL reference. To show the logic running, I built an analogue on local Spark 4.2.0: SQL functions and a session variable standing in for the current user. That analogue uses an ordinary function call inside a query, which is not what Unity Catalog does (UC attaches the function to the table so users can't skip it); it only demonstrates what such functions compute.

docs.title: Row filters
docs.text:
A row filter is a SQL user-defined function that returns a boolean for each row. Rows where it returns FALSE (or NULL) are excluded. It's bound to a table with ALTER TABLE ... SET ROW FILTER:

CREATE FUNCTION prod.sec.us_filter(region STRING)
RETURN IF(IS_ACCOUNT_GROUP_MEMBER('admin'), true, region = 'US');

ALTER TABLE prod.sales.customers SET ROW FILTER prod.sec.us_filter ON (region);
ALTER TABLE prod.sales.customers DROP ROW FILTER;

(The function body follows the documentation's example; names are invented.) Anyone who queries customers now gets only region = 'US' rows unless they're in the admin account group. The filter is part of the table, so it applies in notebooks, jobs, SQL warehouses and BI tools alike.

docs.title: Column masks
docs.text:
A column mask is a SQL function that receives the column's value and returns what the user should see; its return type must match or be castable to the column's type. Each column can have one mask, and a mask can take additional columns as inputs:

CREATE FUNCTION prod.sec.mask_email(email STRING)
RETURN CASE WHEN IS_ACCOUNT_GROUP_MEMBER('compliance') THEN email
            ELSE CONCAT(SUBSTR(email, 1, 1), '***@', SPLIT(email, '@')[1]) END;

ALTER TABLE prod.sales.customers ALTER COLUMN email SET MASK prod.sec.mask_email;
ALTER TABLE prod.sales.customers ALTER COLUMN email DROP MASK;

Syntax per the reference: ALTER TABLE t ALTER COLUMN c SET MASK fn [USING COLUMNS (...)] and ... DROP MASK.

docs.title: The logic, running locally
docs.text:
To see what these functions compute, I ran the same two functions on local Spark, with a grants table and a session variable who as the "current user":

DECLARE OR REPLACE VARIABLE who STRING DEFAULT 'nobody';
CREATE OR REPLACE TEMPORARY FUNCTION region_ok(r STRING) RETURNS BOOLEAN
  RETURN EXISTS(SELECT 1 FROM grants g WHERE g.usr = who AND (g.region = '*' OR g.region = r));
CREATE OR REPLACE TEMPORARY FUNCTION mask_email(e STRING) RETURNS STRING
  RETURN CASE WHEN EXISTS(SELECT 1 FROM grants g WHERE g.usr = who AND g.role = 'admin') THEN e
              ELSE concat(substr(e,1,1), '***@', split(e,'@')[1]) END;

SET VAR who = 'alice';
SELECT id, mask_email(email) AS email, region, salary FROM customers WHERE region_ok(region) ORDER BY id;

With grants = (alice, analyst, US), (erin, analyst, EU), (root, admin, *):

alice (US analyst)            erin (EU analyst)           root (admin)                       mallory (not in grants)
 1 a***@x.com US 50000         2 b***@y.org EU 72000       1 ana@x.com US   50000            (no rows)
 3 c***@z.net US 64000                                     2 bo@y.org  EU   72000
                                                           3 cy@z.net  US   64000
                                                           4 di@w.io   APAC 58000

Alice sees US rows with masked emails, Erin sees one EU row, root sees all rows unmasked, and a user absent from the table gets no rows: the filter fails closed. That's the property to design for: the default for an unknown user must be "nothing". (A mask that returned the real value when a lookup found nothing would fail open.)

docs.title: Why not just use views?
docs.text:
A dynamic view wraps tables in a view that filters/masks using functions like is_account_group_member(), and users get access to the view but not the base table. It still works, and the documentation recommends it when you want to expose a curated, transformed or joined version of data to people with no access to the underlying tables. But it has weaknesses for pure security: you must remember to not grant the base table, every view is another object to maintain, and the same rule is copied into many views.

Approach Attaches to Managed by Best for Row filter / column mask One table or column Table owner or MANAGE Table-specific logic ABAC policy Tables/columns matched by tags, at catalog/schema/table (or metastore) scope Whoever owns/MANAGEs the scope One rule across many tables Dynamic view A view over base tables The view's SQL Curated or joined slices

docs.title: ABAC: policies matched by tags
docs.text:
Attribute-based access control moves the rule from the table to the classification of the data. You tag columns (pii, class = ssn) using governed tags (tags whose allowed values and who may apply them are controlled), then write one policy that says "mask every column tagged pii for these principals". New tables that carry the tag are covered automatically, and because policies are attached at catalog or schema level by higher-level admins, table owners can't remove them.

CREATE OR REPLACE POLICY mask_pii_email
ON SCHEMA prod.sales
COLUMN MASK prod.sec.mask_email
TO `analysts` EXCEPT `compliance`
FOR TABLES
MATCH COLUMNS has_tag('pii') AS pii_col
ON COLUMN pii_col;

This follows the documented CREATE POLICY grammar: ON { METASTORE | CATALOG | SCHEMA | TABLE }, a body of ROW FILTER fn or COLUMN MASK fn, TO principals [EXCEPT principals], FOR TABLES, optional WHEN condition (table-level tags), MATCH COLUMNS condition [AS alias], and ON COLUMN alias for masks. To create one you need MANAGE on the securable (or ownership) and EXECUTE on the function. Tag functions has_tag() and has_tag_value() work in WHEN (checking tags on the table, including inherited from catalog/schema) and MATCH COLUMNS (checking tags on the column itself). The statement above wasn't parseable by sqlglot and I couldn't run it; treat it as documented syntax, not tested code. ABAC can also grant and deny privileges (GRANT policies; DENY policies are in Beta per the documentation).

docs.title: Performance and safety rules (from the docs)
docs.text:
• The engine always chooses the secure plan over the optimized plan when they conflict, so filters and masks can slow queries. Keep functions small: simple CASE over lookups; few arguments; few distinct masks per table.
  • Use deterministic, non-throwing expressions. An expression that can error (ANSI division by zero) blocks optimizations because the error could leak information about values before filtering. Prefer try_divide.
  • Prefer SQL over Python UDFs.
  • Type mismatch trap. If a function parameter is INT but the column is STRING, Databricks casts implicitly. With ANSI mode off, uncastable values silently become NULL, which can make a filter return all rows, or a mask hide the wrong ones. Keep ANSI mode on, and match types exactly.
  • Drop the filter before dropping the function: otherwise the table can become inaccessible (ALTER TABLE ... DROP ROW FILTER repairs it).
  • REPLACE TABLE retains existing row filters and masks (when columns match), a safety feature that can also surprise you.
  • Only one distinct row filter can resolve per user and table, so combine rules with AND in the function.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: When a query reads a protected table, the planner replaces the table scan with the scan wrapped in the filter or mask expressions, before the user's own predicates and projections can see raw values. That rewrite happens in the engine for every query on the table, in any language, which is why a user can't bypass it by writing SELECT * or using a different tool. Because the function runs as part of the plan, anything it calls (group membership checks, lookups) is evaluated per row or per batch; hence the performance guidance. Fine-grained access also affects what compute can run it: the documentation ties it to standard (Lakeguard-isolated) compute or serverless so users' code cannot read unfiltered files directly (check the current compute requirements for your runtime).

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Fail-open functions: unknown users or NULL lookups returning the real data.
  • Masking in a view but granting the base table to the same people.
  • Per-table copies of the same rule instead of ABAC.
  • Complicated functions with joins and Python, then wondering why queries slow down.
  • Implicit cast bugs from mismatched parameter types with ANSI mode off.
  • Dropping the function first, leaving the table inaccessible.
  • Forgetting derived data: a copy of a masked table's unmasked output (an extract written to a file) is no longer protected.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Extend the local analogue so that salary is masked to a range (50k-60k) for non-admins, and a second mask rule shows the real number to users with role hr.
  2. Add a unit test that proves the filter fails closed for a user not in grants, and for a NULL region.
  3. Write the ABAC policy (documented syntax) to mask every column tagged pii in prod.hr for the group analysts except hr, and the row filter policy that restricts prod.sales tables tagged regional by region.
  4. Choose, for a table with 10 sensitive columns used by 30 teams, between per-column masks, ABAC and a dynamic view, and justify the choice.

docs.title: 05 · Lineage, Audit & System Tables
docs.text:
Governance isn't only about blocking access; it's about being able to answer questions afterward. Which dashboards break if I change this column? Who read the customer table last week? What did we spend yesterday? Unity Catalog records the answers automatically, in lineage views and in system tables you query with SQL.

What was run, and what wasn't

System tables and lineage exist only in a Unity Catalog workspace, so no real system-table output appears in this lesson. Table names, columns, retention periods and requirements come from the Databricks documentation (lineage and system-tables pages, October 2026). To show what the queries do, I ran them on local Spark 4.2.0 against small mock tables that I wrote to mimic a few columns of system.access.table_lineage and system.access.audit. The mock rows are invented; the real tables have many more columns and rows, and you must check the current schema in your workspace.

docs.title: Lineage
docs.text:
Per the documentation, Unity Catalog automatically captures lineage for queries run on Databricks, down to the column level, and aggregates it across all workspaces attached to the metastore. Nodes can be tables and views, model versions, external assets and file paths, and the entities that read or write them (notebooks, jobs, pipelines, dashboards, SQL queries).

What it is for: impact analysis (what depends on this table or column?), root-cause investigation (where did this number come from?), sensitive-data tracking for audits, and understanding cross-team dependencies.

Requirements and limits worth knowing (all from the docs):

  • Tables must be registered in Unity Catalog; queries must use the Spark DataFrame API or Databricks SQL interfaces. Lineage isn't captured for every access pattern, and the lineage system tables explicitly "represent a subset of all read/write events" because it's not always possible to infer lineage.
