  • To view lineage you need at least BROWSE on the parent catalog (and permissions on notebooks/jobs/dashboards you want to see details of).
  • External systems (Salesforce, MySQL, Tableau, Power BI) can be registered as external lineage assets to extend the graph.
  • Lineage in Catalog Explorer is retained indefinitely for lineage captured after 1 September 2024 per the docs, while the lineage system tables keep a rolling one-year window.

docs.title: The two lineage system tables
docs.text:
Table One row per Selected columns system.access.table_lineage Read or write event on a table or path source_table_full_name, target_table_full_name, source_type, target_type, entity_type (e.g. JOB, NOTEBOOK, PIPELINE, DASHBOARD_V3), entity_id, entity_run_id, created_by, event_time, event_date system.access.column_lineage Column read/write source_column_name, target_column_name plus table identifiers

An event with a source and no target (a dashboard reading a table) has target_table_full_name = NULL. Column lineage excludes events with no source (an INSERT of literal values).

docs.title: Impact analysis, run on mock data
docs.text:
Mock rows for a small estate: raw CSV → bronze → silver → gold, a feature table built from silver, and a dashboard reading gold:

CREATE OR REPLACE TEMP VIEW table_lineage AS SELECT * FROM VALUES
 ('prod.raw.orders_csv',   'prod.bronze.orders',  'PIPELINE','p1', TIMESTAMP'2026-10-20 01:00:00'),
 ('prod.bronze.orders',    'prod.silver.orders',  'PIPELINE','p1', TIMESTAMP'2026-10-20 01:05:00'),
 ('prod.silver.orders',    'prod.gold.daily_rev', 'JOB',     'j7', TIMESTAMP'2026-10-20 01:30:00'),
 ('prod.silver.customers', 'prod.gold.daily_rev', 'JOB',     'j7', TIMESTAMP'2026-10-20 01:30:00'),
 ('prod.gold.daily_rev',   NULL,                  'DASHBOARD_V3','d3', TIMESTAMP'2026-10-20 08:00:00'),
 ('prod.silver.orders',    'prod.ml.features',    'NOTEBOOK','n9', TIMESTAMP'2026-10-19 12:00:00')
 AS t(source_table_full_name, target_table_full_name, entity_type, entity_id, event_time);

"If I change prod.bronze.orders, what is downstream?" is a graph walk. Spark 4.2 supports recursive CTEs, so:

WITH RECURSIVE down(tbl, depth) AS (
  SELECT 'prod.bronze.orders', 0
  UNION ALL
  SELECT l.target_table_full_name, d.depth + 1
  FROM table_lineage l JOIN down d ON l.source_table_full_name = d.tbl
  WHERE l.target_table_full_name IS NOT NULL AND d.depth < 10)
SELECT DISTINCT tbl, depth FROM down ORDER BY depth, tbl;

Local output on the mock data:

|prod.bronze.orders |0|
|prod.silver.orders |1|
|prod.gold.daily_rev|2|
|prod.ml.features   |2|

and the non-table consumers (rows with a NULL target) found the dashboard:

|DASHBOARD_V3|d3|prod.gold.daily_rev|

So a change to bronze reaches silver, the gold revenue table and the ML feature table, and ultimately dashboard d3. Real lineage has cycles (a table that reads itself), so keep the depth limit; and because the system table is a sample of events, treat the result as "at least these", not as proof nothing else depends on the table.

docs.title: The audit log
docs.text:
system.access.audit records account activity. Documented columns include event_time, event_date, workspace_id, service_name (for example unityCatalog), action_name (for example getTable), user_identity, request_id, request_params (a map whose contents depend on the request) and response. Notes from the docs: filter on event_date for performance; some request_params keys containing SQL are omitted unless you are an account admin or in the databricks_pii_access group; and deleting a workspace removes its audit events older than 14 days.

An access review on mock audit rows (columns simplified to user_email and object_name):

SELECT user_email, action_name, count(*) AS n, min(event_time) AS first_seen
FROM audit
WHERE object_name = 'prod.silver.customers'
GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY first_seen;

|mallory@x.com|getTable         |2|2026-10-20 09:05:00|
|admin@x.com  |updatePermissions|1|2026-10-21 02:00:00|

On the real table you'd pull the user from user_identity.email and the object from request_params, and the available action_name values differ by service. Check the audit documentation for exact keys; I have not validated them against a live workspace. Good habits: alert on permission changes (update...Permissions actions), unusual hours or volumes of reads on sensitive tables, and failed authorization events.

docs.title: Other system tables you'll use
docs.text:
The system catalog also hosts (from the system-tables index) compute and warehouse tables, billing and pricing, query history, jobs and pipeline events, marketplace, model serving, data classification and more. Level 4 · 06 uses billing tables for cost. Access requires Unity Catalog and an account admin to enable the relevant schemas; reading them is governed by normal GRANTs on the system catalog objects, and the docs strongly discourage copying this data out of the platform because it can expose sensitive information.

-- the shapes of the queries you'll write (not run; check columns first)
SELECT * FROM system.access.table_lineage WHERE event_date >= current_date() - INTERVAL 7 DAYS LIMIT 10;
SELECT usage_date, sku_name, SUM(usage_quantity) FROM system.billing.usage GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY 1 DESC LIMIT 20;

docs.title: Tags, classification and discovery
docs.text: Governance metadata complements lineage: tags (key/value labels on catalogs, schemas, tables and columns), governed tags (with controlled values, used by ABAC in Lesson 04), comments, certification and deprecation markers, and data classification, which the documentation describes as automatically classifying and tagging sensitive data. BROWSE plus Catalog Explorer search makes this discoverable without exposing data.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: Lineage is captured by the engine as queries execute: when a Spark plan reads and writes governed tables, the runtime reports (source, target, columns, entity) events to the control plane, which aggregates them into the lineage graph and exports them to the system tables. That's why lineage appears only for supported interfaces and is "a subset": a query run through a path that doesn't report (certain libraries, direct file reads outside UC) leaves no edge. The audit log is produced by the Unity Catalog service itself for each API action (including authorization decisions), so it is complete for UC operations in a way lineage is not.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Treating lineage as complete. Absence of an edge is not proof of no dependency.
  • Reading audit data without filtering on event_date and scanning a year of events.
  • Granting broad access to system tables, which expose user names, queries and request parameters.
  • Never alerting on the audit log, so it is only read after an incident.
  • Copying system-table data to external stores without a security review.
  • Forgetting retention: lineage tables keep one year; audit retention follows the docs table for your plan.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Extend the mock lineage with a cycle and show that the depth limit stops the recursion. What does UNION vs UNION ALL do to the recursion termination?
  2. Write the query that lists, for a given table, all entities (jobs, notebooks, dashboards) that read it, with their last read time.
  3. Design three audit-log alerts for a PII table and write the SQL shape for each.
  4. In a workspace, enable system tables and compare system.access.table_lineage with Catalog Explorer's lineage graph for the same table. Where do they differ?

docs.title: 06 · Lakeflow Spark Declarative Pipelines
docs.text:
In Level 2 you wrote a bronze/silver/gold pipeline by hand: streams, checkpoints, foreachBatch, MERGE, ordering and retries. Declarative pipelines invert that. You declare what each dataset is (a query), and the framework works out the dependency graph, execution order, incremental processing, checkpoints and retries. On Databricks this is Lakeflow Spark Declarative Pipelines (the successor to Delta Live Tables), built on the Apache Spark Declarative Pipelines framework.

What was run, and what wasn't

PySpark 4.2.0 includes the open-source Spark Declarative Pipelines framework (pyspark.pipelines and the spark-pipelines command), so the first half of this lesson was actually executed locally: the three-file pipeline below, two refreshes, and the table contents shown. The open-source runtime has real limits compared with Databricks, discovered while running it: its tables are plain Parquet, not Delta; it exports no expectation decorators (dir(pyspark.pipelines) lists table, materialized_view, temporary_view, append_flow, create_streaming_table, create_auto_cdc_flow, create_sink and a few others, but nothing named expect); and it needs a persistent catalog to re-run (see below). Everything about expectations, the pipeline UI, the event log, serverless compute, AUTO CDC behaviour and pipeline modes is from the Databricks documentation (October 2026) and was not run.

docs.title: Two dataset types
docs.text:
Streaming table Materialized view Defined by A query over a stream (append-only source) A batch query over tables Processing Incremental: each row processed once Refreshed; the engine may update it incrementally when it can, else recomputes Typical layer Bronze ingestion, append-style silver Aggregated silver and gold, joins Python @dp.table returning a streaming DataFrame @dp.materialized_view SQL (Databricks) CREATE STREAMING TABLE ... AS SELECT ... FROM STREAM(...) CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW ... AS SELECT ...

Plus views (@dp.temporary_view, CREATE TEMPORARY VIEW) that exist only for the pipeline run, and flows (append, update, AUTO CDC) that feed a table from one or many sources. Pipeline mode is independent of table type: triggered mode refreshes available data and stops (cheap; fine for 10-minute-to-daily freshness), while continuous keeps tables fresh (an always-on cluster; for seconds-to-minutes freshness), per the documentation.

docs.title: A runnable pipeline (open-source Spark 4.2)
docs.text:
Project layout, created with spark-pipelines init --name orders_pipe, then edited:

orders_pipe/
├── spark-pipeline.yml
├── transformations/
│   ├── bronze.py
│   ├── silver.sql
│   └── gold.py
└── landing/            # JSON files arrive here

spark-pipeline.yml:

name: orders_pipe
storage: file:///path/to/orders_pipe/pipeline-storage      # checkpoints live here
libraries:
  - glob:
      include: transformations/**
configuration:
  spark.sql.shuffle.partitions: "4"

transformations/bronze.py (a streaming table: it returns a streaming DataFrame):

from pyspark import pipelines as dp
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

LANDING = "file:///path/to/orders_pipe/landing"

@dp.table(comment="Raw order events, appended incrementally from JSON files")
def bronze_orders():
    return (spark.readStream.schema("order_id STRING, customer STRING, amount STRING, status STRING").json(LANDING)
            .withColumn("_ingested_at", F.current_timestamp()))

transformations/silver.sql (SQL and Python files mix freely in one pipeline):

CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW silver_orders AS
SELECT CAST(order_id AS INT) AS order_id, customer, CAST(amount AS DECIMAL(10,2)) AS amount, status
FROM bronze_orders
WHERE try_cast(order_id AS INT) IS NOT NULL AND try_cast(amount AS DECIMAL(10,2)) >= 0;

transformations/gold.py:

from pyspark import pipelines as dp
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

@dp.materialized_view(comment="Revenue per customer")
def gold_revenue():
    return (spark.read.table("silver_orders").where("status = 'ok'")
            .groupBy("customer").agg(F.sum("amount").alias("revenue"), F.count("*").alias("orders")))

Notice what's absent: no checkpoint paths, no trigger, no writeStream, no ordering. silver_orders reads bronze_orders by name, and gold_revenue reads silver_orders; that's the whole dependency graph.

The first file a.json held five events, including a non-numeric id (x) and a negative amount. Running the pipeline from the project folder:

export SPARK_HOME=$(python -c "import pyspark,os;print(os.path.dirname(pyspark.__file__))")
spark-pipelines --conf spark.sql.catalogImplementation=hive run

the log showed each flow queued, then bronze_orders, silver_orders, gold_revenue run in dependency order, each COMPLETED, and Run is COMPLETED. Reading the output tables:

bronze_orders (5)   1 ana 10.50 ok | 2 bo 20.00 ok | 3 ana -4 ok | 4 ana 7.25 refund | x cy 5 ok
silver_orders (3)   1 ana 10.50 ok | 2 bo 20.00 ok | 4 ana 7.25 refund        <- 'x' and '-4' filtered out
gold_revenue  (2)   ana 10.50 (1 order) | bo 20.00 (1 order)

Then I added a second file b.json (orders 5 and 6) and ran again:

bronze_orders (7)   the five previous rows + 5 bo 4.00 ok + 6 dee 30.00 ok     <- only new rows were added
silver_orders (5)   1 ana | 2 bo | 4 ana | 5 bo | 6 dee
gold_revenue  (3)   ana 10.50 (1) | bo 24.00 (2) | dee 30.00 (1)

The streaming table ingested only the new file (its checkpoint in pipeline-storage/_checkpoints remembered the first), while the materialized views were recomputed from their inputs. The numbers reconcile: bo's 24.00 is 20.00 + 4.00.

Things I hit running it (worth knowing before you try):

  • Without the extra --conf spark.sql.catalogImplementation=hive, the first run worked but the second run failed with [LOCATION_ALREADY_EXISTS] Cannot name the managed table ... as its associated location ... already exists: the default in-memory catalog forgets the tables between runs while their folders remain. Setting the option in spark-pipeline.yml didn't work either (CANNOT_MODIFY_STATIC_CONFIG), because it must be set when the server starts; passing --conf to spark-pipelines did. This is a local-development quirk, not how Databricks behaves.
  • A catalog:/database: key in the YAML fails with SCHEMA_NOT_FOUND unless that schema already exists.
  • The local tables are Parquet. On Databricks they are Delta tables governed by Unity Catalog.

docs.title: Expectations: data quality as declarations
docs.text:
from pyspark import pipelines as dp

@dp.table
@dp.expect("valid_id", "order_id IS NOT NULL")                   # keep row, record the violation
@dp.expect_or_drop("non_negative_amount", "amount >= 0")         # drop violating rows
@dp.expect_or_fail("known_status", "status IN ('ok','refund')")  # fail the update
def silver_orders():
    return spark.readStream.table("bronze_orders")

The decorator names above are from the Databricks Python reference. In SQL the equivalent is a CONSTRAINT name EXPECT (condition) [ON VIOLATION DROP ROW | FAIL UPDATE] clause. Per the documentation, each expectation's counts of valid and invalid records are logged with the dataset's metrics, expect_or_fail stops a single flow without failing other flows, and the expect_all* variants take a dictionary. Compare with Level 2 · 10, where quarantine tables required hand-written code: expectations count and drop but do not quarantine; to keep failing rows you still write them to a separate table.

docs.title: AUTO CDC
docs.text: The AUTO CDC APIs (successors with the same syntax to APPLY CHANGES) compute SCD Type 1 or Type 2 targets from a change feed or from snapshots, handling ordering by a sequence column, deletes and out-of-order events. In Python this is dp.create_auto_cdc_flow(...), and the open-source package exports create_auto_cdc_flow too (I didn't run it). It replaces the hand-built SCD2 MERGE from Level 2 · 01.

docs.title: Operations
docs.text:
• Compute: serverless or classic; the pipeline owns the cluster, with autoscaling.
  • Updates: a normal update refreshes; --full-refresh (open-source CLI) or a full refresh in the UI resets selected datasets and recomputes from scratch. A full refresh of a streaming table reprocesses all source data and, for sources that have deleted history, can lose data; check the docs before running one.
  • Monitoring: a pipeline event log (also queryable) records flow progress, expectation metrics and lineage; the UI shows the graph and each flow's status. Pipelines run as tasks inside Lakeflow Jobs (next lesson).
  • Materialized views refresh incrementally when the engine can compute the change, with a documented set of supported operations; otherwise they recompute. Look at the refresh type in the event log to see what happened.

docs.title: When to use declarative pipelines
docs.text: Good fit: standard ingest-clean-aggregate flows, CDC, anything where retries, checkpoint plumbing and ordering are your main source of bugs. Poorer fit: highly custom per-batch logic (foreachBatch with external side effects), operations the framework doesn't model, or teams that need to run the same code on a cluster without the framework. The code is portable in spirit only: open-source Spark pipelines and Lakeflow share the programming model, but features differ, as shown above.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
When you run a pipeline, the framework first registers every dataset definition (executing your Python files and parsing SQL, but without running the queries) to build a graph: each dataset is a node, and each read.table("x") or FROM x is an edge. It validates the graph (no cycles, all references resolve), then executes flows in topological order, running independent branches in parallel. For a streaming table, it runs a Structured Streaming query with a framework-managed checkpoint (Level 2 · 07); for a materialized view, it runs the batch query and replaces or incrementally updates the stored result.

Because the framework owns the checkpoints and the graph, it can retry a failed flow, rerun only downstream datasets, and reset a single dataset (--full-refresh) consistently. That's what you paid for with all the hand-written code in Level 2.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Putting side effects in dataset functions (writing files, calling APIs): they may run during planning or more than once.
  • Using a streaming source in a materialized view, or a batch read in a streaming table by accident.
  • Full-refreshing a streaming table whose source no longer holds all the history.
  • Expecting expectations to quarantine rows (they drop, keep or fail).
  • Running continuous mode for hourly data, paying for an idle cluster.
  • Testing only on Databricks: you can unit-test transformation logic locally (Level 4 · 02) and keep the pipeline files thin.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Reproduce the local pipeline. Add c.json with a duplicate of order 5 and see what each table contains afterward. (Predict first: which layer deduplicates, if any?)
  2. Add a fourth dataset gold_status_counts as a SQL materialized view and rerun. Does the log show it running in parallel with gold_revenue?
  3. Convert silver_orders to use the Databricks expectation decorators (don't run), and decide which rule should drop, which should fail.
  4. Run spark-pipelines run --full-refresh bronze_orders locally. What happens to bronze_orders when the landing folder still has both files? What would happen on a real source that had expired old files?

docs.title: 07 · Lakeflow Jobs: Orchestrating Workloads
docs.text:
A pipeline defines how data is transformed; a job decides when and in what order things run, what happens when something fails, and who gets told. Lakeflow Jobs is Databricks' orchestrator: a DAG of tasks (notebooks, pipelines, SQL, Python scripts, dbt, other jobs) with triggers, parameters, retries and notifications.

What was run, and what wasn't

Jobs run only on Databricks, so nothing below was executed on the platform. Task types, trigger behaviour, run-if conditions, limits and parameter syntax come from the Databricks documentation on jobs (October 2026). I did run two local things: a YAML parse of the job definition below (to check it is well-formed YAML only; it was not validated against the Jobs schema or deployed), and a small Python model of the dependency and retry rules, which is my reading of the documented behaviour, not Databricks code, and simplifies the real repair semantics.

docs.title: Jobs, tasks, triggers
docs.text:
• A job is the unit you schedule and monitor. It has a trigger, parameters, notifications and optional Git settings, and up to 1,000 tasks per job (documented limit; a workspace is limited to 2,000 concurrent task runs).
  • A task is one unit of work: notebook, Python script, wheel/JAR, SQL (query, file, alert, dashboard), pipeline, dbt, another job (Run Job), plus control-flow tasks If/else and For each.
  • A trigger starts the job: a schedule (Quartz cron with a time zone; the docs state a minimum 10-second interval between scheduled runs), a file arrival trigger, a continuous trigger, a model-update trigger, or manual/API/run now.

File arrival triggers watch a Unity Catalog external location or volume path (recursively, including subdirectories) and check for new files "best effort every minute" per the docs, costing only the cloud provider's listing charges. They suit irregular arrivals, where a fixed schedule either wastes runs or adds latency.

docs.title: A job definition
docs.text:
Jobs are defined in the UI, with the REST API/SDKs, or as code in bundles (next level). This is a four-task job in bundle YAML (field names follow the Jobs API; it is untested and the notebook paths are invented):

resources:
  jobs:
    orders_daily:
      name: orders-daily
      schedule:
        quartz_cron_expression: "0 30 2 * * ?"      # 02:30 every day
        timezone_id: UTC
      parameters:
        - name: run_date
          default: "{{job.start_time.iso_date}}"
      tasks:
        - task_key: ingest
          notebook_task:
            notebook_path: ../src/ingest.py
            base_parameters:
              run_date: "{{job.parameters.run_date}}"
        - task_key: pipeline
          depends_on: [{task_key: ingest}]
          pipeline_task:
            pipeline_id: ${resources.pipelines.orders_pipeline.id}
        - task_key: publish
          depends_on: [{task_key: pipeline}]
          max_retries: 2
          notebook_task:
            notebook_path: ../src/publish.py
        - task_key: notify
          depends_on: [{task_key: publish}, {task_key: pipeline}]
          run_if: ALL_DONE
          notebook_task:
            notebook_path: ../src/notify.py

Points to notice:

  • depends_on builds the DAG. Tasks with no dependency between them run in parallel.
  • run_if: ALL_DONE makes notify run whether publish and pipeline succeeded or failed.
  • max_retries retries this task on failure. The docs say the default for most configurations is no retries, that serverless jobs auto-optimize retries by default, and that continuous jobs use exponential backoff.
  • {{job.parameters.run_date}} and {{job.start_time.iso_date}} are dynamic value references: double-curly-brace strings replaced at run time. The docs stress that braces are not evaluated as expressions (no functions or arithmetic), and that a non-existent reference is a syntax error.

docs.title: Run-if conditions
docs.text:
A task's Run if dependencies field controls when it executes relative to its upstream tasks:

Condition Runs when All succeeded (default) Every upstream task succeeded; otherwise the task is marked Upstream failed At least one succeeded Any upstream succeeded None failed No upstream failed, and at least one actually ran All done Upstream tasks have finished, whatever their result

(The UI also offers failure-oriented options such as "at least one failed" and "all failed" for error-handling branches; check the current run-if page for the full list.) Use All done for cleanup and notification tasks that must run regardless. Beyond run-if, If/else branches on a boolean expression (for example, only transform if ingestion added rows, with the value passed between tasks as a task value), and For each loops a task over an array of inputs.

docs.title: A runnable model of the semantics
docs.text:
This model implements topological ordering, the run-if conditions above, per-task retries and a "repair" that keeps already-successful tasks:

"""Teaching model of Lakeflow Jobs task-dependency semantics (run-if conditions, retries, repair).
Written from the documented rules. NOT Databricks code, no API calls."""
from graphlib import TopologicalSorter

class Task:
    def __init__(self, name, fn, deps=(), run_if="ALL_SUCCEEDED", retries=0):
        self.name, self.fn, self.deps, self.run_if, self.retries = name, fn, tuple(deps), run_if, retries

def should_run(task, status):
    d = [status[x] for x in task.deps]
    if not d: return True
    ok = [s == "SUCCESS" for s in d]
    ran = [s in ("SUCCESS", "FAILED") for s in d]
    return {"ALL_SUCCEEDED": all(ok), "AT_LEAST_ONE_SUCCEEDED": any(ok),
            "NONE_FAILED": all(s != "FAILED" and s != "UPSTREAM_FAILED" for s in d) and any(ran),
            "ALL_DONE": True}[task.run_if]

def run_job(tasks, status=None, log=print):
    status = dict(status or {})
    order = TopologicalSorter({t.name: t.deps for t in tasks}).static_order()
    by = {t.name: t for t in tasks}
    for name in order:
        t = by[name]
        if status.get(name) == "SUCCESS": log(f"  {name}: already SUCCESS (repair keeps it)"); continue
        if not should_run(t, status): status[name] = "UPSTREAM_FAILED"; log(f"  {name}: UPSTREAM_FAILED (run-if {t.run_if})"); continue
        for attempt in range(t.retries + 1):
            try: t.fn(); status[name] = "SUCCESS"; log(f"  {name}: SUCCESS (attempt {attempt+1})"); break
            except Exception as e: status[name] = "FAILED"; log(f"  {name}: FAILED attempt {attempt+1}: {e}")
    return status

state = {"warehouse_up": False}
def ingest(): pass
def validate(): pass
def transform():
    if not state["warehouse_up"]: raise RuntimeError("warehouse not reachable")
def publish(): pass
def notify(): pass
tasks = [Task("ingest", ingest), Task("validate", validate, ["ingest"]),
         Task("transform", transform, ["validate"], retries=1),
         Task("publish", publish, ["transform"]),
         Task("notify_always", notify, ["publish", "transform"], run_if="ALL_DONE")]
print("run 1:"); st = run_job(tasks)
print("statuses:", st)
state["warehouse_up"] = True
print("\nrepair run (only failed/skipped tasks re-run):"); st = run_job(tasks, st)
print("statuses:", st)

Output of running it:

run 1:
  ingest: SUCCESS (attempt 1)
  validate: SUCCESS (attempt 1)
  transform: FAILED attempt 1: warehouse not reachable
  transform: FAILED attempt 2: warehouse not reachable
  publish: UPSTREAM_FAILED (run-if ALL_SUCCEEDED)
  notify_always: SUCCESS (attempt 1)
statuses: {'ingest': 'SUCCESS', 'validate': 'SUCCESS', 'transform': 'FAILED', 'publish': 'UPSTREAM_FAILED', 'notify_always': 'SUCCESS'}

repair run (only failed/skipped tasks re-run):
  ingest: already SUCCESS (repair keeps it)
  validate: already SUCCESS (repair keeps it)
  transform: SUCCESS (attempt 1)
  publish: SUCCESS (attempt 1)
  notify_always: already SUCCESS (repair keeps it)
statuses: {'ingest': 'SUCCESS', 'validate': 'SUCCESS', 'transform': 'SUCCESS', 'publish': 'SUCCESS', 'notify_always': 'SUCCESS'}

transform failed twice (one retry), publish never started because its run-if condition wasn't met, and notify_always ran anyway. The repair re-ran only the two tasks that hadn't succeeded, so ingest and validate (which could be expensive) were not repeated. In the real product, Repair run re-runs failed and skipped tasks of an existing run; how it treats an ALL_DONE task that already ran is a detail my model glosses over (it simply keeps it), and I did not verify it. Read the repair-failures documentation before relying on it.

docs.title: Parameters and task values
docs.text:
• Job parameters are key/value pairs pushed to every task that declares them (via dynamic references or widgets). Define them once at job level; override on manual runs and backfills.
  • Task values let one task publish a small value for downstream tasks (the dbutils.jobs.taskValues utility), for example a row count that an If/else task checks.
  • Dynamic value references include job and task metadata ({{job.run_id}}, {{job.start_time.iso_date}}, task values).
  • The documentation has a dedicated page on backfilling jobs over date ranges; the principle is to select the date with parameters, never by editing code.

Parameters for a notebook arrive as widgets (Level 1 · 02), so the same notebook runs interactively and in a job.

docs.title: Compute for jobs
docs.text: A job task can run on serverless compute (no cluster to manage; auto-optimized retries), on job compute (a classic cluster created for the run and terminated after, cheaper than all-purpose), or on an existing all-purpose cluster (avoid: higher price and shared interference). Several tasks in a job can share one job cluster to avoid repeated startup.

docs.title: Operating jobs
docs.text:
• Notifications by email, Slack, webhooks on start/success/failure and on duration thresholds.
  • Timeouts per task so a hung task doesn't hold the job forever.
  • Concurrency: limit maximum concurrent runs (commonly 1 for jobs that must not overlap).
  • Permissions: view, manage-run and manage levels; run jobs as a service principal so the identity doesn't depend on a person (and Unity Catalog grants go to the principal).
  • Observability: run history UI, plus job and task run system tables for cost and reliability analysis (look up the exact table names in the system tables documentation; I did not verify them).
  • Git: run notebooks and files from a Git ref rather than workspace copies, so deployments are versioned.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: When a trigger fires, the jobs service creates a run record and a task-run per task. It performs a topological walk of the DAG: tasks whose dependencies are resolved (and whose run-if condition is true) are submitted to compute; others are marked skipped or upstream failed. Each task run is an independent execution (a notebook run on a cluster, a pipeline update, a SQL statement) with its own logs, retries and status; the job run's status is derived from them. Because task runs are separate records, a repair can create a new attempt for specific tasks while keeping the original run's successful results. (That last sentence describes the documented user-visible behaviour; the internal record-keeping is my inference.)

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• One giant notebook task instead of several tasks (no partial retry, no parallelism, no per-step visibility).
  • Overlapping runs because max concurrent runs wasn't limited.
  • Retrying non-idempotent tasks (a retry duplicates side effects); make tasks idempotent first (Level 2).
  • Running production on all-purpose clusters or as a person's identity.
  • Hard-coding dates in notebooks instead of job parameters, making backfills code changes.
  • Using the schedule for irregular arrivals when a file-arrival trigger fits better.
  • No notification on failure: jobs fail silently until someone looks.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Add a fifth task to the model, cleanup with run-if "none failed" depending on publish, and predict its status in both runs before running.
  2. Modify the model so that repair also re-runs ALL_DONE tasks whose upstream changed status. Is that more or less like what you would want?
  3. Write the job YAML for a file-arrival-triggered job (consult the Jobs API reference for the trigger field names) that runs the pipeline when files land in /Volumes/prod/raw/landing/orders/.
  4. Choose retry counts for four tasks (ingest from a flaky API, transform, publish to a warehouse, send a notification) and justify each.

docs.title: 08 · OpenSharing (Formerly Delta Sharing): Sharing Data Across Organizations
docs.text:
Eventually someone outside your workspace needs your data: a partner, a customer, another business unit on another cloud, or a team that uses a different tool. The traditional answers (export CSVs, copy to a bucket, give out credentials) create stale copies and lose governance. Databricks' answer is a sharing protocol that exposes governed tables live, read-only, without copying.

A naming note, and what was run

The current Databricks documentation calls this feature OpenSharing (its documentation hub is at the old delta-sharing URL path, and API paths still contain delta-sharing); older material and the open-source Python client call it Delta Sharing. I use OpenSharing, and mention the old name so searches work. I did not verify whether the open-source project has been renamed. Nothing was run against a Databricks workspace. The concepts and SQL come from the documentation (October 2026). Locally I installed the open-source Python client (delta-sharing 1.4.2, from PyPI) and checked its API surface and how it fails when no server is reachable, against a reserved .invalid host, so no real server was contacted.

docs.title: Concepts
docs.text:
• A share is a read-only collection of data assets that a provider exposes: tables and table partitions, and (for Databricks recipients) also views (including dynamic views with row and column rules), streaming tables, materialized views, volumes, models and notebooks. In Unity Catalog a share is a securable object; dropping it cuts off every recipient.
  • A recipient is the named identity that consumes shares. It is an object in the provider's metastore.
  • A provider, from the recipient's side, is the organization that shares with you.

Three ways to share, from the documentation:

Mode Recipient What you get Databricks-to-Databricks A Unity Catalog workspace No tokens to manage; shares appear as a catalog; supports notebooks, volumes, models, views, plus governance, auditing and usage tracking on both sides Databricks-to-Open Any platform (Spark, pandas, Power BI, Iceberg clients...) A credential file with a bearer token or OIDC federation; tabular data Self-hosted open-source server Anyone You run the sharing server; the Databricks docs don't cover setting it up

docs.title: Providing data: the SQL
docs.text:
CREATE SHARE IF NOT EXISTS partner_sales COMMENT 'Orders and revenue for ACME Corp';

ALTER SHARE partner_sales ADD TABLE prod.gold.daily_revenue COMMENT 'Daily revenue per customer' WITH HISTORY;
ALTER SHARE partner_sales ADD SCHEMA prod.gold_public;

CREATE RECIPIENT IF NOT EXISTS acme_corp COMMENT 'ACME data team';
GRANT SELECT ON SHARE partner_sales TO RECIPIENT acme_corp;

Syntax follows the reference: CREATE SHARE [IF NOT EXISTS] name [COMMENT ...]; ALTER SHARE name ADD [TABLE] t [COMMENT] [PARTITION ...] [AS alias] [WITH HISTORY | WITHOUT HISTORY] (also SCHEMA, VIEW, MATERIALIZED VIEW, MODEL, REMOVE, RENAME, OWNER); CREATE RECIPIENT [IF NOT EXISTS] name [USING ID sharing_identifier] [COMMENT ...] [PROPERTIES (...)]; and GRANT SELECT ON SHARE s TO RECIPIENT r. SELECT is the only privilege you can grant on a share. The names are invented and none of it was run; sqlglot can't parse sharing DDL, so I checked each form against the SQL reference pages. Creating a share needs CREATE SHARE on the metastore; creating a recipient needs CREATE RECIPIENT (or metastore admin).

Two design choices in the syntax matter:

  • WITH HISTORY shares the table's history, which lets recipients time-travel and read the change data feed; without it they see only the current version. It also exposes your past data, including rows you may have deleted, so choose deliberately.
  • Partitions: you can share only some partitions (for example one customer's data), but a plain table share exposes everything. For per-recipient data, prefer a view or a dynamic view (Databricks recipients only) over many partition shares.

docs.title: Recipients without Databricks (open sharing)
docs.text: For a recipient outside Databricks you create a recipient with token-based authentication; Databricks produces an activation link or a credential file (a small JSON profile with the endpoint and a bearer token, possibly with an expiry). The provider controls expiry and rotation. Treat it like a password: send it over a secure channel, never commit it to Git. The documentation also describes OIDC federation for recipients, IP access lists, and network egress controls for the provider.

docs.title: Databricks recipient
docs.text:
A privileged user (metastore admin, or someone with CREATE CATALOG plus USE PROVIDER) creates a catalog from the share:

SHOW PROVIDERS;
SHOW SHARES IN PROVIDER `acme_provider`;
CREATE CATALOG acme_shared USING SHARE `acme_provider`.partner_sales;
GRANT USE CATALOG, USE SCHEMA, SELECT ON CATALOG acme_shared TO `analysts`;
SELECT * FROM acme_shared.gold.daily_revenue;

(CREATE CATALOG ... USING SHARE provider.share is in the CREATE CATALOG syntax; the other statements are standard.) The shared catalog is read-only, and Unity Catalog privileges inside it follow the normal hierarchy. One documented quirk: the information_schema of a shared catalog is updated from the provider only when you query a shared table or run a command like DESCRIBE, so it can look stale.

docs.title: Any other platform: the open-source client
docs.text:
The open-source Python client reads a profile file and speaks the sharing REST protocol:

import delta_sharing

client = delta_sharing.SharingClient("config.share")
client.list_all_tables()
df = delta_sharing.load_as_pandas("config.share#partner_sales.gold.daily_revenue")
# Spark: spark.read.format("deltaSharing").load("config.share#partner_sales.gold.daily_revenue")

The usage pattern (profile#share.schema.table, load_as_pandas, load_as_spark, the deltaSharing Spark format and versionAsOf for shared history) follows the Databricks documentation. Locally, with a dummy profile pointing at a reserved .invalid host, the client's API listed SharingClient, load_as_pandas, load_as_spark, load_table_changes_as_pandas, get_table_version and friends, and a list_shares() call failed with a ConnectionError for https://example.invalid/delta-sharing/shares: confirming the client calls <endpoint>/shares. I couldn't test real reads without a share.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
OpenSharing is a REST protocol with one clever trick: the server never streams your data. A recipient asks for a table; the server checks the token and the share, then returns a list of pre-signed URLs to the table's Parquet files in cloud storage (plus the table's metadata and version). The client then downloads those files directly from the cloud storage using the URLs, which expire quickly. The data doesn't pass through the sharing server, the recipient never receives cloud credentials, and the provider's storage serves the bytes. For Databricks-to-Databricks sharing the same idea applies with Unity Catalog doing the authentication.

Consequences: (1) reading is a file listing plus downloads, so egress costs fall on the provider's cloud account (the docs cover egress management and cost considerations; check them before sharing large tables across regions or clouds); (2) data is live, so recipients see new versions as the provider commits them; (3) recipients can read and copy what they can see, so sharing is not a way to retain control over data once seen; and (4) shared Delta features depend on the recipient's client supporting the table's reader protocol.

docs.title: Operating shares
docs.text:
• Audit: sharing activity is recorded in the audit log system table and in provider/recipient usage views (the docs have an audit-logs page for sharing).
  • Revoke: REVOKE SELECT ON SHARE s FROM RECIPIENT r stops access at the next request; rotate bearer tokens periodically.
  • Schema changes: adding columns is generally safe; dropping or renaming columns can break recipients. Treat a shared table as an API with a contract and version it (orders_v1).
  • PII: share a curated gold or a dynamic view, never the raw table. Row/column rules on shared dynamic views apply for Databricks recipients.
  • Marketplace and clean rooms are built on the same protocol: public listings, and joint analysis without exposing raw rows.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Sharing a bronze table that includes data you didn't mean to expose, with WITH HISTORY exposing deleted rows too.
  • Committing the credential file to a repository or emailing it unencrypted.
  • Forgetting egress cost for a large shared table that many recipients scan fully.
  • No contract on schema: a column rename breaks someone you've never met.
  • Using shares as an access-control substitute inside one organization; use Unity Catalog grants there.
  • Expecting to revoke what was already copied.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Write the full provider-side SQL to share only the gold aggregates for one customer using a view, and explain why a view beats a partition share when you have 200 customers.
  2. Decide for each case whether to use Databricks-to-Databricks or open sharing: (a) another business unit on Databricks, (b) a partner who uses Power BI, (c) a university running R.
  3. Install delta-sharing locally and write a function that validates a profile file (required keys present, token not committed in the working tree). Test it with a fake profile.
  4. Estimate the monthly egress cost of 50 recipients each reading a 200 GB table once a day, using your cloud's published pricing. State your assumptions and what would reduce the cost.

docs.title: 09 · Databricks SQL, Warehouses & Dashboards
docs.text:
Not everyone who needs your data writes Spark. Analysts, BI tools and applications want to run SQL, fast, with predictable cost. Databricks SQL is the SQL-first surface of the lakehouse: a query editor, SQL warehouses (compute for SQL), dashboards, alerts, and connectors (JDBC/ODBC, Python, REST) for other tools.

What was run, and what wasn't

SQL warehouses and dashboards exist only on Databricks, so none of this lesson's platform behaviour was executed. Warehouse types, defaults and sizing advice come from the Databricks documentation pages for SQL warehouses and dashboards (October 2026); defaults and prices change, so re-check them. Locally I installed the open-source databricks-sql-connector package to check its import path and connection signature, and tried it against a reserved .invalid host; what happened is described in the connector section.

docs.title: SQL warehouses
docs.text:
A SQL warehouse is compute dedicated to SQL (and SQL-based) workloads, available in three types:

Type Engine features (per docs) Notes Serverless Photon, Predictive IO, Intelligent Workload Management Starts in seconds (the docs say typically 2 to 6), rapid up- and down-scaling; compute runs in Databricks' account; the recommended default Pro Photon, Predictive IO Classic-plane compute with more features than classic Classic Photon Basic, runs in your cloud account

(A newer Lakehouse Real-Time warehouse type for sub-second, high-concurrency reads is described as Beta in the docs.)

docs.title: The settings that matter
docs.text:
• Cluster size (2X-Small to the largest sizes): the resources of one cluster. Bigger means lower latency for heavy queries; the default per the docs is X-Large. The docs advise for serverless: start with one larger warehouse and size down if needed, since it is usually cheaper to size down than to start small and scale up. If the query profile shows spilling to disk, increase the size.
  • Scaling (min/max clusters): how many same-size clusters Databricks may run in parallel to handle concurrency. The default is 1 to 1. The docs recommend about one cluster per 10 concurrent queries. Watch the Peak Queued Queries metric on the monitoring page.
  • Auto stop: how long idle before shutting down. Defaults per the docs: 45 minutes for pro and classic (minimum 10), 10 minutes for serverless (minimum 5 in the UI; the API allows as low as 1). Idle warehouses accrue DBU and cloud charges until stopped, so for classic/pro this is a cost lever; for serverless the short default is part of its appeal.
  • Type, tags (for cost attribution; Level 4 · 06) and permissions (CAN USE, CAN MANAGE).

Size vs. clusters is the central design question: size improves single-query speed; clusters improve concurrency. A dashboard used by 200 people at 9am needs more clusters, not a bigger one; a monthly report scanning terabytes needs a bigger one. Separate warehouses for separate workloads (ETL, BI, ad-hoc) also isolate them from one another.

Per the docs, serverless uses Intelligent Workload Management: when a query arrives, the system predicts its resource needs; if capacity exists it starts at once, otherwise it queues, and if queue wait times rise the autoscaler provisions more clusters; when demand drops it scales down while keeping enough capacity for recent peaks. When a configuration change recycles clusters, the old cluster may linger up to 24 hours for running queries, after which long-running queries could be terminated; so keep queries well under a day.

docs.title: Writing and tuning queries
docs.text:
Everything from Levels 1 and 2 applies: columnar Delta tables, data skipping, clustering. Warehouse-specific tools:

  • Query history records each query's duration, rows, the user and warehouse; a table in the system catalog holds the same data for analysis (system table list, Lesson 05).
  • Query profile shows the plan with time and rows per operator, spill, and scan statistics (files read vs pruned). This is where you confirm Level 2's advice (skipping works; join strategy; skew).
  • Caching: results can be reused when the same query runs again over unchanged data, and disk caching speeds repeat scans. The exact caching behaviours and settings are in the docs; the practical rule is that a repeated dashboard query should be fast the second time, and a first slow run isn't representative.
  • EXPLAIN gives the plan as text (it worked on local Spark in Level 2).
  • Materialized views (Lesson 06) precompute expensive aggregates; dashboards over a materialized view are cheap and consistent.
-- Typical analyst query shape: filter on a clustering/partition column, aggregate, limit output
SELECT order_date, customer_id, SUM(amount) AS revenue
FROM prod.gold.orders
WHERE order_date >= current_date() - INTERVAL 30 DAYS
GROUP BY ALL
ORDER BY revenue DESC
LIMIT 100;

docs.title: AI/BI dashboards
docs.text:
Dashboards are authored from datasets (tables, views or custom queries), with visualizations (AI-assisted or manual), filters at global, page and widget level, cross-filtering, and calculated fields. Per the docs, published dashboards can be shared with anyone registered in the account, even people without workspace access. Practical points:

  • A dashboard's data permissions are either the viewer's own (each viewer sees what Unity Catalog lets them see, so row filters and masks from Lesson 04 apply) or the publisher's embedded credentials (everyone sees the publisher's view). Choosing the second one for sensitive data is a governance decision, not a convenience setting; check the dashboard sharing documentation for the exact options.
  • Dashboards run on a SQL warehouse; each refresh runs the dataset queries. Use materialized views and the dashboard's caching options to keep cost predictable.
  • Dashboards can be exported/imported, and managed in Git and in bundles (Level 4 · 01).
  • Alerts run a query on a schedule and notify when a condition is met (they can also be a job task).
  • Genie spaces let users ask questions in natural language over curated tables (Level 4 · 05).

docs.title: Connecting from code and tools
docs.text:
JDBC/ODBC drivers connect BI tools (Power BI, Tableau and others) to a warehouse. For Python there is the Databricks SQL Connector:

from databricks import sql
import os

with sql.connect(server_hostname=os.getenv("DATABRICKS_SERVER_HOSTNAME"),
                 http_path=os.getenv("DATABRICKS_HTTP_PATH"),
                 access_token=os.getenv("DATABRICKS_TOKEN")) as connection:
    with connection.cursor() as cursor:
        cursor.execute("SELECT * FROM samples.nyctaxi.trips LIMIT ?", [2])      # parameterized: never f-string user input
        for row in cursor.fetchall():
            print(row)

This is the documented usage pattern; it was not run against a real warehouse. Authentication options in the docs include personal access tokens (fine for experiments), OAuth for users (auth_type="databricks-oauth"), and OAuth for service principals (machine-to-machine) which is what production applications should use. The connector also supports query tags, and the REST SQL Statement Execution API is available when you can't use a driver.

What I observed locally with databricks-sql-connector 4.7.0: sql.connect takes server_hostname, http_path, access_token and further keyword arguments. Pointed at a reserved .invalid hostname (no real server), the default call kept retrying for more than three minutes before I stopped it, so a wrong hostname or a network problem can look like a hang in a scheduled job. With short retry settings (I used the underscore-prefixed _retry_stop_after_attempts_duration=5, _retry_stop_after_attempts_count=1 and _socket_timeout=5, which I did not find in the documentation's public option list, so treat them as unsupported internals) it failed after about 3 seconds with MaxRetryError ... NameResolutionError. The practical lesson: wrap connector calls in your own timeout and retry policy, and never let an unbounded retry run inside a job with no task timeout (Lesson 07).

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
A warehouse is a cluster (or several) of executors running the same Spark/Photon engine you used in Levels 1 and 2, with a front end that accepts SQL statements over HTTP, manages a queue, and returns results. A query is parsed, planned and authorized against Unity Catalog (Lesson 02), optimized (partition and file skipping, AQE), then executed in Photon, the vectorized C++ engine, reading Delta files directly from cloud storage with credentials vended by Unity Catalog. Results are cached and returned in chunks, which is why very large result sets should be written to a table rather than downloaded by a BI tool.

Serverless adds a pool of pre-initialized capacity in Databricks' account, which is why starting takes seconds, and a control loop (IWM) that watches queue length to add and remove clusters. Classic and pro warehouses must provision VMs, so starting takes minutes and scaling is slower.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Using one big warehouse for everything so a runaway ad-hoc query slows the executive dashboard.
  • A bigger size to fix concurrency, or more clusters to fix a single slow query.
  • Leaving classic/pro auto stop at a long idle time on a warehouse used twice a day.
  • Dashboards on raw tables instead of gold tables or materialized views, re-aggregating on every refresh.
  • Publishing with embedded credentials for sensitive data.
  • Concatenating user input into SQL instead of using parameters.
  • Downloading millions of rows through a BI tool instead of aggregating first.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. A BI dashboard has 120 users, most active 9:00 to 10:00, and each load runs eight 2-second queries. Propose the warehouse type, size, min/max clusters and auto stop; justify each setting, citing the docs' guidance, and say what metric you'd watch.
  2. Rewrite a query that scans prod.silver.orders to read from a materialized view, and describe how the dashboard's cost changes (qualitatively).
  3. Write a small Python script with databricks-sql-connector that runs a parameterized query and writes the result to CSV. Add the environment variables it needs and an OAuth service principal variant.
  4. In a workspace, run the same query twice and compare the query profile and duration. What changed, and why?

docs.title: 10 · Project — Design a Governed Data Platform
docs.text:
You can't run Unity Catalog on a laptop, but you can treat your governance design as code: a declarative spec of catalogs, schemas, groups and grants; a generator that turns it into SQL; and a linter with tests that catches the mistakes from this level before anyone runs a GRANT. That is also how teams review access changes in practice: as a pull request on a spec, not as clicks in a UI.

What was run, and what wasn't

The Python below (generator, linter and tests) was run locally with Python 3.12, and all output in this lesson is copied from that run. The generated SQL was not executed against Unity Catalog; it follows the syntax in the Databricks SQL reference (Lessons 01 to 04). The lint rules are my encoding of the rules documented in this level (usage privileges, inheritance, ownership, ALL PRIVILEGES excluding MANAGE, no overlapping external locations), so passing the linter means "consistent with those rules", not "will succeed on a workspace". The bucket names, group names and catalog layout are invented.

docs.title: The design being encoded
docs.text:
A small company, one production catalog prod, with a medallion layout (Level 2 · 09):

Schema Content Who may read Who may write prod.bronze Raw data Data engineers, the ETL service principal The ETL service principal prod.silver Cleaned, contains PII Data engineers only Data engineers prod.gold Aggregates for the business Analysts, data engineers Data engineers

Principles: grant to groups and service principals, never to individuals; owners are groups; analysts can discover the catalog (BROWSE) but only read gold; managed storage is set at catalog level inside an external location; external locations never overlap.

docs.title: The code
docs.text:
uc_platform.py holds the spec, the SQL generator and the linter:

"""Governance-as-code: turn a platform spec into Unity Catalog SQL and lint it against the rules from Level 3.
Pure Python (no Databricks needed). The generated SQL is NOT executed here; it follows the documented syntax."""
import re, sys

SPEC = {
    "env": "prod",
    "locations": {"raw": "s3://acme-raw/landing", "lake": "s3://acme-lake/prod"},
    "catalogs": {"prod": {"owner": "platform-admins", "managed_location": "s3://acme-lake/prod/uc"}},
    "schemas": {   # catalog.schema -> settings
        "prod.bronze": {"owner": "data-engineers", "sensitive": False},
        "prod.silver": {"owner": "data-engineers", "sensitive": True},
        "prod.gold":   {"owner": "data-engineers", "sensitive": False},
    },
    "groups": {"analysts", "data-engineers", "platform-admins", "etl-service"},
    "grants": [   # (principal, privilege(s), securable kind, securable name)
        ("analysts", ["USE CATALOG", "BROWSE"], "CATALOG", "prod"),
        ("analysts", ["USE SCHEMA", "SELECT"], "SCHEMA", "prod.gold"),
        ("data-engineers", ["USE CATALOG", "USE SCHEMA", "CREATE TABLE", "SELECT", "MODIFY"], "CATALOG", "prod"),
        ("etl-service", ["USE CATALOG"], "CATALOG", "prod"),
        ("etl-service", ["USE SCHEMA", "SELECT", "MODIFY", "CREATE TABLE"], "SCHEMA", "prod.bronze"),
    ],
}

def generate(spec):
    out = []
    for c, o in spec["catalogs"].items():
        out.append(f"CREATE CATALOG IF NOT EXISTS {c} MANAGED LOCATION '{o['managed_location']}';")
        out.append(f"ALTER CATALOG {c} OWNER TO `{o['owner']}`;")
    for s, o in spec["schemas"].items():
        out.append(f"CREATE SCHEMA IF NOT EXISTS {s};")
        out.append(f"ALTER SCHEMA {s} OWNER TO `{o['owner']}`;")
    for who, privs, kind, name in spec["grants"]:
        out.append(f"GRANT {', '.join(privs)} ON {kind} {name} TO `{who}`;")
    return out

def contains(a, b): a = a.rstrip("/") + "/"; return (b.rstrip("/") + "/").startswith(a)

def lint(spec):
    problems = []
    # 1. owners are groups, not people
    for kind, items in (("catalog", spec["catalogs"]), ("schema", spec["schemas"])):
        for name, o in items.items():
            if o["owner"] not in spec["groups"] or "@" in o["owner"]:
                problems.append(f"OWNER: {kind} {name} is owned by {o['owner']!r}, which is not a known group")
    # 2. grants go to known groups only
    for who, privs, kind, name in spec["grants"]:
        if who not in spec["groups"]: problems.append(f"PRINCIPAL: grant to unknown principal {who!r}")
    # 3. usage prerequisites: any SELECT/MODIFY/CREATE TABLE on schema or catalog needs USE CATALOG (+ USE SCHEMA at/under schema)
    def privs_of(p, kind, name):
        return {x for w, ps, k, n in spec["grants"] if w == p and k == kind and n == name for x in ps}
    for p in {g[0] for g in spec["grants"]}:
        for s in spec["schemas"]:
            cat = s.split(".")[0]
            eff = set()
            for w, ps, k, n in spec["grants"]:
                if w != p: continue
                if (k == "CATALOG" and n == cat) or (k == "SCHEMA" and n == s): eff |= set(ps)
            data = eff & {"SELECT", "MODIFY", "CREATE TABLE"}
            has_cat = "USE CATALOG" in privs_of(p, "CATALOG", cat)
            has_sch = "USE SCHEMA" in eff
            if data and not has_cat: problems.append(f"USAGE: {p} has {sorted(data)} on {s} but no USE CATALOG on {cat}")
            if data and not has_sch: problems.append(f"USAGE: {p} has {sorted(data)} on {s} but no USE SCHEMA (granted on schema or inherited from catalog)")
    # 4. catalog-wide SELECT must not reach a sensitive schema for non-engineering groups
    for who, privs, kind, name in spec["grants"]:
        if kind == "CATALOG" and "SELECT" in privs and who not in ("data-engineers", "platform-admins"):
            sens = [s for s, o in spec["schemas"].items() if s.startswith(name + ".") and o["sensitive"]]
            if sens: problems.append(f"INHERIT: catalog-level SELECT for {who} reaches sensitive schema(s) {sens}")
    # 5. ALL PRIVILEGES shortcut
    for who, privs, kind, name in spec["grants"]:
        if "ALL PRIVILEGES" in privs: problems.append(f"ALLPRIV: {who} granted ALL PRIVILEGES on {name}; it excludes MANAGE, list explicit privileges")
    # 6. managed locations must sit inside an external location and external locations must not overlap
    locs = list(spec["locations"].items())
    for i, (n1, u1) in enumerate(locs):
        for n2, u2 in locs[i+1:]:
            if contains(u1, u2) or contains(u2, u1): problems.append(f"OVERLAP: external locations {n1!r} and {n2!r} overlap")
    for c, o in spec["catalogs"].items():
        if not any(contains(u, o["managed_location"]) for u in spec["locations"].values()):
            problems.append(f"LOCATION: catalog {c} managed location {o['managed_location']} is not inside any external location")
    return problems

if __name__ == "__main__":
    print("-- generated SQL --"); print("\n".join(generate(SPEC)))
    print("\n-- lint --"); probs = lint(SPEC)
    print("\n".join(probs) if probs else "OK"); sys.exit(1 if probs else 0)

test_platform.py mutates the spec in eight ways and asserts the linter's verdict for each:

import copy
from uc_platform import SPEC, lint

def mutate(fn):
    s = copy.deepcopy(SPEC); fn(s); return lint(s)

cases = {
 "baseline spec is clean": lambda s: None,
 "person owns a schema": lambda s: s["schemas"]["prod.gold"].update(owner="dana@acme.com"),
 "analysts get SELECT on whole catalog": lambda s: s["grants"].append(("analysts", ["SELECT"], "CATALOG", "prod")),
 "SELECT on schema but no USE CATALOG": lambda s: s["grants"].remove(("etl-service", ["USE CATALOG"], "CATALOG", "prod")),
 "ALL PRIVILEGES shortcut": lambda s: s["grants"].append(("etl-service", ["ALL PRIVILEGES"], "SCHEMA", "prod.gold")),
 "overlapping external locations": lambda s: s["locations"].update(raw_all="s3://acme-raw"),
 "catalog storage outside any location": lambda s: s["catalogs"]["prod"].update(managed_location="s3://other/uc"),
 "grant to unknown principal": lambda s: s["grants"].append(("contractors", ["USE CATALOG"], "CATALOG", "prod")),
}
failed = 0
for name, fn in cases.items():
    probs = mutate(fn)
    expect_clean = name.startswith("baseline")
    ok = (not probs) if expect_clean else bool(probs)
    failed += not ok
    print(f"[{'PASS' if ok else 'FAIL'}] {name}")
    for p in probs: print("        ->", p)
print("\nall tests passed" if not failed else f"\n{failed} FAILED")

docs.title: Reading the results
docs.text:
• The catalog-wide SELECT mutation triggers two different rules, which shows why linting beats eyeballing. The INHERIT rule catches the real danger (inheritance reaches silver, which holds PII). The two USAGE messages are a quirk of my linter: analysts hold SELECT on the whole catalog, which covers bronze and silver as well, but they have USE SCHEMA only on gold, so those schemas would not actually be readable. The linter is conservative: it flags a privilege that can't take effect, because an unusable grant usually means a mistake in intent.
  • The USE CATALOG mutation reproduces the lesson 02 trap in a form you can review in a pull request.
  • The overlap check uses a trailing-separator comparison, so landing-archive isn't mistaken for a child of landing (Lesson 03).

docs.title: What this project doesn't do
docs.text: It doesn't read actual state from a workspace (a real tool would compare the spec to SHOW GRANTS output or the information_schema privilege views and report drift), doesn't model row filters, masks or ABAC policies (Lesson 04), doesn't create storage credentials or external locations (they need cloud-side setup), and doesn't model group membership from your identity provider. In production this role is played by Terraform's Databricks provider, Declarative Automation Bundles for workspace objects (Level 4 · 01), or the Databricks SDK; check their current docs, as I did not run them.

docs.title: Extensions
docs.text:
1. Add owners_must_be_groups for tables and a rule that no securable has both MODIFY for analysts and SELECT only for engineers (a likely inversion).
  2. Add a masks section: columns tagged pii must have either a mask policy for analysts or no analyst access to the schema. Generate the CREATE POLICY statements from Lesson 04.
  3. Add drift detection: parse a pasted SHOW GRANTS output into the same structure and diff it against the spec.
  4. Add a rule that environments (dev, prod) never share a managed location.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: The pattern is desired-state configuration: the spec states what should exist, the generator produces idempotent statements (IF NOT EXISTS, GRANT and REVOKE which are both safe to repeat), and the linter is a policy engine that rejects specs violating organization rules before they reach a workspace. Tools like Terraform add the missing piece (state): they compare the desired spec to what exists and compute the minimal changes. Everything in this lesson would still be true if the generator emitted Terraform instead of SQL.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Making grants by hand in a UI with no review or history.
  • A linter nobody maintains: encode each incident as a new rule and test.
  • Generating REVOKE blindly from a spec that is incomplete and removing legitimate access.
  • Treating a clean lint as proof of security: it checks consistency with rules, not correctness of the rules.
  • No separation between environments in the spec.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Run both scripts. Then add a finance schema with PII and a finance-readers group; make the linter pass.
  2. Write two new tests: one where a schema is owned by a service principal not listed in groups, one where a group has MODIFY on a schema but no SELECT. Decide what the linter should say.
  3. Add the Delta Sharing/OpenSharing share from Lesson 08 to the spec (a share and a recipient) and a lint rule that shares may only include tables from gold.
  4. Write down three governance rules your organization has that this linter cannot check, and how you would check them.

docs.title: Level 4 · Development, ML & Operations
docs.text:
Level 4 is about running the platform as a team over years rather than as a single person for an afternoon: shipping changes safely, testing them, tracking models, controlling cost and speed, keeping tables healthy, moving in from other systems, and planning the whole thing.

What was run, and what wasn't

As before, open-source Spark 4.2.0 and Delta Lake 4.4.1 ran locally, and so did several other open-source tools used here: MLflow 3.17.2, scikit-learn, pytest, sqlglot and the delta-sharing and databricks-sql-connector clients. Platform-only features (bundle deployment, Model Serving, AI Functions, Genie, AI Search, Predictive Optimization, Photon, serverless compute, billing system tables) were not run and are described from the Databricks documentation (October 2026); the cost lesson uses invented mock billing rows and says so. Two local experiments gave weak or no results (a caching micro-benchmark with no measurable gain, and a Python UDF timing that hung), and the performance lesson reports them as they happened. Several product names changed recently; the lessons note the old and new names.

Prerequisites: Levels 1 to 3.

docs.title: Modules
docs.text:
1. Declarative Automation Bundles & CI/CD: databricks.yml, dev vs production mode, a CI workflow and a bundle linter.
  2. Testing PySpark & Delta Code Locally: pure transforms, pytest, assertDataFrameEqual, a caught bug.
  3. MLflow: Tracking Experiments: runs, comparison, and the skops trust finding.
  4. Model Registry & Serving: aliases, signatures, a local REST server and Databricks Model Serving.
  5. AI Functions, Genie Agents & AI Search: using AI features responsibly, plus a retrieval toy.
  6. Cost Management: DBUs, Budgets & System Billing: attribution, retractions and levers.
  7. Performance: Photon, Serverless & Caching: a tuning order and honest measurements.
  8. Table Maintenance & Predictive Optimization: deletion vectors measured, purge and vacuum.
  9. Migrating to Databricks: convert, clone, Hive to Unity Catalog, and dialect translation pitfalls.
  10. Capstone: An End-to-End Platform Plan: a plan as data and a checker.

docs.title: After the course
docs.text: Use the exercises as a checklist for a real workspace: nearly every lesson names something you can verify on a Free Edition account that this course could only describe.

docs.title: 01 · Declarative Automation Bundles & CI/CD
docs.text:
Clicking jobs together in a UI works for one person on one afternoon. A team needs the job, its pipeline, its schedule, its permissions and its code in Git, reviewed in pull requests, tested automatically and deployed the same way to dev and prod. Declarative Automation Bundles (the new name for what was Databricks Asset Bundles; older material uses the old name) are Databricks' infrastructure-as-code answer for workspace resources.

What was run, and what wasn't

The Databricks CLI wasn't installed on the machine this course was written on, and there was no workspace, so no databricks bundle command was run: nothing was validated against the real bundle schema or deployed. What I did run locally: the YAML files below were parsed with PyYAML, and a small linter I wrote (shown below) applied a few of the documented best practices to them. Field names and behaviours come from the Databricks documentation pages on bundles and deployment modes (October 2026). Treat the YAML as a documented-pattern sketch to adapt and validate with databricks bundle validate.

docs.title: What a bundle is
docs.text:
A bundle is a project folder with a root databricks.yml that declares: the bundle's name, targets (environments), variables, and the resources to deploy: Lakeflow Jobs, pipelines, dashboards, model-serving endpoints, MLflow experiments and registered models, plus source files (notebooks, Python, wheels) and tests. The CLI then validates, deploys and runs them:

databricks bundle init                  # start from a template
databricks bundle validate -t dev       # check configuration
databricks bundle deploy -t dev         # create/update resources in the dev workspace
databricks bundle run orders_daily -t dev
databricks bundle destroy -t dev        # delete what the bundle created

(Commands from the documentation, not run here.) Deployment is idempotent and declarative: you describe the end state; the CLI works out what to create, update or delete, and tracks what it deployed in a state file.

docs.title: databricks.yml
docs.text:
This is the root file I used (the lint output is further down):

bundle:
  name: orders_platform

include:
  - resources/*.yml

variables:
  catalog:
    description: Unity Catalog catalog for this environment
    default: dev
  warehouse_id:
    description: SQL warehouse used by SQL tasks

targets:
  dev:
    mode: development
    default: true
    workspace:
      host: https://dev-workspace.example.cloud.databricks.com
    variables:
      catalog: dev

  prod:
    mode: production
    workspace:
      host: https://prod-workspace.example.cloud.databricks.com
      root_path: /Workspace/Shared/.bundle/${bundle.name}/${bundle.target}
    git:
      branch: main
    run_as:
      service_principal_name: "00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000"
    permissions:
      - group_name: data-engineers
        level: CAN_MANAGE
      - group_name: analysts
        level: CAN_VIEW
    variables:
      catalog: prod

Reading it:

  • include pulls resource definitions from other files, keeping the root small.
  • variables are declared once, referenced as ${var.catalog}, and given per-target values. The warehouse_id has no default, so supplying it is required wherever it's used.
  • Targets are environments. dev is the default for local work. prod uses mode: production and run_as.
  • ${bundle.name}, ${bundle.target} and similar are substitution variables resolved at deploy time.

docs.title: The two deployment modes
docs.text:
From the deployment-modes documentation:

mode: development mode: production Resource names Prefixed with [dev <your short name>] and tagged dev, so many developers can deploy the same bundle side by side No prefix Schedules and triggers Paused, so a dev deploy never starts a nightly job Active Concurrent runs Enabled for faster iteration As configured Pipelines development: true Validated as development: false Git Not checked Current branch must match the target's git.branch (override with --force) Identity You Databricks recommends a service principal via run_as; without it, run_as and permissions must be stated explicitly Cluster override --cluster-id can override job clusters Not allowed Deployment lock Disabled for speed Enabled

Presets let you customize these defaults. The lesson: development is for you, production is guardrails.

docs.title: A resource file
docs.text:
resources:
  jobs:
    orders_daily:
      name: orders-daily-${bundle.target}
      schedule:
        quartz_cron_expression: "0 30 2 * * ?"
        timezone_id: UTC
      max_concurrent_runs: 1
      parameters:
        - name: catalog
          default: ${var.catalog}
      tasks:
        - task_key: build_silver
          spark_python_task:
            python_file: ../src/build_silver.py
            parameters: ["--catalog", "${var.catalog}"]

The job name embeds ${bundle.target}, so dev and prod deployments never collide. ${var.catalog} makes the same code write to dev or prod Unity Catalog catalogs depending on the target (Level 3 · 01), a pattern that replaces hard-coded catalog names inside notebooks. max_concurrent_runs: 1 prevents overlapping runs (Level 3 · 07). Paths in python_file are relative to the resource file.

docs.title: Checking the bundle with a linter
docs.text:
A real databricks bundle validate checks against the schema. My stand-in checks a few things the docs recommend, so you can run them without a workspace:

"""Tiny static checks for a Declarative Automation Bundle project. Not the Databricks CLI: it cannot validate against the real schema."""
import re, sys, glob, yaml
root = sys.argv[1]
cfg = yaml.safe_load(open(f"{root}/databricks.yml"))
problems = []
declared = set(cfg.get("variables", {}))
text = "".join(open(f).read() for f in [f"{root}/databricks.yml", *glob.glob(f"{root}/resources/*.yml")])
for ref in sorted(set(re.findall(r"\$\{var\.([A-Za-z0-9_]+)\}", text))):
    if ref not in declared: problems.append(f"variable ${{var.{ref}}} is used but not declared")
for name, t in cfg["targets"].items():
    if name.startswith("prod"):
        if t.get("mode") != "production": problems.append(f"target {name}: prod-like target should set mode: production")
        if "run_as" not in t: problems.append(f"target {name}: no run_as (use a service principal)")
        if "permissions" not in t: problems.append(f"target {name}: no permissions block")
        if "@" in str(t.get("workspace", {}).get("root_path", "")): problems.append(f"target {name}: root_path points into a user's folder")
for f in glob.glob(f"{root}/resources/*.yml"):
    r = yaml.safe_load(open(f))
    for jn, j in r["resources"].get("jobs", {}).items():
        if j.get("max_concurrent_runs") is None: problems.append(f"job {jn}: max_concurrent_runs not set")
        keys = [t["task_key"] for t in j["tasks"]]
        if len(keys) != len(set(keys)): problems.append(f"job {jn}: duplicate task_key")
print("targets:", list(cfg["targets"]), "| variables declared:", sorted(declared))
print("\n".join(problems) if problems else "OK: no problems found by these checks")

On the project above:

targets: ['dev', 'prod'] | variables declared: ['catalog', 'warehouse_id']
OK: no problems found by these checks

On a copy where I removed mode: production and run_as from prod, pointed root_path into a person's folder, deleted the catalog variable declaration and removed max_concurrent_runs:

targets: ['dev', 'prod'] | variables declared: ['warehouse_id', 'wh']
variable ${var.catalog} is used but not declared
target prod: prod-like target should set mode: production
target prod: no run_as (use a service principal)
target prod: root_path points into a user's folder
job orders_daily: max_concurrent_runs not set

This catches obvious mistakes in seconds in CI, but it knows nothing about the real schema, so it complements databricks bundle validate and doesn't replace it.

docs.title: CI/CD with GitHub Actions
docs.text:
A typical flow: pull request runs unit tests and bundle validate; merging to main deploys to production with a service principal; secrets live in the CI system, never in the repo. This workflow follows that shape (it parses as YAML; it wasn't run in GitHub Actions, and databricks/setup-cli is the CLI setup action named in the Databricks documentation, which you should pin to a version rather than @main in real use):

name: deploy
on:
  pull_request:
  push:
    branches: [main]
jobs:
  test-and-validate:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with: {python-version: "3.12"}
      - run: pip install -e ".[test]" && pytest -q
      - uses: databricks/setup-cli@main
      - run: databricks bundle validate -t prod
        env:
          DATABRICKS_HOST: ${{ secrets.DATABRICKS_HOST }}
          DATABRICKS_CLIENT_ID: ${{ secrets.DATABRICKS_CLIENT_ID }}
          DATABRICKS_CLIENT_SECRET: ${{ secrets.DATABRICKS_CLIENT_SECRET }}
  deploy-prod:
    if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
    needs: test-and-validate
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: production
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: databricks/setup-cli@main
      - run: databricks bundle deploy -t prod
        env:
          DATABRICKS_HOST: ${{ secrets.DATABRICKS_HOST }}
          DATABRICKS_CLIENT_ID: ${{ secrets.DATABRICKS_CLIENT_ID }}
          DATABRICKS_CLIENT_SECRET: ${{ secrets.DATABRICKS_CLIENT_SECRET }}

Design points:

  • Test first (Lesson 02): unit tests of transformation code run on the CI runner with local Spark; no cluster needed.
  • Validate on PRs, deploy on main, with the environment: production gate giving you an approval step.
  • Authenticate as a service principal with OAuth client credentials (DATABRICKS_CLIENT_ID/SECRET), not a person's token.
  • A typical promotion path is dev (every developer), staging (merge to a release branch, integration tests on real data), prod (tag or main). The same bundle with different targets and variables means the code under test is the code that ships.
  • Add an integration test step that runs the deployed job in a staging target and asserts on output tables.

docs.title: Secrets and configuration
docs.text: Don't put secrets in YAML. Use Databricks secrets (secret scopes backed by Databricks or your cloud's secret manager) and read them at run time with dbutils.secrets.get(scope, key); CI secrets only authenticate the deploy. Environment-specific non-secret settings belong in variables/targets.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: bundle deploy does three things. It builds artifacts (such as a Python wheel); it uploads source files to the workspace folder named by root_path (default under the deployer's home, keyed by bundle name and target); and it applies resources by calling the Jobs/Pipelines/other REST APIs, creating objects it hasn't seen and updating those it has, recording the mapping from bundle resource name to workspace object ID in its state. That state is how destroy knows what to delete and how a rename is detected. Documentation describes both Terraform-based and a newer "direct" deployment engine; the YAML you write is the same either way. Because everything flows through the same APIs you could call yourself, a bundle is a convenience and a discipline, not a new capability.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Deploying prod from a laptop with a personal token instead of CI with a service principal.
  • Hard-coded catalog/schema/warehouse IDs in notebooks rather than variables.
  • Dev deployments that start production schedules (use development mode, which pauses them).
  • Editing deployed jobs in the UI; the next deploy overwrites the change (drift).
  • One giant databricks.yml instead of included resource files.
  • Unpinned actions/CLI versions in CI, so a pipeline changes behaviour on its own.
  • Skipping tests because "it's just config": job config is code.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Add a pipeline resource (Lesson 06 of Level 3) to the bundle and make the job depend on it. Extend the linter to flag any pipeline in a production target with development: true.
  2. Add a staging target with its own variables and workspace host, and decide which mode it should use (justify).
  3. Write down the exact steps for rolling back a bad production deploy using Git and the CI workflow above.
  4. (Needs the CLI) Install the Databricks CLI, run databricks bundle init with a default template, and compare the generated databricks.yml with this one; list three differences.

docs.title: 02 · Testing PySpark & Delta Code Locally
docs.text:
Notebook code that was only ever "tested" by looking at a display() is a liability. The good news from Level 1 is that the same Spark runs on a laptop, so ordinary unit tests can cover most transformation logic in seconds, with no cluster, no workspace and no cloud bill. This lesson sets up that project and is honest about what such tests cannot prove.

What was run

The project and tests below were executed with pytest on local Spark 4.2.0 (Python 3.12); the pass count and the failure message are copied from those runs. Anything that depends on the Databricks runtime, Unity Catalog, serverless compute, Photon, Auto Loader or Lakeflow semantics is outside what these tests can see (see the last section).

docs.title: Structure code so it can be tested
docs.text:
