The single most useful habit: keep transformations as pure functions that take DataFrames (and plain parameters) and return a DataFrame, with no reading, writing, spark.sql against catalogs, or dbutils inside them. I/O goes in a thin "main" notebook or script that reads, calls the function and writes. That thin layer is covered by an integration test on the platform (Lesson 01's staging target); the logic is covered by fast local tests.

tproj/
├── src/orders/transforms.py     # pure functions
└── tests/
    ├── conftest.py              # a shared SparkSession fixture
    └── test_transforms.py

src/orders/transforms.py:

"""Pure DataFrame-in, DataFrame-out functions: easy to test, no I/O, no global state."""
from pyspark.sql import DataFrame, Window, functions as F


def clean_orders(df: DataFrame) -> DataFrame:
    """Type the raw columns; unparseable or negative amounts are returned in the 'rejects' flag instead of failing."""
    return (df.withColumn("order_id", F.expr("try_cast(order_id AS INT)"))
              .withColumn("amount", F.expr("try_cast(amount AS DECIMAL(10,2))"))
              .withColumn("is_valid", F.col("order_id").isNotNull() & F.col("amount").isNotNull() & (F.col("amount") >= 0)))


def latest_per_key(df: DataFrame, key: str, order_col: str) -> DataFrame:
    w = Window.partitionBy(key).orderBy(F.col(order_col).desc())
    return df.withColumn("_rn", F.row_number().over(w)).where("_rn = 1").drop("_rn")


def revenue_by_customer(df: DataFrame) -> DataFrame:
    return (df.where(F.col("status") == "ok")
              .groupBy("customer").agg(F.sum("amount").alias("revenue"), F.count("*").alias("orders")))

tests/conftest.py creates one Spark session for the whole test run (starting Spark costs seconds; creating one per test would make the suite crawl):

import pytest
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession


@pytest.fixture(scope="session")
def spark():
    s = (SparkSession.builder.master("local[2]").appName("tests").config("spark.sql.shuffle.partitions", "2")
         .config("spark.ui.enabled", "false").getOrCreate())
    yield s
    s.stop()

tests/test_transforms.py:

import sys, pathlib
sys.path.insert(0, str(pathlib.Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1] / "src"))
from decimal import Decimal
import pytest
from pyspark.testing import assertDataFrameEqual
from orders.transforms import clean_orders, latest_per_key, revenue_by_customer


def test_clean_orders_flags_bad_rows(spark):
    raw = spark.createDataFrame([("1", "10.50"), ("x", "5"), ("3", "-4"), ("4", "abc")], "order_id string, amount string")
    got = clean_orders(raw).select("order_id", "is_valid")
    want = spark.createDataFrame([(1, True), (None, False), (3, False), (4, False)], "order_id int, is_valid boolean")
    assertDataFrameEqual(got, want)


def test_latest_per_key_keeps_newest(spark):
    df = spark.createDataFrame([(1, "old", 1), (1, "new", 2), (2, "only", 1)], "id int, v string, ts int")
    got = latest_per_key(df, "id", "ts").select("id", "v")
    assertDataFrameEqual(got, spark.createDataFrame([(1, "new"), (2, "only")], "id int, v string"))


def test_revenue_ignores_refunds(spark):
    df = spark.createDataFrame([("ana", Decimal("10.00"), "ok"), ("ana", Decimal("5.00"), "refund"), ("bo", Decimal("2.50"), "ok")],
                               "customer string, amount decimal(10,2), status string")
    got = revenue_by_customer(df)
    want = spark.createDataFrame([("ana", Decimal("10.00"), 1), ("bo", Decimal("2.50"), 1)], "customer string, revenue decimal(20,2), orders bigint")
    assertDataFrameEqual(got, want, checkRowOrder=False)


def test_empty_input_does_not_crash(spark):
    empty = spark.createDataFrame([], "customer string, amount decimal(10,2), status string")
    assert revenue_by_customer(empty).count() == 0


def test_latest_per_key_tie_is_a_bug_magnet(spark):
    """Documenting a real hazard: with equal timestamps the winner is not defined, so the result may vary."""
    df = spark.createDataFrame([(1, "a", 1), (1, "b", 1)], "id int, v string, ts int")
    assert latest_per_key(df, "id", "ts").count() == 1     # we can assert the count, but not which row survives

Running pytest -q from the project folder with PYSPARK_PYTHON set (Level 1 · 10):

.....                                                                    [100%]
5 passed in 9.27s

Five tests in about nine seconds, most of it Spark's start-up. Adding fifty more tests costs little, because the session is shared.

docs.title: assertDataFrameEqual
docs.text:
PySpark ships pyspark.testing.assertDataFrameEqual (and assertSchemaEqual). It compares schema and rows, ignores row order unless you ask (checkRowOrder=True), and produces a diff. Here is what it reported when I deliberately introduced the classic bug of forgetting the status = 'ok' filter in revenue_by_customer:

[DIFFERENT_ROWS] Results do not match: ( 100.00000 % )
*** actual ***
! Row(customer='ana', revenue=Decimal('15.00'), orders=2)

*** expected ***
! Row(customer='ana', revenue=Decimal('10.00'), orders=1)

(The colour codes in the terminal output are removed.) That is precisely why tests are written against known tiny inputs: the failure tells you what the code did wrong, at a glance.

Details worth knowing:

  • Types are part of equality. The expected frame declares revenue decimal(20,2); Spark widened decimal(10,2) sums to decimal(20,2). A test written with the wrong decimal precision fails even when the numbers agree, which is a good thing: schema drift is a bug.
  • Floating point: use rtol/atol arguments for doubles, or better, use DECIMAL.
  • Row order is not defined in Spark; do not assert on it unless the code sorts.

docs.title: What to test
docs.text:
1. The happy path with a handful of rows.
  2. Edge cases that real data produces: NULLs, empty input (the empty-DataFrame test above), duplicates, the boundary of a filter (amount = 0), a single row, unicode strings, timestamps around daylight-saving shifts.
  3. Data-quality rules as functions: clean_orders returns a flag instead of failing, and the test pins the exact behaviour for 'x', '-4' and 'abc'.
  4. Properties where examples are awkward: "output rows never exceed input rows", "sum of revenue before = sum after".
  5. Known hazards written down as tests. The last test documents that latest_per_key with tied timestamps keeps one row but which row is undefined (Level 1 · 04's tie trap). A test that asserts only what is guaranteed is honest, and a reader sees the hazard.

docs.title: Testing Delta behaviour locally
docs.text: Delta-specific code (MERGE, schema evolution, CDF) can be tested with open-source Delta on local Spark, using a temp directory per test (tmp_path fixture) and the configure_spark_with_delta_pip builder from Level 1. For example, a merge function can be tested by creating a table in tmp_path, running the function twice and asserting the second run changed nothing (idempotence, Level 2 · 10). Be aware that open-source Delta differs from the Databricks runtime in defaults and available features, so a local pass says "the logic is right", not "it will behave identically on the platform".

docs.title: Mocking the platform
docs.text: dbutils, spark.table("catalog.schema.t") against Unity Catalog and secrets don't exist locally. Options: pass the table names and DataFrames in as parameters; wrap platform calls in a small adapter class you can fake in tests; and avoid importing dbutils at module level. If you need dbutils in a library, the Databricks SDK and Databricks Connect can run Spark code from your IDE against a real remote compute resource (documented; not run here), which is useful for integration-style tests but needs a workspace and bills compute.

docs.title: What local tests cannot prove
docs.text:
• Performance and scale: ten rows say nothing about skew, shuffles or memory (Level 2 · 05 and 06).
  • Platform behaviour: Unity Catalog permissions, serverless library restrictions, Photon differences, Auto Loader semantics.
  • Concurrency and failure recovery: retries, conflicts, partial failures.
  • Real data shapes: your production data will contain cases you didn't invent. Feed anonymized samples or property-based generators into tests.

So the full pyramid is: many fast local unit tests, some integration tests on a staging target with real catalogs and realistic data volumes, and monitoring in production (Level 4 · 06 and 08). CI runs the first two (Lesson 01).

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: pytest collects the test functions, builds the session-scoped spark fixture once, and injects it into each test by name. Each test constructs tiny DataFrames with createDataFrame (in-memory, schema-declared), applies the function under test (which only builds a plan), and assertDataFrameEqual triggers actions on both sides, collects both results to the driver, and compares schema and rows. Because local[2] runs Spark in one process, nothing leaves your machine and failures give normal Python stack traces.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• A new SparkSession per test (slow) or sharing mutable global state between tests.
  • Tests that read production tables: slow, flaky, expensive, and risky.
  • Asserting on show() output or on row order.
  • Skipping the empty and NULL cases that cause most production incidents.
  • Putting logic in notebooks only: unit-testable code belongs in a package or files imported by notebooks (Git folders and bundles make this straightforward).
  • Trusting a green local suite as proof the platform job works.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Add tests for clean_orders with an amount of "0", "1e3" and a 9-digit amount that overflows decimal(10,2). Decide what the function should do and encode it.
  2. Fix the tie hazard: add a deterministic tie-breaker parameter to latest_per_key and a test proving the winner is stable.
  3. Write a Delta test (using the Level 1 builder) that merges a batch into a table twice and asserts the table is unchanged after the second run.
  4. Add a GitHub Actions job (Lesson 01) that runs pytest on every pull request. What must the runner have installed for Spark to start?

docs.title: 03 · MLflow: Tracking Experiments
docs.text:
Machine learning code produces many near-identical experiments, and "which settings gave that 0.96 AUC last Tuesday?" is a question people regularly fail to answer. MLflow is the open-source standard for recording the answer, and Databricks provides a managed MLflow integrated with Unity Catalog. The tracking API is the same in both places, which means you can learn and test it locally.

What was run

Everything in the "runnable" sections used open-source MLflow 3.17.2 with scikit-learn 1.9.1 on a laptop, tracking to a local SQLite file; output blocks are copied from that run. The data is synthetic (make_classification), so the AUC values only illustrate the workflow and say nothing about any real problem. Databricks-specific behaviour (managed tracking server, notebook experiments, autologging, Unity Catalog model registry) is from the Databricks MLflow documentation (October 2026) and was not run.

docs.title: Concepts
docs.text:
• An experiment groups related runs (for example "churn-demo").
  • A run is one execution: its parameters (inputs such as C=0.01), metrics (numbers such as auc, optionally logged over time), tags (free labels), and artifacts (files: plots, the serialized model, input examples).
  • A model logged to a run can later be registered, loaded and served (next lesson).
  • The tracking store holds run metadata (a database or the Databricks backend); the artifact store holds the files.

docs.title: Tracking four runs
docs.text:
import mlflow, numpy as np, os, warnings
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")
from sklearn.datasets import make_classification
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score, accuracy_score

mlflow.set_tracking_uri("sqlite:///mlflow_demo.db")
mlflow.set_experiment("churn-demo")
X, y = make_classification(n_samples=4000, n_features=12, n_informative=5, weights=[0.8, 0.2], random_state=7)
Xtr, Xte, ytr, yte = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.25, random_state=7, stratify=y)

def run(name, model, params):
    with mlflow.start_run(run_name=name) as r:
        mlflow.log_params(params); mlflow.set_tag("team", "growth")
        model.fit(Xtr, ytr)
        p = model.predict_proba(Xte)[:, 1]
        mlflow.log_metric("auc", roc_auc_score(yte, p)); mlflow.log_metric("accuracy", accuracy_score(yte, p > 0.5))
        mlflow.sklearn.log_model(model, name="model", input_example=Xte[:2], skops_trusted_types=["sklearn.tree._tree.Tree"] if params["model"] == "rf" else None)
        return r.info.run_id

ids = {}
for C in (0.01, 1.0):
    ids[f"logreg_C{C}"] = run(f"logreg_C{C}", LogisticRegression(C=C, max_iter=500), {"model": "logreg", "C": C})
for d in (3, 12):
    ids[f"rf_depth{d}"] = run(f"rf_depth{d}", RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=100, max_depth=d, random_state=7), {"model": "rf", "max_depth": d})

df = mlflow.search_runs(experiment_names=["churn-demo"], order_by=["metrics.auc DESC"])
print(df[["tags.mlflow.runName", "params.model", "metrics.auc", "metrics.accuracy"]].round(4).to_string(index=False))
best = df.iloc[0]["run_id"]; print("best run:", df.iloc[0]["tags.mlflow.runName"])
m = mlflow.sklearn.load_model(f"runs:/{best}/model"); print("reloaded model predicts:", m.predict(Xte[:5]), "truth:", yte[:5])
print(sorted(os.listdir("mlruns"))[:3] if os.path.exists("mlruns") else "no mlruns dir")
art = [r for r in os.walk(".") if r[0].endswith("/artifacts") or "/artifacts" in r[0]]
print("artifact files for one run:", sorted({f for _, _, fs in art[:6] for f in fs})[:8])

Output of the run:

tags.mlflow.runName params.model  metrics.auc  metrics.accuracy
         rf_depth12           rf       0.9600             0.928
          rf_depth3           rf       0.8671             0.839
       logreg_C0.01       logreg       0.8467             0.838
        logreg_C1.0       logreg       0.8447             0.848
best run: rf_depth12
reloaded model predicts: [1 0 0 0 0] truth: [1 0 0 0 0]
artifact files for one run: ['MLmodel', 'conda.yaml', 'input_example.json', 'model.skops', 'python_env.yaml', 'requirements.txt', 'serving_input_example.json']

What happened:

  1. set_tracking_uri("sqlite:///...") chose a local SQLite database as the tracking store (the model files still went to a local ./mlruns folder: the run listing printed ['1'], the experiment's artifact directory). On Databricks the URI is databricks and you don't set it.
  2. Each start_run logged parameters, two metrics, a tag and the model. search_runs returns a pandas DataFrame, here sorted by AUC, which is the comparison table you'd otherwise keep in a spreadsheet. Random forest with depth 12 won on this synthetic data, and deeper trees beating shallow ones is just a property of this made-up dataset.
  3. The model was reloaded from the run with runs:/<run_id>/model and predicted the first five test labels correctly. The artifact folder contains the serialized model plus MLmodel (the flavor and signature metadata), environment files (conda.yaml, python_env.yaml, requirements.txt) and an input example. Those environment files are what make a model reproducible elsewhere.

docs.title: A security finding worth knowing
docs.text:
My first run failed when logging the random forest:

mlflow.exceptions.MlflowException: The saved sklearn model references untrusted types. If you are sure loading these types is safe,
set the 'skops_trusted_types' parameter when calling 'log_model' or 'save_model' to the list of trusted types. Root error: Untrusted
types found in the file: ['sklearn.tree._tree.Tree'].

In this MLflow version the default scikit-learn serialization is the skops format (model.skops above), not pickle. Pickle files can execute arbitrary code when loaded, whereas skops refuses types it hasn't been told to trust. The tree-based models contain sklearn.tree._tree.Tree, and the error text explains that a malicious file could set out-of-range node indices that crash or read out-of-bounds memory when predict is called. I passed skops_trusted_types=["sklearn.tree._tree.Tree"] for the random forest only, after reading that explanation, and the logistic regression needed no allowance. The general rule: loading a model is executing someone else's artifact, so treat model files like code, and trust only types you have reviewed. This is an MLflow 3.x behaviour as observed here; behaviour in other versions may differ.

docs.title: Autologging
docs.text: Instead of calling log_param yourself, mlflow.autolog() instruments supported libraries (scikit-learn, XGBoost, PyTorch, Spark ML and others) to record parameters, metrics and the model automatically. Per the Databricks documentation, when you attach an interactive Python notebook to a cluster, Databricks Autologging calls mlflow.autolog() for you (generally available with Databricks Runtime 10.4 LTS ML or above), so training sessions in notebooks are tracked without code. The convenience has a cost: you log whatever the integration decides to, so explicitly log business-specific things (the data version, the git commit, the training table's Delta version) yourself.

docs.title: MLflow on Databricks
docs.text:
From the documentation:

  • Experiments are either workspace experiments (created in the UI/API, usable by any notebook by name or ID) or notebook experiments (created automatically when you start a run with no active experiment). Experiment names are workspace paths such as /Users/you@example.com/churn-demo.
  • Tracking is a managed service: no server to run, runs appear in the Experiments UI and are governed by workspace permissions.
  • MLflow 3 adds Logged Models and Deployment Jobs, and extends tracking to GenAI: traces, evaluation, prompt management.
  • The model registry lives in Unity Catalog (next lesson), so models get the same three-level names, grants, lineage and audit as tables.
  • Stale experiments are purged from workspaces (a GDPR-related policy noted in the docs), so do not treat the tracking store as your only record of a model you must keep. Register models you need.

A typical Databricks notebook snippet (documented pattern; not run):

import mlflow
mlflow.set_registry_uri("databricks-uc")          # Unity Catalog as the model registry
mlflow.set_experiment("/Users/you@example.com/churn-demo")
with mlflow.start_run():
    ...
    mlflow.log_param("training_table_version", 42)

docs.title: What to log (and why)
docs.text: Log Why Hyperparameters and the random seed Reproduce the run Training data identity: table name and Delta version or snapshot timestamp "Same code, different data" explains most unreproducible results (use time travel, Level 1 · 08) Code version (git SHA; Databricks records it for notebooks in Git folders) Know which code produced the model Metrics on a held-out set, and on slices that matter (per region) A single AUC hides failures on sub-populations Model signature and input example Serving validates inputs against the signature Plots and confusion matrices as artifacts Faster review

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
The tracking client is a thin wrapper that talks to a tracking store. start_run creates a run row with a generated ID; log_param and log_metric insert rows (a metric row also stores a timestamp and a step, which is how training curves work); log_model serializes the model into a temporary folder and uploads the folder to the run's artifact location, then records a reference. search_runs is a query against the store with a small filter language (metrics.auc > 0.9 and params.model = 'rf') that returns a DataFrame. runs:/<run_id>/model is a URI the loader resolves to that artifact folder.

On Databricks the store is the managed backend and the artifact location is cloud storage governed by the platform; for models in Unity Catalog, versions are stored in the schema's managed storage (Level 3 · 01), which is why registered models inherit the catalog's permissions.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Not logging the data version, then being unable to explain a metric change.
  • Comparing runs on different test sets or after tuning on the test set.
  • Logging only the best run, losing the record of what didn't work.
  • Treating autologging as complete.
  • Loading models from untrusted sources (serialization is code execution).
  • Keeping the only copy of a model in an experiment that may be purged.
  • Huge artifacts per run that bloat storage: log what you need.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Run the script. Then add a HistGradientBoostingClassifier run and a metric logged per step (step= argument) for a model that trains iteratively. View it however you like.
  2. Use mlflow.search_runs(filter_string="metrics.auc > 0.85 and params.model = 'rf'") and print the run names.
  3. Add the training data identity (a hash of Xtr) as a tag, and demonstrate that two runs on different seeds have different tags.
  4. Replace the skops trust parameter with serialization_format="cloudpickle" for the random forest if your MLflow version supports it, and write two sentences on the trade-off against the skops approach.

docs.title: 04 · Model Registry & Serving
docs.text:
A model sitting in an experiment run is a file. A model in a registry is a governed, versioned asset with a name, an owner, an audit trail and a way to say "this version is the one production uses". Serving exposes it behind an API. This lesson runs the registry and a REST server locally with open-source MLflow, then maps each piece to Databricks.

What was run

The registry and server below were open-source MLflow 3.17.2 on a laptop (SQLite registry, mlflow models serve on 127.0.0.1), using the models from the previous lesson; outputs are copied from those runs. Databricks Model Serving, the Unity Catalog model registry, serverless endpoints and ai_query were not run; they're described from the Databricks documentation (October 2026). Local serving has none of the platform's autoscaling, authentication, monitoring or governance.

docs.title: Registering a model
docs.text:
import mlflow
from mlflow import MlflowClient

mlflow.set_tracking_uri("sqlite:///mlflow_demo.db"); mlflow.set_registry_uri("sqlite:///mlflow_demo.db")
c = MlflowClient()
best = mlflow.search_runs(experiment_names=["churn-demo"], order_by=["metrics.auc DESC"]).iloc[0].run_id

mv = mlflow.register_model(f"runs:/{best}/model", "churn_model")        # -> version 1
c.set_registered_model_alias("churn_model", "champion", mv.version)

model = mlflow.pyfunc.load_model("models:/churn_model@champion")        # load by alias, not by number

Local results: registered version 1; alias -> 1; the loaded object was a PyFuncModel carrying a signature. Registering a second run's model created version 2, and the champion alias stayed on version 1 until explicitly moved, while a challenger alias could point at version 2:

champion  -> 1
challenger -> 2

Concepts:

  • A registered model (churn_model) has numbered, immutable versions. Each version points at the logged model files and records its source run.
  • Aliases (champion, challenger) are mutable named pointers to a version. Consumers load models:/churn_model@champion, so promoting a new version is a single alias update with no consumer code change, and rollback is moving the alias back.
  • Tags and descriptions annotate versions (validated_by = qa-bot was stored and read back).
  • The older stages (Staging, Production) in the classic workspace registry are the legacy mechanism; Databricks documentation steers new work to Unity Catalog and aliases.

MLflow printed a warning during registration, "Run ... has no artifacts at artifact path 'model', registering model based on models:/m-... instead": in MLflow 3, log_model creates a Logged Model entity (with its own m-... ID) and the run refers to it, so registering from the run's path is redirected to the logged model. It worked; it's a sign that the "model is a file under a run" picture from MLflow 2 is outdated.

docs.title: Signatures: contracts you can enforce
docs.text:
The loaded model's signature was:

inputs:  [Tensor('float64', (-1, 12))]
outputs: [Tensor('int64', (-1,))]

Passing 5 features instead of 12 raised MlflowException: Failed to enforce schema ... Shape of input (2, 5) does not match expected shape (-1, 12). The signature was inferred automatically from the input example logged in the previous lesson. For tabular models trained on a DataFrame, log a named-column signature (use a pandas DataFrame input example) so a request with a missing or misspelled column fails clearly. In my example the inputs were a NumPy array, hence an unnamed tensor.

docs.title: Serving over REST (locally)
docs.text:
export PATH=<venv>/bin:$PATH MLFLOW_TRACKING_URI=sqlite:///mlflow_demo.db MLFLOW_REGISTRY_URI=sqlite:///mlflow_demo.db
mlflow models serve -m "models:/churn_model@champion" --env-manager local -p 5055 --host 127.0.0.1

Requests and local responses (two 12-feature rows; then a bad shape):

POST /invocations  {"inputs": [[0.0]*12, [1.0]*12]}            -> 200 {"predictions": [0, 1]}
POST /invocations  {"dataframe_split": {"columns": [...12 names...], "data": [[0.0]*12]}}   -> 200 {"predictions": [0]}
POST /invocations  {"inputs": [[0.0]*5]}                       -> 400 {"error_code": "INVALID_PARAMETER_VALUE",
                       "message": "Failed to predict data ... Shape of input (1, 5) does not match expected shape (-1, 12)."}
GET  /ping                                                      -> 200

Two things I hit: my first attempt failed with a launcher error "returned non zero return code. Return code = 127" because uvicorn wasn't on PATH (the serve command shells out to it; the virtual environment's bin folder needs to be on PATH); and the server needed --env-manager local to reuse the current environment instead of building a fresh one, which in production you'd avoid (building an isolated environment from the model's requirements.txt is the reproducible way).

docs.title: Databricks Model Serving
docs.text:
Per the documentation, Model Serving deploys models behind a REST API with a managed, serverless, autoscaling service:

  • What can be served: custom models in MLflow format (scikit-learn, XGBoost, PyTorch, Hugging Face transformers...), agents, and foundation models; registered in Unity Catalog (or the legacy workspace registry).
  • Interfaces: the serving UI, the REST endpoint POST /serving-endpoints/{name}/invocations, the MLflow Deployments SDK, and SQL via the ai_query function (batch inference inside a query). The payload formats documented include dataframe_split and dataframe_records for tabular models and tensor inputs: the same shapes the local server accepted.
  • Auth: a token or OAuth credential, with permission to query the endpoint (look up the exact permission name in the docs); the call looks like curl -X POST -u token:$DATABRICKS_API_TOKEN $ENDPOINT_INVOCATION_URL -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"dataframe_split": ...}' per the docs' example.
  • Scale: endpoints autoscale with demand, and you can choose to scale to zero when idle; the docs say scale to zero is not recommended for production endpoints, because capacity isn't guaranteed and the first request pays a cold-start latency.
  • Traffic splitting between model versions for canary or A/B rollout is a common serving feature; I did not verify the current Databricks mechanism, so check the endpoint configuration docs.
  • Monitoring: inference logging and metrics export; endpoint request and cost tables in system tables (look them up in the system tables docs).
  • Pre-deployment validation and a debugging guide exist for the common failure of a model whose dependencies don't resolve on the serving image.

For batch scoring you rarely need an endpoint: load the model as a Spark UDF (mlflow.pyfunc.spark_udf) in a job and write predictions to a table, which is cheaper and simpler than millions of REST calls.

docs.title: Governing models in Unity Catalog
docs.text: Models in Unity Catalog use the same three-level names (catalog.schema.model), CREATE MODEL on a schema (plus USE CATALOG and USE SCHEMA) to register, EXECUTE to use, lineage to the training data, and audit logging (Level 3). The docs state that in MLflow 3 on Databricks the default registry URI is databricks-uc, and that creating a serving endpoint for a Unity Catalog model requires USE CATALOG, USE SCHEMA and EXECUTE on the model. They also say the compute for registering models must use a Unity Catalog-compatible access mode (dedicated, for ML workloads). I didn't verify these requirements on a workspace.

docs.title: A promotion workflow
docs.text:
1. Training job logs candidate versions with metrics and the data version.
  2. An evaluation job loads the challenger, scores a fixed holdout set plus slices, and compares with champion.
  3. If it passes thresholds, the job sets the champion alias to the new version (and tags it with the evaluation run).
  4. Serving picks up the alias (or a deployment job updates the endpoint).
  5. Rollback is one alias update. Put steps 1 to 3 in a Lakeflow job (Level 3 · 07) and the endpoint in a bundle (Lesson 01).

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: The registry is two tables of metadata (registered models; model versions with source, status, tags and aliases) plus the model files in artifact storage. models:/name@alias resolves the alias to a version, the version to a source URI, and loads that artifact. The local server loads the model once at startup into a scoring app; each request body is parsed into a DataFrame or array, validated against the signature, passed to predict, and the result serialized as JSON. Databricks serving wraps the same MLflow scoring contract in a container that is built from the model's recorded environment, run on managed compute with authentication in front, which is why the payload shapes match.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Loading models:/name/3 by number in production code, making every promotion a code change. Use aliases.
  • No signature, so bad inputs fail inside the model with an unreadable error (or silently produce nonsense).
  • Promoting on a single aggregate metric with no slice checks.
  • Serving a model whose training dependencies aren't pinned (the container build fails or behaves differently).
  • Using endpoints for batch inference and paying per-request overhead.
  • Treating --env-manager local as production-ready.
  • Forgetting that registered-model permissions are Unity Catalog permissions (Level 3 · 02).

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Re-run the registration locally, register a third version, move challenger to it, and use search_model_versions to list versions. Notice what the last call in my run returned for aliases ([[], []]) and find out why it differs from get_model_version_by_alias.
  2. Log the model with a pandas DataFrame input example so the signature has named columns; call the server with dataframe_split using a misspelled column and record the error.
  3. Write a script that scores a holdout set with champion and challenger and refuses to move the alias unless AUC improves by at least 0.01 on every one of two slices you define.
  4. Sketch the Lakeflow job and bundle YAML for the promotion workflow above (don't run it).

docs.title: 05 · AI Functions, Genie Agents & AI Search
docs.text:
Databricks' AI features sit on top of the platform you have already built: your governed tables become inputs to LLM calls, to natural-language question answering, and to retrieval for RAG applications. This lesson is an orientation for a data engineer: what each feature does, what it needs, what it costs you in correctness, and where it can hurt.

What was run, and what wasn't

None of the Databricks AI features could be run (they need a workspace, serverless/managed model compute, and in some cases specific regions). Function names, syntax overviews, requirements and renamed products come from the Databricks documentation (October 2026). These features change quickly; names have already changed (below), so verify against the current docs. I did run one small local program: a TF-IDF keyword-retrieval toy that mirrors the shape of vector search and shows, with real output, why plain keyword matching isn't enough. I also make no claims about the accuracy or cost of any model: I have no measurements.

docs.title: Names that changed
docs.text: The documentation currently says Genie Agents (formerly Genie Spaces) and AI Search (formerly Databricks Vector Search). Older tutorials, blog posts and many code samples still use the old names. Likewise Lakeflow Spark Declarative Pipelines and Declarative Automation Bundles replaced older names (earlier in this course), and sharing is now OpenSharing. When a search for a feature fails, look for its new name.

docs.title: AI Functions: LLMs inside SQL
docs.text:
AI Functions are built-in SQL functions that apply models to data stored on Databricks, callable from Databricks SQL, notebooks, pipelines and jobs. From the docs:

  • There are task-specific functions (purpose-built and maintained by Databricks) and one general-purpose function, ai_query, where you supply a prompt and choose a supported model or serving endpoint. The reference lists functions including ai_classify, ai_extract, ai_summarize, ai_translate, ai_analyze_sentiment, ai_mask, ai_fix_grammar, ai_parse_document, ai_similarity, ai_forecast and ai_query (check the current list; it grows).
  • Requirements: they are not available on classic SQL warehouses; Databricks Runtime 15.4 LTS or above is required (18.2 or above recommended for performance and newest features).
  • Your query runs on your compute, but model inference may run on separate Databricks-managed infrastructure that is billed in addition to that compute.
  • Unity Catalog permissions can restrict which task-specific functions an organization may use.
-- Shapes only (not run). Check each function's current signature and options in the SQL reference.
SELECT ticket_id,
       ai_classify(body, ARRAY('billing', 'bug', 'feature request')) AS category,
       ai_query('my-llm-endpoint', CONCAT('Summarize in one sentence: ', body)) AS summary
FROM prod.support.tickets
WHERE created_at >= current_date() - INTERVAL 1 DAY;

ai_classify(content, labels) classifies text by custom labels (the docs describe adding label descriptions and instructions to improve accuracy); ai_extract pulls structured fields according to a schema you provide; ai_query(endpoint, request) calls a model serving endpoint (Lesson 04) or a hosted foundation model.

docs.title: Using them responsibly in pipelines
docs.text:
1. Batch, not row-by-row loops. Run AI Functions in SQL over a table and let the platform parallelize; but remember each row is a model call with latency and cost proportional to rows × tokens.
  2. Filter first. Apply WHERE clauses and deduplicate before calling a model. Do not classify the same boilerplate email a million times.
  3. Materialize results to a table (a Delta table, or a streaming/materialized view in a pipeline) so downstream queries read stored labels instead of re-calling the model.
  4. Model output is not deterministic data. The same input can give different outputs across runs and model versions; treat results as probabilistic features, store the model/function version alongside them, and validate on a labeled sample (Lesson 02's testing mindset applies).
  5. Handle failures. Expect NULLs, timeouts, rate limits and refusals. Count them (reconcile like Level 2 · 09).
  6. Mind the data. Prompts built from table columns send that data to a model; governance for sensitive columns (Level 3 · 04) and your organization's rules about which models may see PII still apply. Check where each function's inference runs and which compliance standards the docs list for it.

docs.title: Genie Agents: natural language over governed data
docs.text:
Per the documentation, Genie lets business users ask questions in natural language. Domain experts configure an agent with datasets (tables and views), sample queries, text instructions and a knowledge store (curated table and column descriptions, synonyms, join relationships, SQL expressions). Genie uses a compound AI system, not a single model, to translate the question into SQL, and responds with the generated query and results; if it can't answer it can ask clarifying questions. The knowledge-store settings are scoped to the agent and do not change Unity Catalog metadata.

What this means for you as the data owner:

  • Quality depends on your metadata. Clear table and column comments, good names, defined joins and certified datasets make answers better; cryptic column names make answers wrong with confidence. Descriptions (Level 3 · 01) are now a product feature.
  • Permissions still apply because queries run under the user's identity on a SQL warehouse (Lesson 09), so row filters and masks (Level 3 · 04) restrict what Genie can show. Check the current docs for the exact identity and sharing model.
  • Always show the SQL. The generated query is the audit trail; encourage users to read it, and have experts add "trusted" example queries for the questions that matter.
  • Use it for exploration, not as a source of record. A number that drives a decision should come from a governed gold table or metric with an owner.

docs.title: AI Search (formerly Vector Search): retrieval for RAG
docs.text:
Retrieval-augmented generation fetches relevant documents and gives them to a model as context. AI Search is the managed index for that: you create an index from a source table (a Delta table, streaming table or similar), it stores embeddings and metadata, and you query it through a REST API (and SDK) for the most similar items. From the docs it supports hybrid keyword-and-similarity search, filtering, reranking, ACLs on endpoints, syncing only selected columns, and automatic sync when the source table changes.

To see the idea (and its limit) without a workspace, here is a keyword-retrieval toy: index five support snippets, "embed" a query, rank by cosine similarity.

"""A TF-IDF retrieval toy: the same *shape* as vector search (index documents, embed a query, rank by cosine similarity).
TF-IDF vectors are sparse keyword vectors, NOT LLM embeddings, so they miss synonyms. Illustration only."""
import numpy as np
from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import TfidfVectorizer
from sklearn.metrics.pairwise import cosine_similarity

docs = {
 "d1": "Refunds are issued to the original payment method within 5 business days.",
 "d2": "To reset your password, use the link on the sign-in page and check your email.",
 "d3": "Our warehouse ships orders Monday to Friday; delivery takes 3 to 7 days.",
 "d4": "Enterprise plans include single sign-on and audit logging.",
 "d5": "If a package is damaged, contact support with photos to get a replacement or your money back.",
}
vec = TfidfVectorizer(stop_words="english", ngram_range=(1, 2)).fit(docs.values())
M = vec.transform(docs.values())
def search(q, k=3):
    s = cosine_similarity(vec.transform([q]), M)[0]
    order = np.argsort(-s)[:k]
    return [(list(docs)[i], round(float(s[i]), 3)) for i in order]
for q in ["how do I reset my password", "get my money back for a broken item", "SSO for large companies"]:
    print(q, "->", search(q))

Output:

how do I reset my password -> [('d2', 0.453), ('d1', 0.0), ('d3', 0.0)]
get my money back for a broken item -> [('d5', 0.277), ('d1', 0.0), ('d2', 0.0)]
SSO for large companies -> [('d1', 0.0), ('d2', 0.0), ('d3', 0.0)]

The first query works because "reset", "password" and "email" literally appear. The second finds the replacement/"money back" document d5 but, notably, not the refunds document d1 (a real answer to the same need) because its words differ ("refunds", "payment method"). The third finds nothing: d4 says "single sign-on" and the query says "SSO", so there's no term overlap. This is the gap that LLM embeddings close: they place texts with similar meaning near each other even without shared words. TF-IDF is not that. A real embedding model would be expected to retrieve d4 for the third query, but I can't show that here, so that's an expectation, not a result.

Pipeline design for RAG on Databricks, in outline: ingest and chunk documents into a Delta table with stable IDs and Change Data Feed (Level 2 · 01) → create an AI Search index synced from that table → at query time embed the question, retrieve the top-k chunks with filters (for example by tenant or by access level) → send chunks plus the question to a model endpoint → log inputs, retrieved IDs and answers for evaluation (MLflow tracing, Lesson 03). Chunk size, filters and evaluation matter more than which model you pick.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: AI Functions are expressions that the SQL engine batches: it collects rows, calls a model endpoint (Databricks-managed or yours) with those inputs, and returns the outputs as a column, handling retries and parallelism. That is why they can be used in any query, and why their cost scales with rows and tokens. Genie's loop retrieves relevant metadata from the knowledge store, asks models to produce a SQL plan, checks and runs it on a warehouse, and shows results. An AI Search index stores each chunk's embedding vector in an approximate-nearest-neighbour structure; a query is embedded with the same model and compared to stored vectors. Embedding the query with a different model than the index is a classic bug: the vectors live in different spaces and rankings are meaningless.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Calling a model on every row of a big table in an interactive query.
  • Not storing the outputs, so every dashboard refresh re-bills.
  • Treating generated labels as ground truth without sampling and measuring.
  • Exposing sensitive columns to models or to Genie without masking.
  • Poor table and column descriptions, then blaming Genie.
  • Mismatched embedding models between index and query.
  • No evaluation set for a RAG system, so quality changes go unnoticed.
  • Relying on a name from an old tutorial (Vector Search, Genie Spaces) and concluding the feature doesn't exist.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Extend the toy: add a synonym dictionary (SSO to "single sign-on") applied to queries and see whether d4 is retrieved. Why doesn't this scale, and what replaces it?
  2. Design a daily job (Level 3 · 07) that labels yesterday's support tickets with ai_classify, stores labels in a Delta table, and reconciles counts (input rows, labelled rows, NULLs). Write the SQL shape and the reconciliation checks.
  3. List ten columns of a table you own that you would NOT send to an LLM function, and what you'd do instead for each.
  4. Write the table and column comments a Genie user would need to ask "revenue by region last quarter" correctly for your gold schema.

docs.title: 06 · Cost Management: DBUs, Budgets & System Billing
docs.text:
Databricks bills in Databricks Units (DBUs): a unit of processing capability per hour, priced per SKU (compute type, cloud and plan). Cost problems on the platform are rarely mysterious; they are usually an idle all-purpose cluster, a job on the wrong compute type, a runaway query, or spend nobody can attribute to a team. This lesson shows how to see the spend, assign it and limit it.

What was run, and what wasn't

I have no Databricks account, so no real billing data was queried. The system-table names, columns and the retraction/ restatement rule come from the Databricks documentation (October 2026). The analysis below runs on local Spark with mock rows that I invented; every quantity and every price in this lesson is made up to illustrate the queries (the documented schema is real, the numbers are not). I give no actual prices: DBU rates vary by SKU, cloud, region, plan and contract, so look them up in the pricing pages and in system.billing.list_prices.

docs.title: What you pay for
docs.text:
• Databricks charges (DBUs) × a rate for the SKU: for example all-purpose compute, jobs compute, SQL, serverless variants, model serving, Lakeflow pipelines. All-purpose (interactive) compute is priced higher than jobs compute for the same cluster, which is one reason production work belongs on job compute or serverless jobs (Level 1 · 02).
  • Cloud charges (classic compute only): the VMs, disks and network in your cloud account, billed by your cloud provider. Serverless compute bundles the infrastructure into the Databricks charge, so there is a single bill (the exact accounting is in the pricing documentation).
  • Storage in your object store, and, for features like AI Functions or model serving, separate usage lines.

docs.title: The billing system tables
docs.text: system.billing.usage is the central table (Lesson 05 of Level 3 covers system tables). Per the docs, records are typically available within 12 hours, and the documented columns include record_id, account_id, workspace_id, sku_name, cloud, usage_start_time, usage_end_time, usage_date, custom_tags (a map), usage_unit (for example DBU), usage_quantity, usage_metadata (a struct with fields such as cluster_id, job_id, warehouse_id, populated depending on the compute type), identity_metadata, record_type, billing_origin_product and product_features. system.billing.list_prices logs SKU prices over time, with a row added whenever a price changes.

docs.title: Corrections: retractions and restatements
docs.text:
If Databricks corrects a usage record it does not edit the original. Per the docs, record_type is ORIGINAL, or RETRACTION (identical to the original except usage_quantity is negative and cancels it) or RESTATEMENT (the corrected record). The docs' own example sums usage so that the retraction negates the original and only the restatement's values remain. Here is what that does on my mock data (seven rows, including a retraction of -40 for job-7 and a restatement of 36):

naive: ORIGINAL rows only              correct: all record types
ALL_PURPOSE_COMPUTE  102.0             ALL_PURPOSE_COMPUTE  102.0
JOBS_COMPUTE          65.0             JOBS_COMPUTE          61.0
SERVERLESS_SQL        30.0             SERVERLESS_SQL        30.0

Filtering to ORIGINAL (a natural-looking cleanup!) overstated jobs compute by 4 DBUs here, because it kept the 40-DBU original and ignored the correction. A plain SUM(usage_quantity) over all record types is right. That lines up with the docs, but check whether you want to restrict by date or ingestion date for reproducible month-end reports (late corrections can change old totals).

docs.title: Attribution with tags
docs.text:
You can't manage what you can't attribute. Per the documentation there are default tags (applied automatically to cloud resources) and custom tags (user-defined on compute and serverless workloads) for tracking by team, project or cost center. Custom tags flow into usage.custom_tags. Warnings from the docs: tag data is stored as plain text and may be replicated globally, so never put personal or sensitive data in tag names or values.

Mock query, using invented prices from an invented price table:

SELECT coalesce(custom_tags['team'], 'UNTAGGED') AS team,
       ROUND(SUM(u.usage_quantity * p.usd_per_dbu), 2) AS usd, SUM(u.usage_quantity) AS dbus
FROM usage u JOIN list_prices p USING (sku_name)
GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY usd DESC;

|data-science|36.00|90.0|
|analytics   |21.00|30.0|
|growth      | 6.10|61.0|
|UNTAGGED    | 4.80|12.0|

(Mock data, with made-up prices.) The UNTAGGED row is the metric to drive to zero. Enforce tagging with compute policies (Level 1 · 02: a policy can require a tag) and, for serverless workloads, budget policies that attach tags to usage. The docs also describe budgets with alerts, in the account console, that notify when spend crosses a threshold; check the current page for the supported actions (alerts versus hard limits).

Other queries from the same mock table: per-job DBUs (job-7 36.0, job-8 25.0, computed from usage_metadata.job_id) and the all-purpose share of total DBUs (52.8% in the mock data). A rising all-purpose share is a classic red flag that production work is running on interactive clusters.

The mock script (runs on local Spark; replace the temp views with system.billing.* tables on a workspace):

from common import spark
s=spark()
# MOCK rows shaped like system.billing.usage (a few columns). SKU names are real-looking labels; quantities and prices are INVENTED.
s.sql("""CREATE OR REPLACE TEMP VIEW usage AS SELECT * FROM VALUES
 ('r1','JOBS_COMPUTE','ORIGINAL',    DATE'2026-10-20', 40.0,  MAP('team','growth'),'job-7'),
 ('r2','JOBS_COMPUTE','ORIGINAL',    DATE'2026-10-20', 25.0,  MAP('team','growth'),'job-8'),
 ('r3','ALL_PURPOSE_COMPUTE','ORIGINAL', DATE'2026-10-20', 90.0, MAP('team','data-science'),NULL),
 ('r4','ALL_PURPOSE_COMPUTE','ORIGINAL', DATE'2026-10-20', 12.0, MAP(),NULL),
 ('r5','SERVERLESS_SQL','ORIGINAL',  DATE'2026-10-20', 30.0,  MAP('team','analytics'),NULL),
 ('r6','JOBS_COMPUTE','RETRACTION',  DATE'2026-10-20', -40.0, MAP('team','growth'),'job-7'),
 ('r7','JOBS_COMPUTE','RESTATEMENT', DATE'2026-10-20', 36.0,  MAP('team','growth'),'job-7')
 AS t(record_id, sku_name, record_type, usage_date, usage_quantity, custom_tags, job_id)""")
s.sql("CREATE OR REPLACE TEMP VIEW list_prices AS SELECT * FROM VALUES ('JOBS_COMPUTE',0.10),('ALL_PURPOSE_COMPUTE',0.40),('SERVERLESS_SQL',0.70) AS t(sku_name, usd_per_dbu)")  # INVENTED
print("naive: ORIGINAL rows only"); s.sql("SELECT sku_name, SUM(usage_quantity) dbus FROM usage WHERE record_type='ORIGINAL' GROUP BY sku_name ORDER BY sku_name").show()
print("correct: all record types (retraction cancels the original, restatement replaces it)"); s.sql("SELECT sku_name, SUM(usage_quantity) dbus FROM usage GROUP BY sku_name ORDER BY sku_name").show()
print("spend by team tag, hypothetical prices"); s.sql("""SELECT coalesce(custom_tags['team'],'UNTAGGED') team, ROUND(SUM(u.usage_quantity * p.usd_per_dbu),2) usd, SUM(u.usage_quantity) dbus
  FROM usage u JOIN list_prices p USING (sku_name) GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY usd DESC""").show()
print("per job (job compute only)"); s.sql("SELECT job_id, SUM(usage_quantity) dbus FROM usage WHERE job_id IS NOT NULL GROUP BY job_id ORDER BY job_id").show()
print("share of all-purpose DBUs"); s.sql("SELECT ROUND(100*SUM(CASE WHEN sku_name='ALL_PURPOSE_COMPUTE' THEN usage_quantity END)/SUM(usage_quantity),1) pct_all_purpose FROM usage").show()

docs.title: Cost levers by compute type
docs.text:
Compute Main levers All-purpose clusters Auto-termination (idle minutes), right-sized nodes, autoscaling, single-node for small work, compute policies capping size, do not run schedules here Job compute Right-size per job, use the cheaper job rate, pools or serverless to cut startup, spot/preemptible workers where interruption is tolerable (classic), fewer, larger jobs vs. many tiny clusters SQL warehouses Auto stop, cluster size vs. max clusters (Level 3 · 09), separate warehouses per workload, query tuning Serverless jobs / notebooks Efficient code (you pay for compute time), avoid long idle sessions, set timeouts Model serving / AI Functions Filter rows first, cache results in tables, scale-to-zero only for non-production, cheaper models for simple tasks Storage VACUUM, delete stale clones/experiments, lifecycle rules on raw landing zones, avoid tiny files (Level 2 · 04)

And the big one: efficiency of the work itself. A query that scans 100× too much data costs 100× too much on any compute type. Everything in Level 2 (data skipping, clustering, joins, small files) is a cost lever, and Level 4 · 07 and 08 cover more.

docs.title: A weekly review routine
docs.text:
1. Total DBUs by SKU and by day: any step change?
  2. Top ten jobs and warehouses by DBUs, with their owners (from tags).
  3. Untagged share, and idle all-purpose clusters (cluster events or compute system tables).
  4. Jobs whose cost per run rose more than, say, 30% (make the threshold your own): look at data volume, retries, skew.
  5. Failed and retried runs: a job that fails after 90% of its work and reruns doubles its cost.
  6. Open an issue for each finding with an owner and a date.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: Each compute resource emits metering events (cluster running time × node DBU rate for classic; resource-seconds for serverless). A billing pipeline aggregates them into usage records, hourly, stamps them with SKU, workspace, tags and metadata, and writes them to the system table; corrections are appended as the retraction-plus-restatement pairs above, never as updates, so the table is append-only and auditable. Prices are a separate versioned log, so cost = usage × the price effective at that time, joined by SKU and time range (my mock join ignored the time range for brevity; a real one must respect price_start_time and price_end_time).

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Filtering record_type = 'ORIGINAL' and missing corrections.
  • Joining list prices without time ranges, or treating list price as what you actually pay (contracts and discounts change that).
  • Production jobs on all-purpose clusters.
  • No auto-termination on interactive clusters.
  • Untagged compute so costs can't be charged back.
  • Putting sensitive values in tags.
  • Optimizing the bill instead of the work (scheduling fewer runs vs. fixing the scan).
  • Forgetting cloud-provider costs on classic compute when comparing with serverless.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Extend the mock to add a second day and a price change on ALL_PURPOSE_COMPUTE; write the time-ranged join and show the spend difference vs. the untimed join.
  2. Write the SQL (shape only) that finds jobs on all-purpose compute, using the fact that job_id is not populated for jobs run on all-purpose compute (per the docs). What does that tell you about how to detect them?
  3. Design the tagging standard for your organization (tag keys, allowed values, enforcement via compute policy, who owns the list).
  4. Decide an alert threshold for a team with a monthly budget of X DBUs, and write the rule in plain words, including what action each threshold triggers.

docs.title: 07 · Performance: Photon, Serverless & Caching
docs.text:
Performance work is mostly about order of operations: fix what the query reads, then how it joins, then what it runs on. This lesson places the platform features (Photon, caches, serverless) in that order, and is candid about a local experiment that produced a weak result and another that hung.

What was run, and what wasn't

Photon, the Databricks disk cache and serverless compute are platform features and were not run; claims about them come from the Databricks documentation (October 2026). Locally (Spark 4.2.0 on a two-core laptop) I ran a caching experiment, which showed the cached plan but no measurable speedup at this tiny scale, and I tried a Python-UDF-versus-built-in-function timing, which hung and so produced no numbers. I report both. I make no performance-ratio claims that I did not measure. Where the documentation states a vendor benchmark ("up to 5x better price/performance" for Photon) I quote it as the vendor's claim; I did not verify it.

docs.title: A tuning order that works
docs.text:
1. Read less. Filter early, select only needed columns, rely on data skipping with good clustering (Level 2 · 03 and 04). Nothing else beats not reading the data.
  2. Shuffle less, and shuffle evenly. Broadcast small tables, fix skew, avoid needless distinct/repartition (Level 2 · 05 and 06).
  3. Avoid row-at-a-time code. Prefer built-in functions to UDFs (below).
  4. Cache only what you reuse.
  5. Then choose the engine and compute (Photon, serverless, size).
  6. Measure with the query profile / Spark UI, not intuition: find the longest stage, the biggest shuffle, the spill.

Steps 1 and 2 are code and layout changes; steps 5 and 6 are configuration. People tend to start at step 5 because it's a setting. It is usually the least effective place to start.

docs.title: Photon
docs.text:
From the docs: Photon is Databricks' native vectorized query engine. For supported operations it replaces the JVM-based Spark SQL execution engine with a native C++ runtime, while the Catalyst optimizer still plans the query; on an unsupported operation it transparently falls back to Spark for the rest of that operation. It processes columnar batches (thousands of rows at a time), can use SIMD instructions, and avoids JVM garbage-collection and warm-up costs. The docs list benefits for scans (filter pushdown, row-group skipping), joins and shuffles (hash joins, a columnar shuffle), writes (a native Parquet writer that speeds Delta, Iceberg and Parquet writes including MERGE, UPDATE, DELETE and CTAS) and the disk cache.

Practical points from the same page:

  • It needs no code changes: SQL and DataFrame APIs in all languages benefit.
  • It helps most for longer-running queries on large data; queries finishing in under about two seconds see no meaningful gain, because planning and scheduling dominate.
  • Enablement: on by default for SQL warehouses and serverless compute; for classic all-purpose, jobs and classic pipelines it is on by default, controlled by a "Use Photon Acceleration" setting, but when you create compute through the Clusters or Jobs APIs you must set it explicitly (runtime_engine set to PHOTON; photon: true for the Pipelines API).
  • It accelerates stateless streaming but not stateful streaming (Level 2 · 07's windowed aggregation would not benefit).
  • Photon can change a workload's DBU consumption and price; I did not verify the current pricing rules, so test with your jobs and check the pricing pages (Lesson 06).
  • Operations Photon doesn't support fall back to the Spark engine (per the docs), so a plan can mix Photon and non-Photon operators; the query profile shows which. I did not verify which specific expressions fall back.

docs.title: Caching: three different things
docs.text:
Cache What it caches How you get it Disk cache (formerly Delta cache / DBIO cache) Parquet/Delta files on workers' local disks Automatic on supported instance types; proprietary Databricks feature Spark cache (df.cache()) A DataFrame's computed result in memory/disk You call it explicitly; per application Query/result cache The result of a SQL query Automatic for SQL warehouses and dashboards; see the caching docs for its rules

The docs recommend using the disk cache instead of the Spark cache for repeated reads of Parquet and Delta data, and note that on SQL warehouses and Databricks Runtime 14.2+ the older CACHE SELECT command is ignored in favour of an enhanced disk-caching algorithm. Use Spark cache() when you reuse a computed intermediate (an expensive join result) several times in one job, and unpersist() it when done: cached data occupies executor memory that your other operations need.

docs.title: A local cache experiment, and what it did and didn't show
docs.text:
I built a DataFrame of 400,000 rows with a SHA-256 hash column, grouped it, and counted the distinct hashes per group, three times uncached and three times after cache() plus one materializing action (local Spark, two cores):

uncached: recomputed every action        runs(s)=[1.18, 0.12, 0.09]
cached (after one materializing count)   runs(s)=[0.15, 0.08, 0.07]

The physical plan after caching did show the cache in use:

HashAggregate(keys=[g], functions=[count(1)])
+- Exchange hashpartitioning(g, 8)
   +- HashAggregate(keys=[g], functions=[partial_count(1)])
      +- InMemoryTableScan [g]
            +- InMemoryRelation [id, h, g], StorageLevel(disk, memory, deserialized, 1 replicas)

But the timings do not demonstrate a benefit. The first uncached run (1.18 s) most likely includes one-time JVM and code-generation warm-up (I did not isolate it); once warm, the uncached runs (0.12 s, 0.09 s) are about as fast as the cached ones (0.08 s, 0.07 s), because this dataset is tiny and the "expensive" lineage (a range and a hash) isn't expensive enough. The lesson is a methodological one: a micro- benchmark on a small laptop dataset can't show a caching effect, and warm-up effects can fool you into seeing one. To see real gains you need data large enough that recomputation costs seconds-to-minutes, repeated runs, and the platform's own metrics. I'd rather show this honestly than print a flattering ratio.

docs.title: UDFs: why they are slow, and a failed measurement
docs.text:
A Python UDF runs your function in a separate Python process: for each batch, Spark serializes rows out of the JVM, calls Python, and serializes results back. Pandas (Arrow-based) UDFs process whole columns at a time, cutting the per-row overhead, and built-in functions run entirely inside the engine (and in Photon, if enabled). The ordering "built-in, then pandas UDF, then row-at-a-time Python UDF" is standard Spark guidance, and Python code can't run inside a native engine, so UDF logic itself isn't accelerated by Photon (my reasoning, not a quote from the docs).

I tried to measure it: the same arithmetic over 300,000 rows with a built-in expression, a Python UDF and a pandas UDF. The script hung with idle Python workers and I killed it after several minutes, so I have no timings to report. I did not find the cause (the same session ran built-in expressions fine, so it was specific to the Python-worker path on that machine's Python 3.12 / pandas 2 / NumPy 2.5 environment). If you try this yourself and see similar behaviour, check that PYSPARK_PYTHON matches the driver's Python (Level 1 · 10) and test with a tiny input first. I'd rather state that failure than substitute figures from memory.

Rule that stands regardless: if a built-in function or a SQL expression can do it, use that.

docs.title: Serverless compute: convenience with constraints
docs.text:
Serverless removes cluster configuration, starts quickly and scales automatically, but the documentation lists limitations worth knowing before you migrate a job (October 2026; the list changes):

  • Only Spark Connect APIs are supported; RDD APIs are not; R is not supported.
  • Spark Connect defers analysis and name resolution to execution time, which can change behaviour of existing code.
  • ANSI mode is on by default (invalid casts and overflows raise errors); the default session time zone is UTC.
  • You must use Unity Catalog to reach external data; DBFS access is limited; dbutils/working-directory assumptions can break (use absolute paths and workspace files).
  • Maven library coordinates aren't supported; UDFs can't access the internet and have a 1 GB memory limit; global temp views aren't supported; and the Spark UI is not available: use the query profile.

None of this makes serverless a bad choice; for most new workloads the docs recommend it. It means test before moving a legacy job.

docs.title: Reading the evidence
docs.text:
Whether in the Spark UI (classic) or the query profile (serverless/SQL):

  1. Sort operators by time; find the one that dominates.
  2. Compare rows/bytes read with rows/bytes returned: a huge scan with a tiny result means filtering or clustering is the fix.
  3. Check shuffle read/write, spill, and task time distribution (skew).
  4. Look at the number of files read and pruned.
  5. Only then change compute (size/type/Photon), and re-measure on the same input.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: Photon sits below the optimizer: Catalyst produces a physical plan, and Photon's planner converts the supported operators into Photon operators running on columnar batches in native code, inserting transitions between Photon and JVM operators where it must fall back. The disk cache sits below the file reader: when a Parquet file is read from cloud storage it is copied to local SSD in a fast format, and later reads for the same file, by any query on that node, hit local disk. The Spark cache sits at the DataFrame level: it stores computed partitions in executors' memory/disk, keyed by the logical plan, so only identical plans reuse it. That's why a disk cache benefits many different queries over the same files while a Spark cache helps only the same reused intermediate.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Changing cluster size first.
  • df.cache() on everything, starving memory.
  • Benchmarking on tiny data (as above) or including warm-up in timings.
  • Row-at-a-time Python UDFs where a built-in exists.
  • Assuming Photon speeds up everything (short queries, Python UDFs and stateful streaming don't benefit).
  • Migrating to serverless without testing RDD/DBFS/relative-path usage.
  • Not looking at the query profile before tuning.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Re-run the cache experiment with 40 million rows (if your machine allows) and a genuinely expensive lineage (a join), and report whether a difference appears. Include a warm-up run that you discard.
  2. Take one of your Level 1 or 2 queries, produce its plan with EXPLAIN FORMATTED, and identify the scan's pushed filters and read columns. Make one change that reduces bytes read.
  3. Write a checklist for migrating an existing job to serverless, using the limitations above.
  4. If you have a workspace, run the same query on a classic warehouse and a serverless warehouse and compare the query profile (not just the wall-clock time).

docs.title: 08 · Table Maintenance & Predictive Optimization
docs.text:
Delta tables don't maintain themselves. Every write adds files; every UPDATE or DELETE leaves old files behind; statistics go stale; clustering decays as new data lands. On Databricks, much of this can now be automated, but you still need to know what the maintenance operations do, because the defaults interact with time travel, cost and correctness.

What was run, and what wasn't

The deletion-vector experiment below ran on open-source Delta Lake 4.4.1 / local Spark 4.2.0, and its numbers are copied from that run. OPTIMIZE and VACUUM behaviour was measured in Level 1 and 2. Predictive Optimization, auto compaction and optimized writes, and automatic liquid clustering are Databricks features that were not run; they are described from the Databricks documentation (October 2026). Their defaults and rollout schedules change, so verify what your account actually does.

docs.title: The four chores
docs.text:
Chore What it fixes Command Compaction / clustering Small files; poor data skipping OPTIMIZE (Level 2 · 03) Cleanup Unreferenced files (storage cost) VACUUM (Level 1 · 08) Statistics Stale table/column stats used by the optimizer ANALYZE TABLE ... COMPUTE STATISTICS Purging deleted data Rows that are "deleted" but still physically present REORG TABLE ... APPLY (PURGE)

The first two you've met. The last two deserve a closer look.

docs.title: Deletion vectors: cheap deletes, deferred cost
docs.text:
Without deletion vectors, changing one row means rewriting the whole Parquet file that contains it. With them enabled, Delta marks rows as deleted in a small side structure and applies it at read time. I measured both on a 200,000-row table in four files (about 14 MB):

CREATE TABLE plain  (...) USING delta TBLPROPERTIES ('delta.enableDeletionVectors' = 'false');
CREATE TABLE withdv (...) USING delta TBLPROPERTIES ('delta.enableDeletionVectors' = 'true');
DELETE FROM plain  WHERE id = 12345;
DELETE FROM withdv WHERE id = 12345;

Operation metrics from the history of each DELETE:

plain   DELETE one row -> numRemovedFiles 1, numAddedFiles 1, numCopiedRows 49999, numDeletedRows 1, numDeletionVectorsAdded 0
withdv  DELETE one row -> numRemovedFiles 0, numAddedFiles 0, numCopiedRows 0,     numDeletedRows 1, numDeletionVectorsAdded 1

Deleting one row rewrote a file and copied 49,999 other rows in the plain table; the table with deletion vectors rewrote nothing and added one deletion vector. The file count stayed 4 in both, and both returned 199,999 rows afterwards. The size of the table with deletion vectors did not change (14,099,290 bytes before and after): the "deleted" row is still physically in the file, just hidden.

That's the catch. Reads must apply the deletion vector, and the deleted data still exists on disk, which matters for privacy (a GDPR erasure request isn't satisfied by hiding a row) and for read performance as vectors accumulate. REORG TABLE ... APPLY (PURGE) rewrites only the files that contain soft-deleted rows:

REORG TABLE withdv APPLY (PURGE);

Locally this reported numFilesAdded=1, numFilesRemoved=1 (a rewritten file of 3,535,050 bytes replacing one of 3,531,929 bytes, consistent with the 4 files and the one that held the deleted row). Afterward the table size matched the plain table's (14,102,411 bytes). Purging doesn't delete the old file from storage either: you still need VACUUM after the retention window to physically remove the pre-purge data (and old versions stay readable by time travel until then).

Enabling deletion vectors also raised the table's protocol (minReaderVersion 3, minWriterVersion 7 locally), so old readers can't read the table (Level 2 · 02's column-mapping warning applies). Per the Databricks docs, deletion vectors accelerate DELETE, UPDATE and MERGE (Photon uses them for predictive I/O on updates), enable row-level concurrency from Databricks Runtime 14.2, and for Delta tables must be enabled explicitly (a workspace setting can enable them on new tables; defaults vary by region); client compatibility varies, with the docs listing runtime versions per operation.

docs.title: Statistics
docs.text:
The optimizer uses table and column statistics (row counts, distinct counts, min/max) to choose join orders and strategies, separate from the per-file min/max used for data skipping (Level 2 · 04).

ANALYZE TABLE prod.silver.orders COMPUTE STATISTICS;
ANALYZE TABLE prod.silver.orders COMPUTE STATISTICS FOR COLUMNS order_date, customer_id;

Stale or missing statistics are a common cause of a bad join strategy (a table believed to be huge never gets broadcast; AQE, Level 2 · 05, repairs some of this at runtime). Predictive Optimization collects statistics for managed tables.

docs.title: Automatic file-size management
docs.text:
From the documentation: Databricks automatically tunes file sizes for Unity Catalog managed tables, and manual tuning recommendations don't apply to them. For external tables and legacy workloads you can configure:

  • Optimized writes (delta.autoOptimize.optimizeWrite): reshuffles data before writing to produce fewer, larger files.
  • Auto compaction (delta.autoOptimize.autoCompact): after a write succeeds, synchronously compacts small files within the partition on the cluster doing the write, only files not compacted before.
  • Target file size settings.

The docs state these reduce the small-file problem but are not a full replacement for OPTIMIZE: for tables larger than about 1 TB they recommend scheduling OPTIMIZE as well, and they recommend liquid clustering for data layout.

docs.title: Predictive Optimization
docs.text:
Per the documentation, Predictive Optimization automatically runs OPTIMIZE, VACUUM and ANALYZE on Unity Catalog managed tables (Delta and Iceberg), identifies the tables that would benefit, queues the operations, and collects statistics at write time. Details to know:

  • It is enabled by default for accounts created on or after 11 November 2024, with a gradual rollout to existing accounts that the docs expect to complete by August 2026, so verify your account.
  • It can be enabled or overridden at account, catalog, schema or table level.
  • It runs on serverless compute for jobs and is billed under a serverless jobs SKU; operations are visible in a predictive optimization system table.
  • OPTIMIZE run by it does not apply ZORDER; for Z-ordered tables it ignores Z-ordered files. With liquid clustering enabled, it triggers incremental clustering, and with automatic liquid clustering it may select new clustering keys itself.
  • VACUUM uses delta.deletedFileRetentionDuration (default 7 days). If you need longer time travel, set the property before you enable it, or it will clean up history you wanted. The docs call this out explicitly.
  • Requirements: Premium plan or above in a supported region, SQL warehouses or Databricks Runtime 12.2 LTS+, and managed tables only. External tables still need your own jobs.

This is the largest operational simplification on the platform, and it changes the question from "who runs OPTIMIZE?" to "what retention and clustering do we want, and are we verifying it happens?"

docs.title: A maintenance policy
docs.text:
Table type Policy UC managed, predictive optimization on Set retention properties deliberately; use liquid clustering; monitor the operations table; run nothing by hand unless investigating UC managed, PO off Scheduled OPTIMIZE (liquid clustering) and VACUUM jobs, ANALYZE for join-heavy tables External / legacy Scheduled OPTIMIZE + VACUUM, optimized writes + auto compaction, own monitoring Tables with erasure obligations Deletion vectors plus REORG ... PURGE plus VACUUM after retention, tested end to end Streaming sinks Auto compaction/optimized writes or periodic OPTIMIZE (many small commits)

Add monitoring: file count and average file size per table (DESCRIBE DETAIL), table size growth, the age of the oldest unvacuumed file, and failed maintenance runs. A table whose average file size drifts toward kilobytes is telling you maintenance is not happening.

DESCRIBE DETAIL prod.silver.orders;     -- numFiles, sizeInBytes -> average file size = sizeInBytes / numFiles
DESCRIBE HISTORY prod.silver.orders;    -- when did OPTIMIZE / VACUUM last run?

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: OPTIMIZE reads small files, writes larger ones and commits add/remove actions marked dataChange = false. VACUUM compares the set of files referenced by versions within the retention window with the files present, and deletes the rest. A deletion vector is a compact bitmap (stored inline or in a side file) of row positions inside a specific data file; the add action for that file carries a reference to it, so a query reading the file filters out those positions. REORG ... PURGE rewrites a file without the marked rows and commits a new add with no vector. Predictive Optimization is a scheduler: it observes table activity (writes, file counts, query patterns), estimates the benefit of each operation, and enqueues OPTIMIZE, VACUUM and ANALYZE onto serverless compute.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Running VACUUM RETAIN 0 HOURS to "save storage now" (kills time travel and can break concurrent writers).
  • Enabling Predictive Optimization before setting retention you need for time travel.
  • Assuming a deletion-vector delete erased the data.
  • Z-ordering a table and expecting Predictive Optimization to maintain the Z-order.
  • Forgetting external tables aren't covered by Predictive Optimization.
  • Optimizing tiny tables or optimizing on every write.
  • No monitoring of file counts, so decay is noticed only when queries slow down.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Reproduce the deletion-vector experiment. Then delete 5,000 scattered rows with and without deletion vectors and compare numCopiedRows. At what point does the advantage shrink?
  2. After REORG ... PURGE, prove the deleted row's bytes are still on disk until VACUUM (search the Parquet file for the id or use time travel), and then remove them.
  3. Write a function that, given DESCRIBE DETAIL output, flags tables whose average file size is below a threshold you choose, and test it on a table with 200 tiny appends before and after OPTIMIZE.
  4. Write the retention and clustering decisions for three tables you own (one audit log, one hot dimension, one erasure-sensitive table) before enabling Predictive Optimization.

docs.title: 09 · Migrating to Databricks
docs.text:
Few teams start on a blank slate. Data sits in Parquet folders, in a Hive metastore, in another warehouse, with SQL and jobs written for another engine. Migration succeeds when it's treated as three separate problems: moving data, moving metadata and permissions, and translating code, each with its own verification.

What was run, and what wasn't

I ran locally (open-source Delta Lake 4.4.1, Spark 4.2.0): an in-place CONVERT TO DELTA, a SHALLOW CLONE, and SQL dialect translation with sqlglot 30.24, whose actual output (including its flaws) is shown below. DEEP CLONE is not supported by this open-source build (error shown), so I could not test it and describe it from the Databricks docs. Hive metastore upgrade tools (SYNC, UCX, upgrade wizards), federation and Unity Catalog behaviour need a workspace and were not run; they are described from the documentation (October 2026). I have not migrated a real system, so the checklist is guidance, not field experience.

docs.title: Parquet to Delta, in place
docs.text:
If you have a folder of Parquet files, you often don't need to copy anything: CONVERT TO DELTA writes a _delta_log that references the existing files.

CONVERT TO DELTA parquet.`/data/legacy` PARTITIONED BY (day STRING);

Local run on a 1,000-row folder partitioned by day:

before:  ['_SUCCESS', 'day=0', 'day=1', 'day=2']
after:   ['_SUCCESS', '_delta_log', 'day=0', 'day=1', 'day=2']
rows read through Delta: 1000        DESCRIBE HISTORY operations: ['CONVERT']

The data folders were untouched; only _delta_log appeared, and the history recorded a CONVERT operation. Points to remember:

  • You must supply PARTITIONED BY with types for partitioned data (Delta can't infer partition column types reliably from directory names).
  • Delta scans the files to collect statistics and the schema, so conversion takes time proportional to the data size, but it doesn't rewrite it.
  • The folder is now a Delta table: writers that don't know Delta (old jobs doing plain Parquet writes into it) will corrupt the table state. Cut writers over before converting, or convert and cut over in the same change.
  • Files written with incompatible Parquet features may need rewriting; test on a copy.

docs.title: Clones: copies, snapshots and sandboxes
docs.text:
CREATE TABLE sandbox SHALLOW CLONE prod.silver.orders;
CREATE TABLE backup  DEEP    CLONE prod.silver.orders;

A shallow clone copies only metadata (the log), so it's instant and tiny, and reads the source's data files by reference. A deep clone copies the data files too. In the local run, after cloning, I deleted 10 rows from the source: the shallow clone still returned all 1,000 rows while the source returned 990, showing the clone is isolated from later changes to the source (it keeps referencing the files that were current when it was made). Cautions: a shallow clone depends on the source's files, so a VACUUM on the source after the retention window can break the clone, and shallow clones aren't backups.

DEEP CLONE failed in my local build with [PARSE_SYNTAX_ERROR] Syntax error at or near 'DEEP', so it appears to be a Databricks feature rather than part of open-source Delta 4.4.1; I used a CTAS copy for the comparison (1,000 rows) instead. In the Databricks docs, CLONE or CTAS is also how you copy Hive tables into Unity Catalog managed tables (they must live in reserved managed storage).

docs.title: Loading from elsewhere
docs.text:
• Files in object storage: register them as external tables/volumes (Level 3 · 03) and ingest with Auto Loader or COPY INTO (Level 2 · 08).
