  • Databases and warehouses: read via JDBC/connectors or Lakehouse Federation (query the remote system in place through a foreign catalog) to avoid copying while you migrate gradually; ingestion tools and CDC feeds for continuous sync (Lakeflow Connect and partner tools are described in the docs; I did not review their current feature sets).
  • Other lake formats: Iceberg and Delta interoperate on Databricks to varying degrees (check "UniForm" and managed Iceberg documentation for your versions).

docs.title: 2. Moving metadata and permissions: Hive metastore to Unity Catalog
docs.text:
From the Databricks documentation: a workspace's legacy Hive metastore appears as a catalog named hive_metastore, usable alongside Unity Catalog, but it doesn't get Unity Catalog's auditing, lineage or access control, and Databricks recommends migrating. Options named in the docs:

Approach Use when SYNC Upgrade Hive external tables (and managed tables stored outside workspace/DBFS-root storage) to Unity Catalog external tables; can re-sync as the source changes. It cannot upgrade managed tables in workspace storage CLONE / CTAS Copy Hive managed tables into UC managed tables (needed for tables in DBFS root) UCX (Databricks Labs, databrickslabs/ucx) A toolkit that assesses readiness and migrates identities, permissions, storage locations and tables Upgrade wizards in the UI Small numbers of tables Hive metastore federation Gradual: mirror the Hive metastore as a foreign catalog governed by UC while you migrate 
SYNC TABLE prod.sales.orders FROM hive_metastore.sales.orders DRY RUN;   -- preview; syntax: SYNC {SCHEMA|TABLE} target [AS EXTERNAL] FROM source [SET OWNER p] [DRY RUN]
CREATE TABLE prod.sales.orders_managed DEEP CLONE hive_metastore.sales.orders_managed;   -- Databricks-only syntax; not run

What does not migrate itself: permissions (Hive table ACLs vs UC grants; design the new grants with Level 3 · 02), mounts and DBFS paths in code (dbfs:/mnt/... becomes external locations and volumes), cluster-scoped credentials (instance profiles become storage credentials), jobs (compute access mode, libraries), init scripts (not supported on some UC compute), and three-part names in SQL. Plan each as workstreams.

docs.title: 3. Translating code: dialects
docs.text:
Machine translation gets you most of the way for SQL and none of the way for stored-procedure logic. I ran four sample queries through sqlglot.transpile(q, read=<dialect>, write="databricks"). The results below are real output, and most of the value is in what the tool got wrong or left alone.

Snowflake to Databricks

in:  SELECT IFF(a > 1,'x','y') f, TO_VARCHAR(ts,'YYYY-MM-DD') d, DATEADD(day,7,ts) w, t.v:name::string n
     FROM t, LATERAL FLATTEN(input => t.arr) x
     QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY k ORDER BY ts DESC) = 1
out: SELECT IF(a > 1,'x','y') AS f, TO_CHAR(ts,'YYYY-MM-DD') AS d, DATEADD(DAY,7,ts) AS w, CAST(t.v:name AS STRING) AS n
     FROM t, LATERAL EXPLODE(input => t.arr) AS x(SEQ, KEY, PATH, INDEX, VALUE, THIS)
     QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY k ORDER BY ts DESC NULLS FIRST) = 1

Good: IFF to IF, QUALIFY retained. Two things to catch: the tool added NULLS FIRST to the descending sort. That preserves Snowflake's semantics (NULLs sort as largest, so first when descending) where Databricks' default for DESC puts NULLs last (the default you saw in Level 1 · 03's window example). And LATERAL EXPLODE(input => ...) AS x(SEQ, KEY, ...) copies Snowflake's FLATTEN output columns onto a function that doesn't have them with a input => argument; I would not trust that line to run on Databricks and would rewrite it by hand as LATERAL VIEW explode(t.arr) or explode(t.arr). I did not run it.

PostgreSQL

in:  SELECT id, NOW() - INTERVAL '7 days' AS wk, data->>'name' AS n, string_agg(tag, ',') FROM events GROUP BY id, data->>'name' LIMIT 10
out: SELECT id, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP() - INTERVAL '7' DAYS AS wk, GET_JSON_OBJECT(data, '$.name') AS n, LISTAGG(tag, ',') FROM events GROUP BY id, GET_JSON_OBJECT(data, '$.name') LIMIT 10

Plausible, but ->> on a JSON string column becomes GET_JSON_OBJECT, which is a different function with its own semantics (and you might prefer a typed VARIANT or from_json), and LISTAGG's availability and ordering behaviour should be checked on your runtime (I did not verify it).

SQL Server (T-SQL)

in:  SELECT TOP 5 ISNULL(a,0) a, GETDATE() now, DATEDIFF(day,d1,d2) dd FROM dbo.t WITH (NOLOCK)
out: SELECT COALESCE(a,0) AS a, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP() AS now, DATEDIFF(DAY, CAST(d1 AS TIMESTAMP), CAST(d2 AS TIMESTAMP)) AS dd FROM dbo.t LIMIT 5

TOP became LIMIT, ISNULL became COALESCE. Notice that WITH (NOLOCK) silently disappeared: a dirty-read hint that has no equivalent, because Delta reads a consistent snapshot. That's usually fine, but it's a semantic change the tool made without telling you. LIMIT without an ORDER BY returns arbitrary rows in both systems.

Oracle

in:  SELECT NVL(a,0) a, SYSDATE, TO_CHAR(d,'YYYY-MM-DD') FROM t WHERE ROWNUM <= 5
out: SELECT COALESCE(a,0) AS a, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP(), TO_CHAR(d,'YYYY-MM-DD') FROM t WHERE ROWNUM <= 5

ROWNUM <= 5 was left unchanged, and Databricks has no ROWNUM: this would fail. Machine translation can emit SQL that looks fine and doesn't run. Never accept translated SQL without executing it, and compare results.

Other well-known sources of mismatch (general knowledge, not tested here): integer division and decimal precision rules, string comparison collation and trailing spaces, date/timestamp time zone handling (Databricks serverless defaults to UTC; Level 4 · 07), NULL ordering, implicit casts (ANSI mode errors), identifier case sensitivity, MERGE semantics, temp tables, and procedural code (PL/SQL, T-SQL procedures), which must be rewritten as notebooks, SQL scripting or Python.

docs.title: 4. Validation: how you know it worked
docs.text:
1. Row counts per table, per partition or day, source versus target.
  2. Aggregates: sums, min/max, null counts, distinct counts on key columns. Compare with tolerance for floating point, exactly for decimals.
  3. Row-level checksums on a sample (hash of the concatenated columns) or full-table hash by key range for critical tables.
  4. Query-result diffs for the top reports, run in parallel for a period ("shadow run").
  5. Performance and cost on realistic data (Level 4 · 06 and 07).
  6. Permissions audit: for each role, test with a user who should and should not have access (Level 3).
  7. Cutover plan with rollback: freeze writes, final sync, switch, keep the old system read-only for a fixed period.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: CONVERT TO DELTA is cheap because a Delta table is "Parquet files plus a log": the command lists the files, reads footers for the schema and statistics, and writes 00000000000000000000.json with an add action per file (Level 1 · 07). Shallow clone writes a log whose add actions point to the source's absolute file paths; deep clone additionally copies the files. SYNC creates or updates a metastore entry pointing at the same storage location, which is why it applies to external data and why it doesn't copy anything. Dialect translation is parse-tree rewriting: the input SQL becomes a tree, rewrite rules replace nodes the target spells differently (IFF to IF), and the tree is printed in the target dialect, which cannot add semantics the tree never represented (a NOLOCK hint or a ROWNUM pseudo-column), hence the failures above.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Converting a folder that other jobs still write to as plain Parquet.
  • Relying on a shallow clone as a backup.
  • Translating SQL and not executing it.
  • Migrating tables but not permissions, mounts and credentials.
  • Cutting over without a validation suite or a rollback path.
  • Treating hive_metastore as permanent because it still works.
  • Forgetting time zones and ANSI-mode differences when comparing numbers.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Reproduce the CONVERT TO DELTA and shallow-clone experiments. Then VACUUM the source with RETAIN 0 HOURS after an update and see whether the shallow clone still reads. Record what you observe.
  2. Run sqlglot.transpile on five queries from your own warehouse. For each output, classify it as correct, needs-edit or wrong, and explain how you decided (executing it counts).
  3. Write a validation script that compares row counts and per-column null counts and sums between two tables and prints a diff.
  4. Draft the cutover runbook for one pipeline: freeze, final sync, switch, verify, rollback, and the exact checks at each step.

docs.title: 10 · Capstone — An End-to-End Platform Plan
docs.text:
You have now met the whole stack: lakehouse and Delta, ingestion and pipelines, governance, orchestration, sharing and serving, delivery, ML, cost and maintenance. The capstone asks you to put it together on paper first, because most expensive platform mistakes are design mistakes. You'll write a platform plan as structured data, then run a checker that applies rules from every level to it.

What was run, and what wasn't

The plan checker is plain Python (PyYAML) and was run locally; its outputs below are copied from that run. It checks a design for consistency against the rules taught in this course; it does not touch Databricks, and a passing plan is not proof that a platform will work, be secure, or be cheap. The company ("acme-retail"), table names, SLAs and numbers are invented. The rules encode guidance from earlier lessons (several of which are themselves from the Databricks documentation, October 2026, and not run).

docs.title: The brief
docs.text: Acme Retail ingests order files from stores into a lakehouse, builds a cleaned orders and customers model, and publishes a daily revenue dashboard. Constraints: customer data is personal data (GDPR-style erasure requests); the analytics team must see revenue but not raw customer details; the platform team is three people; a production incident must be recoverable within a day.

docs.title: What a good plan answers
docs.text: Area Questions the plan must answer Lessons Data Which layers, tables and owners? Retention? Layout (clustering vs partitioning)? L1 · 06 to 09, L2 · 03, 04, 09 Pipelines Trigger, compute type, idempotence, retries, SLA, alerting? L2 · 07 to 10, L3 · 06, 07 Governance Catalog layout, groups, privileges, PII controls, erasure procedure? L3 · 01 to 05, L4 · 08 Serving Warehouse type/size, dashboards, sharing? L3 · 08, 09 Cost Tags, budgets, review cadence? L4 · 06 Delivery IaC, tests, CI/CD, deploy identity, rollback? L4 · 01, 02 Operations Maintenance, monitoring, disaster recovery? L4 · 07, 08

docs.title: The plan (as data)
docs.text:
plan.yml:

platform: acme-retail
environments: [dev, prod]
catalogs: {dev: {owner: platform-admins}, prod: {owner: platform-admins}}
tables:
  - {name: prod.bronze.orders_raw,  layer: bronze, owner: data-engineers, retention_days: 365, layout: "append-only, no clustering", pii: false, tests: [reconciliation]}
  - {name: prod.silver.orders,      layer: silver, owner: data-engineers, retention_days: 90,  layout: "liquid clustering by order_date, customer_id", pii: true, pii_control: abac_mask, tests: [unit, reconciliation, expectations]}
  - {name: prod.silver.customers,   layer: silver, owner: data-engineers, retention_days: 90,  layout: "liquid clustering by customer_id", pii: true, pii_control: abac_mask, erasure: "deletion vectors + REORG PURGE + VACUUM", tests: [unit]}
  - {name: prod.gold.daily_revenue, layer: gold,   owner: analytics-eng,  retention_days: 30,  layout: "liquid clustering by order_date", pii: false, tests: [reconciliation]}
pipelines:
  - {name: orders_ingest,  owner: data-engineers, trigger: "file arrival", compute: serverless, idempotent: true, retries: 2, sla_minutes: 30, alert: "pagerduty", reads: [landing volume], writes: [prod.bronze.orders_raw]}
  - {name: orders_silver,  owner: data-engineers, trigger: "after orders_ingest", compute: serverless, idempotent: true, retries: 1, sla_minutes: 45, alert: "slack", reads: [prod.bronze.orders_raw], writes: [prod.silver.orders, prod.silver.customers]}
  - {name: revenue_gold,   owner: analytics-eng,  trigger: "02:30 UTC daily", compute: serverless, idempotent: true, retries: 1, sla_minutes: 60, alert: "slack", reads: [prod.silver.orders], writes: [prod.gold.daily_revenue]}
serving: {dashboards: [revenue], warehouse: {type: serverless, size: Medium, max_clusters: 3, auto_stop_minutes: 10}}
cost: {tags_required: [team, env, cost_center], budget_alerts: [50, 80, 100], review: weekly}
governance: {groups_only: true, owners_are_groups: true, predictive_optimization: true, retention_set_before_po: true}
delivery: {iac: bundles, ci: [unit tests, bundle validate], deploy: "service principal from main", rollback: "redeploy previous tag; RESTORE affected tables"}

Some design reasoning behind it:

  • Serverless everywhere for jobs and the warehouse: a three-person team shouldn't manage clusters (Level 1 · 02, Level 3 · 09), and serverless's constraints (Level 4 · 07) don't hit this workload, as far as the plan author knows. Verify with a test run.
  • Bronze is append-only with 365 days of retention so silver and gold can be rebuilt after a bug (Level 2 · 09); silver keeps 90 days and gold 30, matching how far back anyone needs to time travel (Level 1 · 08). These retention numbers are illustrative.
  • Personal data lives in silver.orders and silver.customers; analysts read gold and masked silver via ABAC (Level 3 · 04); customers has an explicit erasure procedure (deletion vectors, then REORG ... PURGE, then VACUUM after retention: Level 4 · 08), and note that bronze also contains the personal data: a complete erasure design must say what happens there (the plan above leaves it unanswered, which is exactly the kind of gap review should find: see Exercise 2).
  • File arrival trigger for ingest (irregular store uploads: Level 3 · 07), chained downstream tasks, and a daily gold job.
  • Delivery through bundles with a service principal deploying from main (Level 4 · 01).

docs.title: The checker
docs.text:
"""Capstone plan checker: cross-cutting rules from Levels 1-4 applied to a platform plan. A design review aid, not a Databricks API."""
import sys, yaml
plan = yaml.safe_load(open(sys.argv[1])); problems = []
tables = {t["name"]: t for t in plan["tables"]}; pipes = plan["pipelines"]
for t in plan["tables"]:
    for k in ("owner", "layer", "retention_days", "layout", "tests"):
        if k not in t: problems.append(f"table {t['name']}: missing '{k}'")
    if t.get("pii") and not t.get("pii_control"): problems.append(f"table {t['name']}: contains PII but no pii_control (mask/ABAC/row filter)")
    if t.get("layer") == "bronze" and "append" not in t.get("layout", ""): problems.append(f"table {t['name']}: bronze should be append-only")
    if "partition" in t.get("layout", "").lower() and "liquid" not in t.get("layout", "").lower(): problems.append(f"table {t['name']}: prefer liquid clustering to partitioning for new tables (Level 2 · 03/04)")
    if t.get("layer") in ("silver", "gold") and not t.get("tests"): problems.append(f"table {t['name']}: no tests listed")
    if t.get("pii") and t["layer"] == "silver" and "erasure" not in t and t["name"].endswith("customers"): problems.append(f"table {t['name']}: personal data table has no erasure procedure")
written = {w for p in pipes for w in p["writes"]}
for name in tables:
    if name not in written: problems.append(f"table {name}: no pipeline writes it")
for p in pipes:
    if not p.get("idempotent"): problems.append(f"pipeline {p['name']}: not idempotent, so retries can duplicate data")
    if p.get("compute") in ("all-purpose", "all_purpose"): problems.append(f"pipeline {p['name']}: production job on all-purpose compute")
    if p.get("retries", 0) > 0 and not p.get("idempotent"): problems.append(f"pipeline {p['name']}: retries without idempotence")
    for k in ("owner", "sla_minutes", "alert"):
        if k not in p: problems.append(f"pipeline {p['name']}: missing '{k}'")
    for w in p["writes"]:
        if w.startswith("prod.") and plan["environments"] and "prod" not in plan["catalogs"]: problems.append(f"pipeline {p['name']}: writes to undefined catalog")
g = plan["governance"]
if not g.get("owners_are_groups"): problems.append("governance: owners must be groups")
if g.get("predictive_optimization") and not g.get("retention_set_before_po"): problems.append("governance: set VACUUM retention BEFORE enabling predictive optimization (Level 4 · 08)")
if len(plan["cost"].get("tags_required", [])) < 2: problems.append("cost: require at least team + env tags")
if "bundles" not in plan["delivery"].get("iac", "") and "terraform" not in plan["delivery"].get("iac", ""): problems.append("delivery: no infrastructure as code")
if not plan["delivery"].get("rollback"): problems.append("delivery: no rollback plan")
w = plan["serving"]["warehouse"]
if w.get("auto_stop_minutes", 999) > 45: problems.append("serving: auto stop above the documented classic default")
print(f"{len(plan['tables'])} tables, {len(pipes)} pipelines checked")
print("\n".join(problems) if problems else "OK: plan passes all checks")
sys.exit(1 if problems else 0)

On the plan above:

4 tables, 3 pipelines checked
OK: plan passes all checks

To see the rules bite, I made a copy of the plan with six deliberate defects (removed the PII control on silver.orders, switched the gold layout to partitioning, put ingest on all-purpose compute, made the gold pipeline non-idempotent while still retrying, turned off "retention set before predictive optimization", and emptied the rollback plan):

4 tables, 3 pipelines checked
table prod.silver.orders: contains PII but no pii_control (mask/ABAC/row filter)
table prod.gold.daily_revenue: prefer liquid clustering to partitioning for new tables (Level 2 · 03/04)
pipeline orders_ingest: production job on all-purpose compute
pipeline revenue_gold: not idempotent, so retries can duplicate data
pipeline revenue_gold: retries without idempotence
governance: set VACUUM retention BEFORE enabling predictive optimization (Level 4 · 08)
delivery: no rollback plan

Seven messages for six defects (the non-idempotent pipeline trips two rules). The checker is deliberately small; its value is that every message points back to a lesson, and that you can add a rule each time an incident teaches you one.

Notice what the checker does not catch in the passing plan: the bronze erasure gap above; whether the clustering columns match real query patterns; whether serverless limitations apply to your libraries; whether the SLAs are achievable; and whether the costs fit the budget. A checker enforces consistency; judgment about trade-offs stays with people.

docs.title: Your capstone
docs.text:
Produce, for a domain you know (or the Acme brief), the following. Each item should be short and specific.

  1. Plan file (like plan.yml) with at least four tables across three layers and three pipelines. Make it pass the checker, then extend the checker with two rules of your own.
  2. Data-flow diagram (boxes and arrows are fine): sources, ingestion, layers, serving, consumers, and where each governance control (mask, filter, grant) applies.
  3. Unity Catalog layout and grants: the spec for Level 3 · 10's generator, including groups and a service principal.
  4. Cost model: tags, expected workloads by compute type, budget thresholds, and the first three queries you'd run weekly (Level 4 · 06). Use real prices from the pricing pages, not guesses.
  5. Failure analysis: for each pipeline, what happens if it fails halfway, runs twice, or receives late data. How do you recover (retry, repair, RESTORE, replay from bronze)?
  6. Test plan: unit tests for transformations (Lesson 02), a reconciliation check per layer, one integration test on a staging target.
  7. Risks and unknowns: what you could not verify without a workspace (be as candid as this course tries to be).

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: A plan checker is a policy engine over a declarative model, the same pattern as the governance linter (Level 3 · 10) and the bundle linter (Lesson 01): represent decisions as data, express rules as functions over that data, run them in CI so a design review becomes a pull request with failing checks instead of a meeting. The leverage comes from the data model: because tables, pipelines and policies are all explicit records, a rule like "every PII table has a control" is five lines. The limit is also the data model: anything not represented (like bronze's personal data) is invisible to every rule.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Designing from tools instead of requirements (picking Photon, serverless or a feature before the SLA and the budget).
  • A plan with no failure analysis.
  • Forgetting that erasure applies to every layer and every copy, including bronze, backups and clones.
  • Treating the checker as the review.
  • A plan nobody updates: keep it in Git next to the bundle, and change it in the same pull request as the code.
  • Over-engineering for a three-person team: every extra layer, job and policy has a maintenance cost; delete what you can't justify.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Run check_plan.py on plan.yml, then on your own mutated copy. Add a rule that every pipeline writing PII tables must run as a service principal (add the field to the data model).
  2. Close the bronze erasure gap: write the procedure (what is deleted, where, in what order, how verified) and add a rule that flags any PII table feeding a bronze table without a documented erasure path.
  3. Estimate which Level 4 lesson's advice would change your plan if the team were 30 people instead of 3, and why.
  4. Present your plan to a colleague, ask them to find one thing the checker missed, and add that as a rule.

docs.title: Where to go next
docs.text: You now have a map of the platform and a habit of testing claims. The best next steps: get a Free Edition workspace and re-run the platform-only lessons that this course could only describe; deploy one small bundle with a pipeline and a job; connect a SQL warehouse dashboard to a gold table; and read the Databricks release notes monthly, since names, defaults and features keep changing, as the renames noted throughout this course (Delta Live Tables, Asset Bundles, Delta Sharing, Genie Spaces, Vector Search) show.
